en: The Second Sandarbha, the Bhagavat-sandarbha, within the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata-sandarbha titled Ṣaṭ-sandarbha.
May the illustrious Śrī Śrī Rādhā-Govinda be victorious!
May the holy Śrīla Rūpa and Sanātana be pleased;
this is now analyzed by the southern Bhaṭṭa. Om.
Having examined the original manuscript of that work— which was disordered, missing, and fragmentary—
and having rearranged it according to its sequence, Jīvaka writes it down. Now,
having thus characterized that reality (*tattva*) in general by way of the characteristic of non-dual gnosis (*advaya-jñāna*), once again—
He specifically defines that particular manifestation of His own being, revealed through the excellence of the qualifications of a lay devotee (upāsaka), with the latter half of this very verse:
"He is called Brahman, the Supreme Self (paramātman), and the Blessed Lord (bhagavān). [BhP 1.2.11]
Now, in this very scripture known as the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata, that single reality is expressed in three ways in various places:
in some instances it is called Brahman, in some Paramātman, and in others Bhagavān.

However, since it is explained by [the author] himself that "here, because of the distinction obtained through the meditative absorption (samādhi) of the illustrious Vyāsa, he is designated as the 'individual soul' (jīva)," those two [terms] are introduced first. In the root text, however, they are arranged in such a way to highlight their specific distinctions in sequence.

This is the meaning: when that single reality, whose nature is indivisible bliss, has attained identity with the multitude of blisses— beginning with the *thutkṛta* and *pārameṣṭhya* states— of the Paramahaṃsas through the power of their spiritual practice (*sādhana*).

Furthermore, when the mind is incapable of grasping the diversity of its own essential nature and powers, that which either flashes forth exactly as it has been generally characterized, or is presented as being just like that through the non-distinction between power (śakti) and the possessor of power (śaktimat), is designated by the term "Brahman."
Now, that single reality, by its own essential power (*svarūpa-bhūtā śakti*), assumes a certain particularity;

it is the foundational substratum for all other powers, and it is the object of experience for the supreme ascetics (*bhāgavata-paramahaṃsas*) whose bliss of Brahman is permeated by the internal abundance of the bliss of experiencing that [reality].

Likewise, that which manifests within and also without the senses— which have been permeated by *bhakti* consisting of a specific power of the bliss of His own essential nature (*svarūpa-ānanda*) that is the most effective means of realization through direct experience—

or that which is presented as such through the distinction between the power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), being clearly differentiated [from them], is designated by the word "Bhagavān."
Thus it was said by the venerable Jaḍabharata:
"Knowledge is pure, the singular ultimate reality, internal and not external— the true Brahman."
"That which the wise call Vāsudeva—the inward-facing, perfectly tranquil one designated by the word 'Bhagavat'";
thus [it is said]. And Śrī Manu also spoke regarding Śrī Dhruva:
"Then you [are established] in the inner Self, the Blessed One, O Infinite One, who consists solely of bliss and in whom all potencies are present.
Thus, "consisting solely of bliss" (ānanda-mātra) is the substantive (viśeṣya), and "all potencies" (samastāḥ śaktayaḥ) are the qualifiers (viśeṣaṇāni); [the Lord is] the qualified (viśiṣṭa).

The term "Bhagavān" has thus arrived [as the subject]. And so, when such specific qualities have been attained, this Bhagavān is of the nature of the indivisible reality (*akhaṇḍatattva*) by virtue of being a complete manifestation.
But since Brahman is manifest yet its specific forms are not revealed, it follows that its manifestation is incomplete; this, however,
shall be examined in detail further on.
The meaning of the word *bhagavat* is declared in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa* [6.5.66–69, 73–75, 79]:
"That which is unmanifest, undecaying, inconceivable, unborn, and imperishable..."
It is indescribable and formless, and not joined with hands, feet, or other such limbs.
The wise indeed behold that which is all-pervading, omnipresent, eternal, the source of all beings, and without cause; that which pervades all, yet is itself not pervaded.
That is Brahman, the supreme abode; that is to be meditated upon by those desiring liberation;
it is the subtle, supreme state of Viṣṇu, proclaimed by the words of the Vedas.
This very nature of the Supreme Self is what is expressed by the word "Bhagavat";
the term "Bhagavat" is the designator of that primordial Being whose essence is the Imperishable (akṣara).

Having said this and more—“O Sage, the letter *bha* possesses two meanings: it signifies the supporter (*sambhartṛ*) and likewise the sustainer (*bhartṛ*); the letter *ga*, moreover, signifies the leader (*netṛ*), the causer to go (*gamayitṛ*), and the creator (*sraṣṭṛ*).”
The term *bhaga* is defined as the designation for the six qualities: complete sovereignty, valor, fame, splendor, knowledge, and dispassion.
"Beings dwell there in that Self of beings, the Self of all;
and He dwells in all beings without exception—therefore, the Imperishable One is the meaning of the syllable *va*. Having said this:
"Knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor, in their entirety..."
Those denoted by the word "Bhagavat" are devoid of qualities and other such factors that are to be abandoned.
Thus, up to the end of [ViP 6.5.79],
here— as before— the state of being qualified by the qualifier and the qualified must be analyzed;
this applies to the qualifier as well.
The fact that [the Self] is not to be abandoned will become manifest.
"Formless" and "unjoined with hands, feet, and so forth"— this refers to the culmination in the manifestation of the pure substantive (viśeṣya) called Brahman.
However, [statements] such as "all-pervading" and "omnipresent" refer to a specific ultimate state;
alternatively, [statements] such as "formless" refer to the absence of ordinary form and so forth.
It is established as a negation;

therefore, it should be understood that by the phrase "devoid of the conjunction of hands, feet, and so forth," only the relationship of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is excluded, and not the relationship of inherence (*samavāya*).
"Vibhu" means endowed with all sovereignty;
"vyāpī" means all-pervasive.

"Unpervaded" means that which cannot be pervaded by anything else. This very nature of Brahman is denoted by the word "Bhagavat"; it is not merely indicated (lakṣya). He determines this very point: this word "Bhagavat" [is used] for that particular river.
It is indeed denotative, like the word "Ganges," and not indicative, like the word "bank";
such being the case, [it is] the true, imperishable...
Relying on the view of the *Nirukta* that "one should explain [words] based on their similarity," he states the meaning of words such as *bhaga* and so forth:
"The sustainer" (*sambhartṛ*) means the leader; that is, the one who causes [the devotee] to attain the fruit of devotion, which is love, and who leads them to his own world.

He is the bestower [of fruits], the creator, and the one who causes the various qualities to arise in His own devotees. It should be understood that His role as the nourisher of the world and so forth occurs only through a traditional succession (paramparā) and not directly.
Sovereignty (aiśvarya) is the power of subjugating all things.
The term "of the complete" applies to every [instance].
Vigor is the efficacy, like that of a jewel or a mantra.
Fame (*yaśas*) is the renown of the excellence of one's speech, mind, and body; prosperity (*śrī*) is success in every respect;
and knowledge (*jñāna*) is omniscience (*sarvajñatva*).
Detachment (*vairāgya*) is non-attachment to the objects of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*). *Iṅganā* means perception (*saṃjñā*).
According to the view that [the names] are identical in their syllables, one should say "Bhagavān" when it ought to be said.
The elision of the *matup* suffix is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) phenomenon.

In the case of "sambhartṛ" and so forth, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) refers precisely to the state of being a sustainer (*sambhartṛtva*) and the like; just as in the rule "a collection of words ending in nominal or verbal suffixes is a sentence," the expression "pacati bhavati" [is considered a sentence].
The meaning is that the "maturation" (*pāka*) of the sentence is intended; or just as in the case of *sattā* [where] in the expressions *asti* and *bhavati*, only the root-meaning itself is intended,
so too in the expression *bhagavān*, the sense of the possessive suffix *matup* is [intended].
It can be so applied.
By another method, he shows the six divisions: "knowledge and power" refers to the knowledge of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
Power is the capacity of the sense faculties;
sovereignty and heroism have been explained;
splendor is radiance.
"Without remainder" means "in their entirety.
Regarding the phrase "denoted by the word 'Bhagavat'": the meaning is that these are indeed qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the Blessed One, and not merely incidental characteristics (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Here, the word "Bhagavān" contains the possessive suffix *matup* in the sense of eternal connection (*nitya-yoga*).
Furthermore, that reality (*tattva*) is the manifestation of the complete form of such a Bhagavān, just as before, [consisting of] the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth.
That which manifests as the controller, or that which is being propounded [as such], is designated by the term "Supreme Self" (paramātman).

Although these words, beginning with "Brahmā," generally refer to one another's meanings, this has been stated here with the intention of emphasizing the specific conventional usage in each respective context. Thus spoke the son of Śrī. [2]
In this very way, he explains through a series of questions and answers. The King said:
"You ought to tell us of the final state of the Supreme Self, the Brahman designated as Nārāyaṇa; for you are the foremost among those who know Brahman. [BhP 11.3.35]

The venerable Pippalāyana said: That which is the cause of the maintenance, emergence, and dissolution of this world, yet is itself without cause; that which exists in the states of dreaming, waking, and deep sleep, and also externally.
"Know that, O Lord of Men, by which the body, senses, life-breath, and heart move when they are enlivened.
Herein lies the meaning of the question.

Of the Blessed One designated as Nārāyaṇa; for he is read as the third in that well-known group beginning with "Brahman" and "Supreme Self," and because this is made clear in the passage: "In Nārāyaṇa, who is called the Fourth (turīya) and designated by the word 'Bhagavat'. [He attained] finality.
The reality (*tattva*). He provides the answer in the sequence of questions with the word "sthitau" (*in the state of persistence*):
that which is the cause of persistence and so forth, yet is itself causeless;
and that which exists within the states of waking and so on, as well as externally.
And that by which the body and so forth are enlivened and move about—
that alone is the supreme reality, [to be understood] through the sequence of questions.
One should connect the text as follows: "Know [it] to have the form of Nārāyaṇa and so forth.
Nevertheless, for the sake of clarifying its erroneous nature, it is explained by way of inversion.

In this regard, the purport of the subsequent statement is that although [the Lord] is one, there is a distinction in His manifestation due to the difference in the qualifications [of the devotees] and because He is presented as being undifferentiated from them, as well as due to the differences in the experiences of the individual persons who worship Him.
This is what is meant:

although it is not itself a cause— being indifferent therein because it consists solely of the manifestation of its own essential power— it is nevertheless [the Supreme Self], which is synonymous with the *paramātman* in its state as the impeller of *prakṛti* and the individual soul (*jīva*).

Know that which, through the person characterized as His own portion (*svāṃśa*), becomes the cause of this [universe's] creation, maintenance, and so forth, to be the form of the Blessed Lord (*bhagavad-rūpa*).
And he says that the state of being the Supreme Self (*paramātmatā*) is established in this very way, by means of which cause—

Know that the Supreme Self is that by which alone the body and other such things— which have been enlivened through the entry of the individual soul (*jīva*), who is a portion of the Agent— are impelled; it is by His very direction that all principles (*tattvas*), beginning with *pradhāna*, move and engage in their respective functions.

Regarding the passage, "Obeisances to that Blessed One, the Brahman, the Supreme Self" (*tasmai namo bhagavate brahmaṇe paramātmane*), found in Varuṇa’s hymn of praise to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the commentary states: "To the Supreme Self means to the controller of all living beings. Because He is the Self (*ātman*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and is superior (*parama*) in relation to it, He is designated by the term "Supreme Self" (*paramātman*).
"It is that very [Self] which is manifested as its associate.
Thus, he says "In a dream," etc., meaning that in this way, only the state of being Brahman— undifferentiated from those [states]— is established.
That very reality which exists through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in dreams and so forth,
and which likewise exists externally within the pure power called the individual soul (*jīva*), and— by the force of the word "and" (*ca*)—
which also exists beyond that through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), being itself undifferentiated, is the nature of Brahman.
"Know this," said Śrī Nārada.
Regarding this very triad, he also speaks of it in the context of accomplishment with three [verses]:
"One should fix the mind on Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Three, whose form is Time;
he attains lordship, which is the field that impels the Knower of the Field."
A yogi who fixes his mind upon me as Nārāyaṇa— the one called the Fourth (turīya), designated by the word "Bhagavat"— shall attain mastery over my attributes.
"Fixing his clear mind upon me, the Brahman devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), he attains supreme bliss wherein all desire ceases.
And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "In the Lord of the three worlds, the controller of the *māyā* consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*)."
Therefore, in the internal ruler (antaryāmin) who is the form of the one who perceives time,
known as the Fourth (turīya);
Virāṭ, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Kāraṇa are the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the Lord; that state which is devoid of these three is known as the Fourth (turīya).
Thus, regarding these characteristics: "The sixfold collection consisting of complete sovereignty, valor, fame, splendor, knowledge, and dispassion is designated by the term *bhaga*. [ViP 6.5.74]
"In that which possesses [those qualities], denoted by the word 'Bhagavat'"; thus [ends] this [verse].
The Blessed Lord:
3. Now, the rebuttal to the first verse beginning with "atha vadanti" is set forth up to the third section.
In order to state that the specific manifestation [of the Lord] is characterized by the specific fitness [of the devotee],
he first describes that fitness regarding the manifestation of Brahman:
"Nevertheless, O Infinite One, of Your majesty whose quality is [immeasurable] greatness..."
It is worthy of being awakened by those with stainless inner selves,
because it is changeless, self-experienced, and formless;
for it is to be realized as the non-dual Self, and not otherwise.

Although it has been stated that [Your nature] is difficult to comprehend both in Your state as Brahman and in Your state as Bhagavān, nevertheless, O Infinite One (bhūman), You who are limitless in both essential form and attributes, You are devoid of qualities (aguṇa) in the sense that Your true form and inherent qualities have not been fully manifested.

That which is majesty, greatness, vastness—that is to say, Brahman-hood—for why is it called "Brahman"? Because of the Vedic scripture: "It expands (bṛṃhati) and it causes [all things] to expand (bṛṃhayati)."
That majesty of yours deserves to be understood by those with stainless inner selves— that is, by those whose internal organs (antahkarana) are pure through their qualities;
for it is revealed in their awakening.
The meaning is that he becomes capable;
from what cause?
To this he says: "From his own experience, because of the awakening to the purity of the object."
But surely, experience is indeed a modification (vṛtti) of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa),
and since that [modification] consists precisely of the transformations of the gross and subtle bodies, how could it take as its object the reality that is the state of being changeless?
To this he replies: "Because it is changeless" (*avikriyat*), that is, because it has abandoned those various modifications.

[Objection: Surely it is only experience (*anubhava*) assuming the form of an object that could grasp the object; however, the entity that is pure consciousness (*śuddhatva-padartha*) would not be an object for anyone, because its nature is inward-facing (*pratyag-rūpatvāt*).

Regarding this, he says: "Formless" (*arūpa*) means that which is not formed (*rūpyate*), that is, not cultivated (*bhāvyate*); [it refers to] the object (*viṣaya*). [The term refers to the state] devoid of the form of that [object], that is, in the absence of the form of the objects associated with the entry into the two bodies (*deha-dvaya-āveśa*).
The meaning is that when [the Self] exists, the referent of the term *svayam* (itself) shines forth as pure.
Now, one might ask: in the experience of the referent as the subtle nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), how can my own nature as Brahman—which consists of the form of full consciousness—manifest?

Regarding this, he says: [The Self is established] by virtue of its being the very nature of non-dual consciousness, by its equality in having the form of pure awareness (*cid-ākāratā*), and by its being the essential nature of that which is to be realized as the identity of the meanings of *tat* and *tvam*.
Although, after such an experience of the Self, there is no further power of the practitioner to effect a state of non-duality with that which is to be realized; [nevertheless, it is so established].

Nevertheless, the sense is that even that [knowledge] arises there solely by the power of the Śrī Bhagavān, who was propitiated through the practice of *sādhana-bhakti*— which was previously performed for that very purpose and is relied upon everywhere.
This was stated immediately after the verse beginning with "vadanti," etc.
The sages, placing their faith in that [teaching] and endowed with knowledge and dispassion,
perceive the Self within the self.
"By devotion acquired through hearing," as stated in the instruction of the Lord Matsya to Satyavrata:
"And my own majesty..."
"That which is designated as the Supreme Brahman, being favored by me through your inquiries, you shall know it revealed within your heart. [BhP 8.24.38] Thus it is said.
Brahmā [said this] to the Blessed Lord:
He described such a manifestation with these two and a half verses:
"Eternal, perfectly tranquil, fearless, consisting of pure awakening..."
The reality of the Supreme Self is pure, equal, and beyond both existence and non-existence;
therein no word exists that possesses multiple agents or has action as its meaning,
and Māyā flees in shame when she comes face to face with it.
That indeed is the station of the Supreme Person, the Blessed One,
which they know as Brahman— eternal bliss, free from sorrow.
This is the meaning.
That which they know as Brahman because of its being the greatest in every respect is indeed the supreme abode of this blessed Person (puruṣa),
since it is the first direct realization through the state of non-conceptuality (nirvikalpa).
And because the Blessed Brahman possesses the nature of non-conceptual existence (*nirvikalpa-sattā-rūpatva*),

the direct realization (*sākṣāt-kṛti*) of the Blessed One— who is distinguished by specific conceptualizations of diverse forms and so forth— arises immediately after that [realization of Brahman]. His...
The meaning is that Brahman, which constitutes its own essential nature, becomes the object of direct realization.
He states the defining characteristic of that non-conceptual Brahman as "mere self-awareness" (*pratibodha-mātra*) and as "eternal bliss" (*ajasra-sukha*).

The meaning is that whatever entity is perceived as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*) to insentience (*jaḍa*) and suffering (*duḥkha*), and whatever is eternal, is of a single form— that is, it has that very nature—
which is the reality of the self (*ātma-tattva*) common to all.
The self is the root.
The meaning is that the self is perceived in its various forms as being self-luminous by nature and as the object of supreme, unconditional love.

Now, he states the reason for the permanence of that nature of bliss: "eternal" (*śāśvata*), "quiescent" (*praśānta*), "everlasting" (*nitya*)—meaning always free from agitation—and likewise "fearless" (*abhaya*), meaning devoid of fear, and "sorrowless" (*viśoka*), meaning free from grief. Furthermore, lest one think that its being of the nature of bliss implies it is produced by merit (*puṇya*), he says: "wherein there is no sound. Wherein...
The meaning is that a word denoting an agent (*puru-kāraka*) does not function for the sake of ritual action (*kriyārtha*), such as sacrifice and the like.

Rather, in the manner of the passage beginning with "But you [should know] the person revealed by the Upaniṣads" (*tvaṃ tv aupaniṣadaṃ puruṣam*), the Upaniṣads alone are the illuminators; this is the sense.
Furthermore, by the words "pure" (*śuddham*) and so forth, [the text] excludes the state of being produced by the sense organs even when [pleasure] has the nature of happiness.
In that context, "pure" means free from defects (*doṣa*).
It is equal, devoid of high and low;
it is beyond existence and non-existence, and stands above the entire range of causes and effects.
Why say more? It is called *māyā*.
And when that [delusion] stands before the multitude of those liberated while living (jīvanmukta) with their faces turned toward them, it departs as if ashamed;
the meaning is that it retreats and goes far away from them.
Śrī Brahmā said to Nārada:
"When the reality of the Blessed Lord is manifested, Brahman itself is manifested;
therefore, the Brahma-saṃdarbha is also considered to be included herein as a subordinate part."
Now, he describes the fitness for the manifestation of the Blessed One: "When the mind was properly fixed and purified through the yoga of devotion, he beheld the perfect Puruṣa."
Thus [it is said in BhP 1.7.4].
This has already been explained.
[7] Thus, it was spoken by Brahmā:
O Lord, you indeed dwell within the lotus-heart of men purified by the yoga of devotion, becoming the object of their hearing and sight.
Thus [it is said]. Śrī Sūta spoke of that manifestation with ten and a half verses:
"To him, the Blessed One, having been honored, [showed] his own world..."
He revealed that which is supreme and beyond the supreme— a state free from affliction, delusion, and fear,
praised by those who have seen their own true nature. //9//
Wherein rajas and tamas proceed, and sattva is mixed with them, there is no influence of time;
where Māyā does not exist, how much less the others of Hari?
Wherein dwell those who follow the minor vows and are honored by gods and asuras. //10//
Dark-complexioned yet radiant, with eyes like hundred-petaled lotuses, clad in saffron garments, of excellent luster and beautiful form—
all possessed four arms and shimmering jewels.
Adorned with exquisite golden ornaments, they were radiant;
possessing the luster of coral, beryl, and lotus stalks, they wore shimmering earrings, crowns, and garlands. //11//
He who shines forth on all sides with the radiant rows of celestial palaces belonging to the great-souled ones,
resplendent with the splendor of the most excellent women and others.
Just as the sky [is filled] with rows of clouds accompanied by lightning. //12//
Where Śrī, personified, pays manifold honors with her various manifestations at the feet of the Wide-strider,
having taken her place upon the swing accompanied by those born of the flower-season.
Being praised, she sings of her beloved’s deeds. //13//
There he beheld the Lord of all the Sātvatas,
the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of sacrifice, and the Lord of the world,
accompanied by Sunanda, Nanda, Prabala, Arhaṇa, and others.
The Lord was attended by the foremost of his own retinue. //14//
[He saw] the one with four arms, wearing a crown and earrings, whose face has eyes reddened by a serene smile, and whose nectar-like gaze is turned toward favoring his servants.
A yellow garment upon his chest, marked by the Goddess Śrī. //15//
He is seated upon a supreme, most worthy throne, surrounded by the four, sixteen, and five Śaktis,
endowed with His own inherent powers as well as other transient ones.
The Lord, rejoicing in his own abode. //16//
With his inner self overflowing with the joy of seeing Him, his body bristling with thrill, and his eyes filled with tears from the weight of divine love,
the Creator of the universe bowed down at His lotus feet.
That which is attained by way of the path of the paramahaṃsas. //17//
To that wise one who had approached him with joy,
worthy of his own command for the creation of progeny,
he spoke with words radiant with a gentle smile.
The beloved one, his mind delighted, touched the beloved one on the hand. //18 [BhP 2.9.9-18] //

To that Brahmā, who was worshipping by means of austerities performed solely for the sake of pleasing Him while stationed within the lotus-navel of the Person named Śrī Nārāyaṇa in accordance with the Lord’s command, the Blessed One— being honored and having been won over by that worship—
revealed His own world, Vaikuṇṭha, the best of all worlds.
He showed it correctly:
that from which there is no other Vaikuṇṭha higher or more excellent than this, because it is the supreme Vaikuṇṭha of the Blessed Lord.

Alternatively, the meaning is that whatever reality called Para-Brahman exists from Vaikuṇṭha is not different from the Supreme; by the manifestation of its specific essential power (svarūpa-śakti), it is unobscured by Māyā, and thus it is of that very form. However, later on...
This will be clarified:
the reason for such a state is that [the mind] is "freed" (vyapeta) and by its own nature (svadṛṣṭitaḥ).
Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the clinging to life are the five afflictions; through these delusions, there is diversity.
In that state where fear and agitation, as well as afflictions and the like,
have departed, even those who know the Self— those for whom the vision of their own [true nature] has been realized— have praised and extolled it from every side, in its entirety.
Then those sages, having seen Vaikuṇṭha— the vessel that brings joy to the eyes— and his abode, Vikuṇṭha, which is self-effulgent, [were filled with wonder].
Having circumambulated the Blessed One, prostrated before him, and taken leave of him,
they returned filled with joy, praising the Vaiṣṇava glory;
thus he again manifests that very same state.
"It proceeds" means that in Vaikuṇṭha, neither *rajas* nor *tamas* proceed.
That *sattva* which is a mixture of those two, their companion, and inert—that too is not it;

rather, it is something entirely different. And that is the *sattva* called "pure," whose nature is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), which exists as a function (*vṛtti*) of that power of the Lord's own essence (*svarūpa-śakti*) which is distinct from *māyā* and will be properly established hereafter.
It will be established in that very context;
the meaning is that it functions precisely where that [context] occurs.
And so, in the *Jitanta-stotra* within the *Nārada-pañcarātra*:
The world named Vaikuṇṭha,
endowed with the six divine qualities,
which is unattainable for those who are not Vaiṣṇavas.
It is devoid of the three qualities.
In the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa*, however, during the description of Vaikuṇṭha, the non-material nature (*aprākṛtatva*) of that reality is clearly demonstrated;
for, immediately after the description of the manifestations of *prakṛti*— [the text continues].
Thus has been described the supreme form of my manifestation in its ordinary aspect;
now listen, O daughter of the Mountain, to the form of my three-quarter manifestation.
Between Pradhāna and the supreme ether flows the auspicious Virajā river, flowing with waters produced from the perspiration of the Vedāṅgas.
Beyond that, in the supreme ether, is the eternal, immortal, perpetual, constant, infinite, and supreme state, which consists of three quarters.
"The divine, imperishable state of Brahman, consisting of pure being," and so forth.
The mutual non-deviation of the primal qualities (*prakṛti-guṇa*) has been stated in the *Sāṅkhya-kaumudī*: "They function as mutual pairs.
And in its commentary: "They are companions of one another, being inseparable (*avinābhāva*)."
That is to say, they are abiding [in that state].
And there is a scriptural authority on this point:
"All are mutually paired."
All go everywhere;
Sattva is the mate of Rajas.
Having begun with these words, [the text continues]:
"Neither their beginning, nor their conjunction, nor their disjunction is perceived. Thus [it is said].
Therefore, in this context, because of the absence of *rajas*, its non-creativity is shown; because of the absence of *tamas*, its indestructibility is shown;
and because of the absence of *sattva* pertaining to *prakṛti*, its nature as being, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*) is demonstrated. The reason for this is as follows:
And there is no "temporal progression" (kāla-vikrama);
for it is by means of temporal progression that sattva and the other guṇas are differentiated through the agitation of primordial matter (prakṛti).

Therefore, the meaning is that where this very progression of time— which is the cause of the six modifications of existence— does not operate, the absence of those [modifications] is all the more certain.
Furthermore, regarding their root...

Thus he says, "it is indeed an axe," meaning that where there is no *māyā*. Here, *māyā* refers to the power (*śakti*) of the Blessed One which is the cause of the creation of the world and so forth, and not merely deceit.
Because that [other-worldly being] is excluded precisely by the negation of kings and so forth;
or alternatively, because even that ordinary existence which constitutes the existence of those two relatives does not occur there.
The "mixed" [state] is the *pradhāna* whose three qualities (*guṇas*) have not yet become separate. First, the distinction between *māyā* and *pradhāna* must be discerned.
[The author] confirms the very point already stated by means of a *kaimutya* (argument from the obvious).
As for the phrase "how much more so others," the explanation that "for those two there is some mixed *sattva*—
that is, mixed with *rajas* and *tamas*— but not [pure] *sattva*" is merely grinding what has already been ground. In general...
For that [sattva] is understood precisely through the negation of rajas and tamas;
and its distinctness from the material (prākṛta) sattva will be explained by Mārkaṇḍeya to the Ṛṣi Śrī Nārāyaṇa in the twelfth [chapter].
O Lord, sattva, rajas, and tamas are the bonds of Your own self, the causes of this world’s maintenance, dissolution, and emergence; yet even though they consist of māyā,
You assume the form of sattva for the sake of peace.
Nor do others [possess] the calamities, delusions, and fears of men, from which [the former two are free].
Therefore, O Blessed One, here in this world, those who are skilled worship Your own beloved white form, which belongs to You;
for the Sātvatas desire that sattva which is the very form of the Supreme Person.
"Since there is no fear from the world, nor any other source of happiness for the self," so it is said.
The meaning of these two [verses] is as follows:
O Lord, although the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas are indeed Your own pastimes produced by Māyā—
pastimes which serve as the causes for the maintenance and so forth of this universe— nevertheless, that which consists of sattva is precisely [that].
It leads to tranquility and supreme happiness;
the other two, consisting of passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas), do not. It is not merely that these two lack tranquility.

But [the Lord] says that it is undesirable as well, using the word "vyasana": "O Blessed One, therefore the wise— those who are skillful and proficient— worship and serve Your pure body consisting of *sattva*, which is the substratum of Your pastimes in the form of Śrī Viṣṇu, and not Your other forms such as Brahmā or Rudra."
They worship and follow [him], but not one in the form of Dakṣabhairava and the like;
in what manner? His own.
Because you also bring peace to the world, she is dear to you as well.
Is it not well known that even my form consists of sentient beings?
If so, how is it that [she is dear] to him as well?
"It is indeed composed of *māyā*;

it is not so, it is not so," say the Sātvatas, the followers of the Śrī-Bhāgavata. For they maintain that the *sattva* which is Your form, O Puruṣa, is what they desire as illumination, and from which *sattva* the world [arises].

That which is called Vaikuṇṭha shines forth as fearless, consisting of the bliss of the Self, and having the nature of the supreme Brahman-bliss; it is described as a particular function of the power of its own essential nature. This is pure *sattva*, denoted by the term Vasudeva.
"In that place, the person moves about unobstructed" (BhP 4.3.23)—
according to such passages which will be cited later—
the reason for being beyond the range of perception is the quality of *prakṛti*.

It is called *sattva* both because it conforms to the established definition of *sattva* as characterized by purity, and because it attains the designation *sattva* as a specific modification of the power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*) that has become such.

And therefore, because it exists as the function of its own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*), it is said to be of the very nature of its own essence; thus it is described as "that fearless bliss which is the Self" (*ātma-sukha*).
This is the case when there is no other object.

In passages such as *bhagavad-vigrahaṃ pratirūpam yad etat* (BhP 2.8.2), there would be a contradiction of the proposition that [the Lord's form] consists solely of the nature of pure goodness (*śuddha-sattva*). Furthermore, in passages such as *abhayam*, there would be a loss of the state of being free from fear (*prāñjalatā*).
It occurs that, when there is a double repetition of the phrase "and *rajas* and *tamas*," there arises a burden of comprehension for only one word;
for even previously, [the two] were already referred to by the dual number in the expression "nor others."

Therefore, there exists an existence (*sattva*) that is one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-bhūta*), distinct from that which is well-known [as the material *sattva*]. This is the opinion of the author of the *Ṭīkā* regarding the passage beginning with "In the eleventh [canto], this body, which is the arrangement of the three worlds... and "knowledge is intrinsic" (*jñānaṃ svataḥ*), concerning that body which [arises] from that existence which constitutes one's essential nature.

By the phrase "the knowledge of those who are supported," and likewise by the passage in the *Śrī-Bharata-Jāpya*, "The Supreme, beyond the *rajas* of the sun-god Jātavedas, the splendor (*bhargas*) of the Divine" (BhP 5.7.14), his doctrine is that "the Supreme" is beyond *rajas*, which is to say, beyond *prakṛti*.
By the words "supremely consisting of pure *sattva*" and so forth;
for this very reason, it is heard in scripture that the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest belong only to the individual soul (*jīva*) and not to the Lord (*īśa*).
Then, in the eleventh [chapter], it is said: "The qualities of goodness, passion, and ignorance belong to the individual soul (jīva), not to Me.
And in the Śrī-Bhagavad-Upaniṣad:
Whatever states of being there are—whether characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa)—know them to proceed from Me alone; yet I am not in them, but they are in Me.
Deluded by these three states consisting of the qualities (guṇas), this entire world does not recognize Me, who am beyond them and imperishable.
"For this divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the gunas, is difficult to overcome;
but those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion" (Gītā 7.14).
As it is said in the tenth [chapter]:
For Hari is indeed directly devoid of qualities, the Supreme Person beyond material nature;
he is the all-seeing witness.
"By worshipping Him, one becomes free from the modes.
And in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"The qualities such as goodness (sattva) and the rest do not exist in the Lord."
And where the material qualities (guṇas) do not exist—
may that primordial Person, who is pure among all pure things, be gracious. Thus [ViP 1.9.44].
In this context, by specifying "ordinary" (prākṛta), it is implied in that very same place that other qualities, which are extraordinary (aprākṛta), certainly exist within Him:
namely, *hlādinī*, *sandhinī*, and *saṃvit*.
"In You, the sole refuge of all, there is a single [nature] that produces both joy and pain; but in You, who are devoid of qualities, there is no mixture of these. (ViP 1.12.69)
And so it was said by Devendra in the tenth [chapter]: "Your abode is pure essence, peaceful, composed of austerity, and with rajas and tamas destroyed."
"This flow of the qualities is composed of illusion;
there is no prior connection for You," thus [it is said in BhP 10.27.4].
This is the meaning.
Dhāma is the power of light that constitutes its very nature;
its purity is expressed by the two qualifying attributes.
And [it is described as] "consisting of austerity (tapas), with rajas and tamas destroyed";
here, "austerity" means knowledge, according to the Vedic scripture: "He performed that austerity."
The meaning is that he consists of austerity and has the nature of abundant knowledge, being devoid even of a trace of dullness.
Just as it is said that "the self consists of knowledge and is pure," by this [statement],
material existence (*prākṛta-sattva*) is also excluded.
For this very reason, this flow of qualities such as *sattva* and the rest does not exist for you, who consist of *māyā*; because that [flow] is a bond caused solely by ignorance.
For this same reason, Brahmā and the others addressed the Blessed Lord with these reasoned arguments:
You resort to pure sattva for the stability of embodied beings; Your form is the means to attain the highest good through Vedic rites, yoga, austerity, and meditative concentration.
By which people strive for your worthy worship.
O Creator, if this sentience were not your own innate nature, which wipes away the distinction between knowledge and ignorance,
you would be inferred only through the manifestations of the *guṇas*.
And that by which, or through which, something is manifested—
this is the meaning:
because it is manifested by *sattva*, the body is delineated as non-different from it.

You resort to and manifest the *sattva* element; how is it? It is pure (*viśuddha*). Even though other [elements] are unmixed with *rajas* and *tamas*, they are not [pure] because, being material (*prākṛta*), they are permeated by a portion of inertia (*jāḍya*).
It is especially pure;
the meaning is that this [state] is exceedingly pure because, by virtue of its nature as the power of its own essence (svarūpa-śakti), it does not even touch a portion of that [impurity].
For what purpose do I take refuge?
It is for the sake of steadying the mind upon my own lotus-feet for the stability of embodied beings, and because of the very bliss of devotion to You which exists everywhere.
The meaning is that it is the primary purpose;
this is evident from Śrī Kuntī’s words in BhP 1.8.19: "for the sake of prescribing the yoga of devotion."
Of what nature is that body? It is the means of attainment and the locus of all the highest human goals (*puruṣārtha*);
the meaning is that its form consists of eternal bliss and supreme bliss.
Therefore, [there is] no difference between that body and you.
The meaning is that this description is merely figurative (aupacārika).
For this very reason, by whatever form one person takes as an object, another person performs worship (arhaṇa) and honor toward that form.
The meaning is: by what means—namely, the Vedas and so forth that have you as their object;
for those [means] common to others are indeed offered only for your worship.
Even if [the body] were established through effort,
it would not be required,
because such a body is the cause for the manifestation [of the self].
They clarify that [the world] has the nature of one's own essence:
"O Creator, if this being— which is your innate consciousness— consists of experience, then its meaning is that it is the power of self-luminosity."
That would not be so;
rather, for you, whose self-luminous nature is free from the distinction of ignorance, the very mode of your experience has attained purification— that is, cleansing.
The meaning is that she alone is what remains in the world, and not even a trace of you exists;
[the opponent objects: "Let this be due to the quality of *sattva* belonging to material nature (*prākṛta*), so what is the use of your own? To this he says:

The meaning is that you are merely inferred through the manifestation of your natural qualities, but you are not directly perceived. Alternatively, if that which is your own essence— the nature of your consciousness and the cleansing away of the division of ignorance— [is realized];

The meaning is this: You do not come into being, nor do You manifest; rather, You are inferred at that time by the manifestations of the qualities of material nature (prakṛti), such as goodness (sattva) and the rest, whereas You are indeed directly perceived through the manifestation of Your own innate existence (nija-sattā).
To clarify that very point, they state that there are two types of inference in this regard: "that of which the quality manifests."

The meaning is that even a quality such as existence (*sattva*), which does not constitute the very nature [of the self], serves as an inferential mark (*liṅga*) for you either merely by virtue of having an invariable connection with you, or merely by virtue of being manifested by you alone. For example, the dawn of the red sun (*aruṇodaya*) is an inferential mark for the proximity of the rising of the sun, or as smoke is for fire.

The sense is that, since it possesses the nature of a mark (*liṅga*), it is logical that in either case there is an absence of its being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for your direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*).
Thus, in this way, [it is established] that for one whose being is non-material (*aprākṛta-sattva*), [the object] consists in the form of its own self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*). By which...
It has been established that the direct realization of You, who are self-luminous,

occurs [in this way]. In this regard, those who consider that which is called *viśuddha-sattva* (pure goodness) to be merely material (*prākṛta*), devoid of *rajas* and *tamas*, and [consequently view] its effect as the Lord—
However, they [the dualists] imagine [the self] to possess conflict and so forth; yet it is not favored by anything at all.

Because it is by nature inherently tranquil due to the absence of connection with *rajas*, and because its form is characterized by indifference toward everything, agitation is impossible for it. Since it consists of pure knowledge (*vidyāmaya*), it merely illumines things as they truly exist.
Because it is the nature of phenomena (dharmatva), and because it is unfit for other conceptual constructions;
as it has been said: "even though it is stated, [it remains] beyond the range [of thought]."
The cause for being within the range of perception is the quality of *sattva*, which is the nature [of the object].
When the range of perception possesses many forms, it is *rajas*;
when those many forms are concealed, it is *rajas*.
Likewise, when they are mutually indifferent, it is *sattva*;
when there is assistance, it is *rajas*; and when there is injury, it is *tamas*.
[The attributes] such as being an object of experience, [and] maintenance, creation, and destruction; and [the attributes] such as indifference, and so forth.
Now, if even a trace of *rajas* were to be admitted therein, the term "pure" (*viśuddha*) would be rendered meaningless; therefore, enough of that view.
Regarding the phrase "by the striking of the jar of passion," in the Vaikuṇṭha-nirūpaṇa section of the Pādmottara-khaṇḍa,
the non-material (aprākṛta) nature of that *sattva* is clearly demonstrated.
As it has been said after the description of the manifestations of Prakṛti:
"Thus, for her whose form is composed of Prakṛti, this is the supreme form of manifestation."
But hear now, O daughter of the mountain, of the form of the three-quartered manifestation.
Between Pradhāna and the supreme ether flows the auspicious Virajā river,
which is made to flow by the waters produced from the perspiration of the Vedāṅgas.
Beyond that, in the supreme ether, is the eternal,
immortal, perpetual, constant, infinite, and supreme state consisting of three-quarters.
"The divine, imperishable state of Brahman consists of pure sattva," and so forth.
This incidental analysis of pure sattva is now concluded; next, the main subject proceeds.

Thus, the verse under discussion is being explained. Now, one might object: "Since qualities and so forth are absent, this world is indeed devoid of distinctions. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] illuminates that the distinction therein is merely a manifestation (*vilāsa*) of that very power—which consists of pure *sattva*—which is not distinct from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
He shows that very distinction with the words "of Hari":
the gods (surāḥ) arise from *sattva*, while the asuras arise from *rajas* and *tamas*; [the Lord] is worshipped by them.
The meaning is that they are the most worthy of offerings among them;
the intention is that this is precisely because they have transcended all qualities (guṇa).
He describes them as follows: "dark-complexioned yet radiant.
They are both dark-complexioned and radiant, brilliant;
they wear yellow garments, are well-adorned, and exceedingly delicate, shining like the finest jewels as if opening their eyes.
Those who possess necklaces (*niṣka*) and ornaments (*padaka*) set with the finest jewels are radiant and glorious;
among them are some others who have attained a form similar to that of the Blessed Lord (*śrī-bhagavat*), such as those known as *pravāla*.
They possess colors similar to coral and other such gems. Furthermore, he describes the world with the word "bhrājiṣṇubhiḥ" (shining).

"Śrīr yatra" means that Śrī—the internal potency (*svarūpa-śakti*)—is present there in her embodied form as the beloved of Him; she bestows honor (*mānam*), that is, worship, through her opulences (*vibhūtibhiḥ*).
Taking on a physical form as her beloved, she received honor and worship through her own attendants who took the forms of her friends;
resorting to playful grace, she engaged in swinging on a swing, while Spring, appearing in the form of flowers, followed after her.
While being sung to in various ways by those bees,
she herself began to sing of the deeds of her beloved Hari;
"she saw"— this is the predicate for the relative pronouns (*yat*) occurring previously in the verse, namely *akhila-loka*.

He is the Lord of all the Sātvatas, the Sātvata Yādava heroes; the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of Sacrifice, the Lord of Creatures, the Lord of Intellects, the Lord of the Worlds, and the Lord of the Earth.
May the Lord, the protector of the Andhakas, Vṛṣṇis, and Sātvatas, and the master of the virtuous, be gracious to me.
This is because it is corroborated by this statement [BhP 2.4.20],
and because, according to the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatamata, it will be established that Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone is the Svayaṃ Bhagavān.
And this very Bhāgavata, consisting of four verses, was taught by the Blessed Lord to Brahmā immediately thereafter; and therein it is said:
"In the past, it was spoken by me to the Unborn One from my navel."
Seated upon a lotus at the beginning of creation,
that supreme knowledge which illumines my own majesty is what the wise call Bhāgavata.
Thus, according to the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa addressed to Uddhava in the third [chapter], [BhP 3.4.13].
To Him who in the beginning created Brahmā and who indeed bestowed the Vedas upon him— to that God, the light of self-knowledge, [I offer my salutations].
"One desiring liberation should indeed go for refuge to Him"— thus,
according to the *Śrī-Gopāla-tāpanī*, it is heard that He is the instructor of that [liberation].

Regarding this, he said: "While I was performing the *brahmasavana* sacrifice, [the Lord] was meditated upon and praised; at the end of a *parārdha*, He awakened, and a Person dressed as a cowherd appeared before me. According to the *Śrīgopālatāpanī Upaniṣad*, in a certain *kalpa*, at the beginning of creation, it was indeed in this very manner that He appeared in the form of Śrī Gopāla.

Furthermore, because it will be established in the *Śrī Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha* that the Lord’s own form was revealed to Brahmā and that His abode is Mahāvaikuṇṭha, one should understand that at the time of His manifestation in Dvārakā, Śrī Prabalā and others were also present, as indicated by their association with Sunanda, Nanda, and the rest who were heard [there].
As it was said in the first [canto]:
"Sunanda, Nanda, Śīrṣaṇya, and those others who are the bulls among the Sātvatas" (BhP 1.14.32); and [it was said]:
"By the grace of the servant" (2.9.15).
One whose very glance intoxicates the beholders like wine;
[he who possesses] on the left side of his chest a mark of golden lines, signifying that he is worthy of the highest honor— these are the four [verses].
The powers (śaktayaḥ) are dharma and the rest;
these alone are described in the Yoga-pīṭha of the Pādmottara-khaṇḍa, and not the external factors such as adharma and the rest. For it is thus:
With the feet consisting of knowledge of Dharma, sovereignty, dispassion, and so forth,
[he is] the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva [Vedas].
"Constantly enveloped by forms in succession"—thus [it is said].
The use of the word "samasta" (all) at the end is an archaic (ārṣa) usage.
And the sixteen powers are Caṇḍā and the others.
And likewise, in that very same [text]: "It is well-guarded by the gatekeepers Caṇḍa and the others, such as Kumuda.
The word "city" (nagarī) connects with what precedes. And they are:
Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa at the eastern gate; Bhadra and Subhadra at the southern [gate].
Jaya and Vijaya are in the west, and Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ are in the north.
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita.
"These are declared to be the lords of the directions here in this most beautiful city.
The remainder [of the meaning] is that Kumuda and the others are the lords of the directions starting from the southeast (āgneyī), two by two.
The five powers (pañca-śaktayaḥ) [are as follows].

Kūrma and the others; and likewise in that very same [text]: "Kūrma, the Nāga king, Vanateya, Trayīśvara, the Vedic meters, and all mantras have assumed the form of the sacred seats (pīṭhas). Thus it is said.
"Trayīśvara" is an epithet of Vainateya (Garuḍa),
because he consists of the Vedas (*chandomaya*).
Although the statement in the Uttara-khaṇḍa refers to the Supreme Void (*paramavyoman*), nevertheless, that—
Furthermore, based on similarity, scriptural authority, and established tradition, the Yoga-pīṭha of Śrī Kṛṣṇa should also be understood in the same way.

Here, the sixteen Śaktis are to be understood as Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, according to the statement from the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa that will be cited earlier in the *Śrī Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha*, or else they are to be understood as Śrutālambinī and the others.
Thus, [the Lord] is endowed with His own essential attributes, such as sovereignty and the rest;
whereas in other cases— namely, among yogis— the meaning is that these are attained through qualities that are impermanent.
He is the Lord (Īśvara) because He delights in His own abodes within the glorious Vaikuṇṭha;
for this very reason, He is not established as dependent on anything else.
Regarding the phrase "tad-darśana" (seeing that):
the statement "that lotus-foot which is reached by the path of the paramahaṃsas" reveals its nature as a mass of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānandaghana*).
The Blessed One spoke thus to that Brahmā, who was feeling affectionate toward him,
regarding the task of creating progeny through his own partial incarnation as a Puruṣa.
Worship is appropriate toward the Teaching (śāsana).

Now, one might object: "Let that person alone bestow grace; however, because the Blessed Lord (Śrī-Bhagavat) exists in a transcendent state (parāvastha), even a connection with Him—the creator of the material world—is no connection at all. Anticipating this doubt, [the author speaks] of His devotee...
He says that this is indeed an excess of affection: "dear" means one who possesses love for Him;
for He too is dear, being under the sway of love.
In that context as well, the qualifiers "being delighted" (*prīyamāṇām*) and "with a joyful mind" (*prītamanāḥ*) indicate at that time an extraordinary intensity of the outpouring of love toward Him,
who bears the marks of the Blessed One.
By means of his gaze, he manifests an exceeding delight even for him there, [as indicated] by the words "with the luster of a slight smile" and "touching the hand with speech.
His status as a worshiper of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is established by the statement of the Śrī Gopāla-tāpanī Upaniṣad.
This has been shown.
And so it is stated in the *Brahma-saṃhitā* (5.22–5):
"There, Brahmā came into being once more, four-faced and master of the four Vedas."
Having been born, he was indeed impelled at that very moment by the power of the Blessed One.
Desiring to create, he formed a thought refined by his prior latent impressions;
he beheld only darkness everywhere and nothing else at all.
Then a divine voice spoke before him, saying to Kṛṣṇa, Govinda: "The people of the cowherds are in love with you."
"This beloved of Vahni shall grant you what is dear;
perform penance with him, and through this, your success will be achieved."
Then he performed austerities for a very long time, pleasing the imperishable Govinda; and so forth.
Śrī Śuka said: //8// [9] Now,
in order to establish once again in particular this point— that the Blessed One is not something superimposed, but is indeed His very own essential nature— another section is commenced.
In that regard,
he states the capacity of that object by means of the two qualifiers of the phrase: "the object here is a real thing to be known."
"Bestowing auspiciousness and uprooting the threefold suffering" (BhP 1.1.2):
"Auspiciousness" (*śiva*) is supreme bliss; its "bestowing" occurs through His own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*).
The "threefold suffering" is the power of *māyā*.
And the eradication of that [bondage] must be accomplished by her alone—thus says Śrī Vyāsa.

(9) [10] Furthermore, those two—the power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*) and the essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*)—are mutually opposed; likewise, their respective functions (*vṛtti*), though many, are mutually opposed within their own respective groups.
Nevertheless, he says that their single treasure is indeed that very one:
"The powers of which belong to the disputing speakers."
They become the ground for dispute and agreement, and they repeatedly cause self-delusion for these beings;
homage to that Infinite One of boundless qualities! [BhP 6.4.26]
Clear. Dakṣa [worships] Śrī Puruṣottama. 10.
[11] Likewise:
"In whom the contradictory courses of fate fall incessantly..."

I take refuge in that Brahman— the source of the universe, the one, infinite, primordial, consisting of pure bliss, and immutable— [from whom] knowledge and other various powers arise in succession. [BhP 4.9.16]

Various powers, existing in their respective classes according to the sequence of superior, middling, and inferior, and though generally following mutually contradictory courses, constantly fall upon that [substratum] which they depend on and perform their respective functions.

Dhruva [worships] Śrī-Pṛśnigarbha. (11) [12] He who, at the beginning of creation and thereafter, sustains this world by means of His powers consisting of substance, action, agency, and consciousness;
Salutation to that Supreme Person, the Creator, whose powers are both fully expanded and restrained;
he "anuruṇaddhi" means he brings about [creation].
Śrī Maitreya said to Vidura:
[12] He speaks of their inconceivability: "The Lord of the Self possesses thousands of powers beyond the reach of logic" (BhP 3.33.3).

This is clear. Furthermore, the inconceivability [of the Lord] was stated at the beginning [in the Sūtra]: "But because the Veda is the source, [the Lord's power is] inconceivable" (Vs 2.1.27), and also in the passage beginning with "And thus in the Self, for there are various... (Vs 2.1.28).
Śrī Devahūti [spoke to] Kapiladeva.
[14] He states that power (*śakti*) is his inherent nature: "In the beginning, there was one [reality] consisting of the threefold [qualities]: sattva, rajas, and tamas."
The Sūtra declares, "I am the Great One," referring to the individual soul (jīva).
Yet it is Brahman alone that shines forth through its vast power in the form of knowledge, action, object, and fruit— that which is both being and non-being, and which transcends both.
Brahman alone, possessing vast power, appears as the possessor of manifold powers;
by the use of the particle *eva*, it is indicated that this power belongs to Brahman alone and is not imagined, thereby making known the inherent nature of that power.
In this regard, the cause is as follows:

that which is Brahman; that which is the gross effect in the form of earth and so forth, being unreal; and that which is the subtle cause in the form of *prakṛti* and so forth—of these two, whose majesty is external, there is the supreme majesty of essential nature, which is Śrī.
The external majesty consists of forms such as Vaikuṇṭha and so forth, as well as the nature of the pure individual soul;
otherwise, those respective states would not be established.
In what form does it possess those various forms?
To this he replies: in the form of knowledge, action, object, and fruit; that is, by way of being the nature of the power of knowledge characterized by the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest.
In the form of the power of activity characterized by the Sūtras and so forth;
in the form of the objects characterized by the Tanmātras and so forth;
and in the form of the unity of all those things characterized as Prakṛti.
In its nature as form, it has the character of both being and non-being;
in its nature as the fruit, it is the supreme state of those two.
Therein lies the fruit.
The reality of consciousness known as the Blessed Lord, which consists of the nature of the goals of human life along with His sovereign power,
and the reality of consciousness known as the pure individual soul (jīva), because it is permitted by Him—
by this [the Lord] manifests in forms such as knowledge and action.
The nature of power (*śaktitva*) has been indicated.
He clarifies, with supporting evidence, that the nature of power is innate:
"In the beginning, that which was the one Brahman became the threefold *pradhāna*—sattva, rajas, and tamas—and from that [arose the world]."
By the power of action (kriyā-śakti) it is the Sūtra, and by the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) it is Mahat;
from that comes Ahaṃkāra, and that very [principle],
characterized as the individual soul (jīva), is the pure essential nature, the individual self (jīvātman), which is indicated by such terms as Vaikuṇṭha and so forth.
And the Vedas proclaim its majesty, such as:
"In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), and so forth.

Since there is first one [entity] and then that very form [appears], the power is established as inherent (*svābhāvika*), because it is impossible for it to be adventitious (*aupādhika*) given the non-existence of anything else;
this is like the majesty of one's own nature being present in every limb and member.
Even though it is eternally established, by its very existence— just as the multitude of solar rays exists through the existence of the sun— it [is manifested].
Because it has attained existence, it must be the material cause (*upādāna*) and the primary source (*tadādika*) of that world;
for the Śruti states: "By its light all this shines" (Kaṭha 2.2.15).
The inconceivability and inherent nature of His potency (śakti) are stated in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Of Him who is devoid of qualities, immeasurable, pure, and of stainless essence..."
"How is it that Brahman is accepted as the agent of creation and so forth?"—
after this question from Maitreya, Śrī Parāśara said:
Since the powers of all entities fall within the domain of inconceivable knowledge,
they therefore belong to Brahman.
O best of ascetics, the powers of manifestation and other such capacities arise from it, just as heat arises from fire. (ViP 1.3.2)
On this point, the commentary of Śrīdhara Svāmī also states:
"Thus, the agency of Brahman in creation and so forth has been described. Regarding that, an objection is raised: 'Of the one devoid of qualities (nirguṇasya)..."
Of that which is devoid of qualities such as existence and so forth,
which is immeasurable, which is undelimited by space, time, and the like, which is pure, bodiless, or devoid of auxiliary causes.
How can there be creation and so forth for such a Brahman— one whose nature is stainless, devoid of the impressions of merit and demerit, or rather, devoid of passion and the like?

The meaning is that agency is accepted [for the Self] precisely because in the world, agency and so forth are observed in things such as pots, which are indeed distinct from this [Self]. He provides the rebuttal with the verse beginning "capacities" (śaktayaḥ) and its half-verse.
For in the world, the powers of all entities— such as jewels, mantras, and so forth— are within the domain of inconceivable knowledge;
that which is inconceivable is beyond the reach of logical reasoning.

Knowledge, which has as its means of valid cognition the impossibility of otherwise accounting for an effect, possesses objects; or rather, they are inconceivable— meaning they cannot be conceptualized through dichotomies such as difference or non-difference—
and exist solely as the objects of knowledge derived from presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Therefore, for this very reason, even in Brahman there exist such powers— namely, the powers of being (*bhāva-śakti*) which are the causes of creation and so forth, and which are established by its own nature (*svabhāva-siddha*),
just like the power of burning and so forth in fire.

Therefore, the meaning is that because Brahman possesses inconceivable power, its status as the creator of the world and so forth is possible, even though it is devoid of qualities and the like; and the Śruti says:
"Of him, neither effect nor instrument exists."
Neither an equal nor one superior to Him is seen;
His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, consisting of innate knowledge, strength, and action. [ŚvetU 6.8]
"But one should know Māyā as Prakṛti (primordial nature), and the Great Lord (Maheśvara) as the wielder of Māyā" [ŚvetU 4.10].
Or rather, the construction is as follows: [He is the cause] of all entities, like the inconceivable power of heat in fire.
Powers indeed exist as the objects of knowledge;
moreover, for Brahman, those powers are its very nature, non-different from its own essence.
According to the Vedic scripture, "His power is heard to be indeed manifold," therefore,
like the heat of fire, they cannot be obstructed by anyone through gems, mantras, or other means. For this very reason,
His sovereignty is unrestrained.
And thus says the Śruti:
"He, indeed, is the controller of all this, the lord of all, the sovereign of all," and so forth (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
Since this is so, creation and the rest proceed from Brahman as their cause; there is no inconsistency whatsoever here.
This is the point.

Here, it should be understood that the question is posed by relying on the position that Brahman is indeed devoid of attributes (nirviśeṣa), whereas the answer is given by relying on the position that it is indeed with attributes (saviśeṣa).
For this very reason, it has also been explained that [the word] "of the pure" (*śuddhasya*) occurs in the question;
for here, purity (*śuddhatva*) is understood as being solitary (*kevalatva*), and that—
This is logical, because power is established in Brahman as the object of refutation; thus,
it is understood that according to the position of the opponent, even power does not exist in Brahman.
Therefore, even in the interrogative statement, the following different meaning should be understood: "of the Nirguṇa," that is, devoid of material (prākṛta) and non-material (aprākṛta) qualities;
and for that very reason, "beyond the scope of the means of valid cognition" (pramāṇāgocara). From that...
Thus, although the Self is pure and stainless,
it is not perceived as otherwise through the reflection of another— as is the case with objects such as crystal;
and so, having established the question by relying upon this state of being devoid of distinctions.

In the refutation, however, within the first interpretation, having disregarded the position of absolute non-distinction (*nirviśeṣa*), powers were established for the purpose of demonstrating Brahman's agency.
In the second interpretation, it is determined that, for the sake of understanding the specific distinction therein,
whereas qualities such as heat might occasionally be adventitious in water and other substances, they cannot be so in Brahman.
This is because of the Vedic scripture stating, "No one equal to Him or superior to Him is seen.

Likewise, the phrase "by means of jewels, mantras, and so forth" serves as a negative example (vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta); therefore, it is demonstrated that the powers of Brahman cannot be overcome by anything else.

Furthermore, by employing the term "Brahman" in the sense of the well-known declaration "All this, indeed, is Brahman," it is acknowledged that although [the Self] is distinct from Māyā— which consists of the qualities (guṇas) such as sattva—
it is nevertheless "devoid of qualities" (nirguṇa), meaning it is untouched by the material qualities (prākṛta-guṇas), and thus those qualities are recognized as being external to it.
This has been accepted.
Thus, this very Śruti passage, "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti," has accepted it;
and just as in the phrase "and Māyā, which rests upon that," because of His status as Maheśvara, He is the substratum of Māyā, which is the external instrument (bahiraṅga), [the text] refers to Him.
And it is also understood that [the Lord] remains having overcome [all things].
Therefore, as before, here too it is established that His mere power is innate and untouched by the defects of *māyā*.
Therefore, in the Śrī Gītā Upaniṣad it is said:
"I shall declare that which is to be known, by knowing which one attains immortality;
the beginningless Supreme Brahman is said to be neither being nor non-being."

"Having hands and feet everywhere," and so forth [Gītā 13.12–13]. Herein is the method: that single supreme reality, by its own inherent and inconceivable power, is at all times indeed [manifested] in the forms of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), its manifestations (*tadrūpavaibhava*), the individual soul (*jīva*), and primordial matter (*pradhāna*).
It abides in four ways:
like the light situated within the solar disk, it exists in the form of the disk itself, the rays extending outside that disk, and the reflected image thereof.

In the same way, the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa* states: "Just as the radiance of a fire situated in one place spreads far and wide, so too is this entire universe the power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Brahman. [ViP 1.22.56]

According to the Vedic scripture, "By whose light all this shines," the impossibility of various types of immersion (*samāveśa*) and so forth due to [the Self's] pervasiveness and other attributes is refuted precisely by the inconceivability (*acintyatva*) of power (*śakti*). This is because that which is difficult to accomplish...
For "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) is indeed inconceivability;
and that power is threefold: internal, external, and intermediate.

Therein, it abides by means of its internal power called *svarūpa-śakti*, in its full essential nature (*svarūpa*) and in the form of the majestic manifestations of its essential nature (*svarūpa-vaibhava*), such as Vaikuṇṭha;
and by means of its marginal power (*taṭastha-śakti*), [in the form of] rays.
In the form of the pure individual soul (jīva), whose essential nature is the one consciousness residing within, there exists—
due to the external adjunct known as Māyā— the insentient aspect born from His external glory, which corresponds to the variegation of colors appearing upon a reflected image.
And by way of its primary form, it constitutes the four elements; for this very reason, considering that the *pradhāna* is of the same nature as the *jīva*,
it possesses the status of an extrinsic power (*taṭastha-śakti*), and with the intention that it is included within *māyā*, [it is called] *śakti*.

Threefold power is enumerated in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "The supreme power of Viṣṇu is declared to be one; likewise, another is called the power of the individual soul (kṣetrajña); and a third power is recognized as that known as ignorance and karma" (ViP 6.7.61).
"And because it is concealed by that [power], O King, the power known as the *kṣetrajña* exists in all beings in varying degrees. [ViP 6.7.63]
The meaning is that *māyā* is so designated because its effect is ignorance (*avidyā*) and action (*karman*);

even though this [power] is external (*bahiraṅga*), it nevertheless has the capacity to veil the individual soul (*jīva*), which consists of the power of the "standing on the bank" (*taṭastha-śakti*).
He says "it has capacity" by means of the word *tayā* (by that).

The meaning is that, through a gradation, the obscuration produced by that [ignorance] exists in bodies ranging from Brahmā down to stationary beings in the form of lightness or heaviness. As it has been said:

As it is said: "The living being is deluded by that very same inconceivable Māyā through which the Knowable is [deluded]" (BhP 1.7.5). Furthermore, the fact that Pradhāna is manifested by Māyā will be demonstrated later.

In this context, the respective similarity among those [factors], which possess a single nature, is based solely on their being internal (*antaraṅga*), external (*bahiraṅga*), or indifferent (*taṭastha*), and not on their identity in every respect; therefore, they are said to occupy the respective positions [of the original elements].
But since it does not possess that respective form [of the object], those various defects find no opportunity there.

Śrī Pippalāyana [praised] Nimi. (14) [15] Thus, having all come together, the Lord, who is the power of both consciousness and unconsciousness, spoke to Brahmā— who was being praised in this very way as the Supreme Lord— by Hiraṇyakaśipu as well:
"To Him who is endowed with the powers of consciousness and matter" (BhP 7.3.34).
This refers to the fact that the reality of consciousness rests upon another reality of consciousness,
just as light— such as the radiance of rays— rests upon light.

It is like being the locus of a mandala. In that regard, the power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti), known as the "indifferent" (taṭastha), shall be explained in due course within the section concerning the Supreme Self (paramātman).
Now, for the purpose of explaining that which is called the internal (antaraṅga), even the external (bahiraṅga) is indicated by the words "that which is lower (aparā) and higher (parā).
It is heard in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"O Soul of all, that power of Yours which exists in all beings is the lower (aparā)."
O Lord of the Gods, salutations to that eternal one who is the locus of all virtues.
"I bow to that supreme Sovereign, who transcends the range of speech and mind, who is without distinctions, and who is to be discerned by the knowledge of the wise. Thus [it is said].
This very [Sovereign] should be understood as possessing many modes of manifestation (*vṛtti*).
Because of the Vedic scripture: "His power is heard to be manifold indeed.
(15) [16] In that regard, he states the external factor: "That which might be perceived apart from an object..."
And it would not be perceived within itself; one should know that to be the illusion of the Self, like a reflection or like darkness. [BhP 2.9.33]

The meaning is that if an object which is the ultimate reality were perceived apart from me, then its perception would be impossible when there is no perception of me; the sense is that its perception occurs only as something external to me.
The meaning is: that which is not perceived in itself, and for which there is no perception independently of its having me as its locus;
such is the definition.
One should know that the *māyā* of me, the Supreme Lord, the reality of all things, is a power called *māyā* which is twofold in nature, consisting of the *jīva-māyā* and the *guṇa-māyā*.
Herein, even for the pure *jīva*, there is consciousness (*cit*)—
Because there is no distinction in their nature as *rūpa* (form) and because they occupy the position of its rays, it is intended that they are indeed included within itself.

In this regard, its designation as having a dual nature is obtained through two types of analogies. Therein, clarifying the similarity of the first part—known as the *jīva* and *māyā*—by means of an analogy:
He dispels the doubt with the words "as it appears" (*yathābhāsa*).
An appearance (*ābhāsa*) is a particular reflection that has somehow surged forth in a location separated from its own light-source by the luminous image; as for that [appearance]:
Therefore, it is perceived only as external, and there is no perception of that [external object] without it; such is the meaning.

By this, its status as what is called "appearance" (*ābhāsa*) is established within that [consciousness], by virtue of its being a property (*dharmatva*) consisting in the manifestation of a semblance (*pratibimba*) or a synonym for appearance.
This has been indicated; therefore, its effect is termed an "appearance" (*ābhāsa*), as in the passage beginning with "Appearance and cessation" (BhP 2.10.7).
In this regard, it is just as when a certain extremely formidable being obstructs the light of the eyes of those whose vision has fallen upon the flash of his own magical power (*svacāścikyacchaṭā*).
And having enveloped him with its own exceedingly fierce brilliance, it agitates the observer's eye and pours forth a variegation of colors in its vicinity.
Sometimes it transforms that very [consciousness] into various forms through its state of differentiation;
in the same way, this [ignorance] also veils the knowledge of the individual soul (jīva).
It emits primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which is insentient, known as the *māyā* of the qualities, and whose form consists of the equilibrium of the qualities such as *sattva*;
at times, it [emits] the qualities such as *sattva* as separate entities.
It should be understood that he also causes the qualities (guṇas) to transform into various forms.
Thus it has been said: "Of the fire situated in one place... and so forth.
And thus say the experts in Ayurveda: "Of that Person who is the source of the world, who is devoid of desire, and whose sole nature is consciousness and bliss,
there exists an eternal primordial nature (prakṛti), like a reflection of the sun."
"Though insentient, through union with the sentience of the Supreme Self, she fashioned the entire impermanent universe like the form of a drama. Thus [it is said].
Thus, it should be analyzed further ahead that the aspect of the *nimitta* (efficient cause) is *jīva-māyā*, while the aspect of the *upādāna* (material cause) is *guṇa-māyā*.
Now, having established this, [we shall consider] the second aspect called *guṇa-māyā*.
He clarifies this with an illustration:
"just as darkness. Here, by the word "darkness," the previously mentioned darkness is intended.
The mixture of colors is called *prāya*.
For example, just as that root-light, though non-existent [independently], cannot occur without having that [root] as its substratum, so too is this [case].
Alternatively, there are two separate illustrations for the purpose of defining "mere illusion" (māyāmātra); among them,
the illustration of the appearance has already been explained.
And there is the illustration of darkness:
just as in the dark, light is perceived only elsewhere,
and not without light itself.
Just as light is not perceived by the eye alone— that is, it is perceived by the eye but not by the back or other parts— it should be understood that this [consciousness] is likewise.
Consequently, its two aspects must be inferred solely through the difference in their modes of activity, and not otherwise.
By way of a distinction between examples:
with the intention of presenting two types of previous examples,
the former is sometimes employed using the term *chāyā* as a synonym for *ābhāsa*, while the latter is designated by the term *tamas* alone.

And so it is; as in the passage, "He created before him the five-fold ignorance by means of his shadow" (BhP 3.20.18), and as in "Where am I? I am great darkness" (BhP 10.14.11) and other such instances.
In the former case, because it functions as the causal power known as *avidyā*, it pertains to the individual soul (*jīva*).
The nature of *māyā*:

the meaning is that in the passage beginning with "Thus he created," at the commencement of creation, Brahmā himself manifested ignorance (*avidyā*) by resorting to *māyā*, which is the power of shadow (*chāyā-śakti*).
O Uddhava, know that knowledge and ignorance are my two primary bodies for embodied beings;
they cause bondage and liberation, and are fashioned by my Māyā.
Because it has been stated thus;
and the difference between the manifestations of these two is heard in scripture.
Among them, regarding the former, in the *Padma-purāṇa* [it is said of] Śrī Kṛṣṇa—
In the *Kārttikamāhātmya* concerning the dialogue with Satyabhāmā, within the hymn to Māyā composed by the hosts of gods:
"Having thus offered praise, those gods beheld him situated in a circle of splendor in the sky, with the quarters of space pervaded by his radiance."
