From the midst of that, they all heard the voice of Sarasvatī moving through the sky:
"I myself, divided threefold, abide by means of the three qualities," and so forth.
In the northern Padmottara-khaṇḍa, there is an immeasurable abode of primordial nature (prakṛti), consisting of dense darkness and devoid of parts.

The Blessed Lord [spoke] to Brahmā. [16] [17] Now, since the activity of everything else would otherwise be impossible, He first describes, by means of two verses, His own internal power known as Svarūpa-bhūtā (the power consisting of His own essential nature).
I bow down to that which is spread within and without like the sky, which the mind, intellect, senses, and vital breaths neither touch nor know.
These— the body, senses, life-breath, mind, and intellect— [are distinct from it].
Only when they are pierced by a portion of that [divine power] do they engage in ritual acts;
at other times, like unheated iron,
they remain in their positions only through the instruction of one who perceives that [reality].

And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "I bow to that Brahman which, though pervasive like space, is not touched by the vital breaths (*asavaḥ*), that is, the powers of action (*kriyā-śakti*), nor is it known by the mind and other faculties through the power of cognition (*jñāna-śakti*). To them...

He states the reason for that knowledge: these bodies, senses, and so forth, being pierced by a portion of which [Self] and entered by a portion of whose consciousness, they function in their respective activities and objects. Just as...
Iron does not burn that which has not been reached by it;
therefore, just as iron, though it becomes a burner solely through the power of fire,
does not burn the fire itself, so too do the body and other elements proceed by means of the powers of knowledge and action residing in Brahman.
The meaning is that they neither touch nor know [it]. Thus ends this [section]. Here, in the *Advaita-śārīraka* as well, Sāṅkhya has been refuted, as follows:
"Now, however, the witness..."
If the causality of the Pradhāna for the act of seeing were to be postulated— just as the causality of fire for the burning of an iron ball and so forth—
then that very thing which is the cause of the Pradhāna’s seeing would be [the Self].

"The omniscient one is the primary cause of the world" [Śaṅkara-bhāṣya, 1.1.5]. And there is a scriptural passage on this point: "Only after Him, as He shines, do all things shine" [Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.2.15].
"For who indeed could breathe, who could live, if this bliss were not in the ether? [TaittU 2.7], beginning with "the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear," and so forth.
Now, regarding the remaining portion of the subject at hand, the commentary says: "In that case, the individual soul (jīva) might know because it is a seer; no, he says."
In the states such as waking and so forth, it attains—that is, reaches—the designation of the seer, the appellation "seer.

There is no other so-called individual soul (jīva) distinct from this, according to the Śruti: "There is no other seer than this" (BAU 3.7.23). Or alternatively, one knows that even the individual soul, which is designated as the seer and bears the name "seer," becomes that very [Brahman] at that time.
But the meaning is not that the living being (jīva) knows that; this is what has been stated:
"He who knows that triad there is the Self, the support of its own support" (BhP 2.10.9).

And in the Śruti: "The so-called jīva is not other than this; it is not self-established, but rather has that [Self] as its very essence"—this is the meaning. Likewise, there is no seer other than this.
The meaning should be explained as follows: for that seer of all, there is no other seer.
Śrī Nārada said to Citraketu:
"Furthermore— body, life-breaths, senses, mental faculties, and the elements..."
He who knows the Supreme does not perceive himself or another;
such a person knows all things and their qualities, yet he does not perceive [himself as] the omniscient one. I praise that infinite Being.
The body, the vital breaths, the senses which are the organs, the minds which are the internal instruments, the elements,
and the subtle measures (tanmātras).
They do not know themselves as their own true nature, nor the "other" consisting of the various objects of their senses, nor the supreme group of deities that presides over both.
The individual soul (pumān jīva), however, [perceives] everything—
both its own self as its true nature and the cognizer other than that— as [its own].
He knows the "foot" of those two— the collection of objects such as the body and the class of deities presiding over them—
as well as those that constitute the root of the body and so forth.
He knows the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest;
yet, even though he knows this much, he does not know that All-Knowing One who is the knower of everything from the body up to the individual soul (*jīva*).
He is infinite because of His great qualities, as it is said: "Him they call infinite" (BhP 1.18.19).
For this very reason, after beginning with "For where there is duality as it were, there one sees another" (BAU 4.5.15), the text describes the individual soul's state of seeing another.

In the passage beginning with "where one's own everything has become the Self alone, by what should one see whom?", the state of being a seer of the Supreme Self is denied for that [individual soul]; however, it is established that the Supreme Self possesses the capacity to see all those things as well as the capacity to see itself.
He said this with the words, "By what means, O Maitreyī, could one know the knower? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).
This is the meaning.
In that manifestation of *māyā* where duality appears as if it were real,
because [the world] is rooted in that,
it is non-different from it; yet, by virtue of being caused by the inconceivable power called *māyā*, it is insentient, impure, and perishable.
Then, through its state of being characterized by difference, that which has been concentrated arises repeatedly as if possessing independent existence; therein,
one living being perceives another object because of the mutual compatibility between his instruments of perception and the objects to be perceived.

This is the state of being. However, within the splendor of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), that Supreme Self (*paramātman*)— who is the Self of this individual soul (*jīva*) which stands in the place of rays and who stands in the place of the solar orb—
has become everything by means of His own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*).
It exists as having existed from time immemorial,
not by entering into that; that other one therein is the individual soul (jīva).
By what other instrument would one perceive what object?
The meaning is that one would perceive nothing by means of anything at all; for rays do not, by their own power, [perceive] the majesty contained within the solar orb.

The sense is that the flames would not illuminate, nor would fire burn. This being so, he whose infinite majesty of essential nature is thus [described]— him, the knower, the omniscient one— [one should know].
"By what other instrument could one know the Supreme Self? By none at all"—this is the meaning.
Thus, when the power of knowledge has been established therein, the powers of action and will are also indicated. Dakṣa [worships] the illustrious Puruṣottama. 18/19.
He speaks of her also as one who has brought Māyā under control:
"For you, having eternally conquered the qualities of the self by your own splendor,
are Time, who has brought under control the power of both creation and the renunciation of what is to be created" (BhP 7.9.22).
"By its own splendor" means by the power of consciousness (*cic-śakti*);

for there is also a commentary stating that "time is the impeller of *māyā*. Furthermore, in this context, "Self" refers to the individual soul (*jīva*), and its "qualities" are *sattva* and the others.
For it has been stated: "Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities of the individual soul (jīva), not of Me. [BhP 11.25.12]
Prahlāda [worships] Śrī Narasiṃha.
//19// [20] And likewise:
He performs the maintenance, dissolution, and emergence of the universe.

Salutations to You, the witness of qualities and actions, upon whom the Māyā— like iron dependent on a magnet— revolves; for that which is desired by the observer is not truly desired by him through his own attributes.
And the commentary [states]: "For that observer, what is desired is for the sake of another;
for if there were absolute lack of desire, observation would be impossible.
But it is not desired for its own sake."
Māyā effects the maintenance of the universe and so forth through her own qualities;
although she is insentient, her activity occurs due to the proximity of the Lord, as illustrated by the example of iron [being moved] by a magnet.

Just as iron revolves due to the cause of a magnet—being dependent upon it and directed toward it—so too [I bow] to Him, the witness of the qualities (guṇas), the actions (karmans), and the unseen potencies (adṛṣṭas) of the individual soul; to Him, salutation! Thus ends this [section]. May there be prosperity!
To the illustrious Lord Varāha.

//20// [21] Now, since liberation (kaivalya) is impossible if there is a mixture with the power of illusion (māyā-śakti), and since even in liberation there would be an absence of experience— and consequently the status of that bliss as an object of value would be untenable— he states that very [power] by means of the proof of "inexplicability otherwise" (anyathānupapatti):
You are the primordial Puruṣa, the manifest Lord, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), having cast aside illusion (māyā) by means of your conscious power (cit-śakti).
Abiding in the self in the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya),
you are yourself the primordial Person, the Blessed Lord;
likewise, you are the Sovereign, the Inner Controller (antaryāmī).
That person who is thus designated is also you alone;
therefore, in both modes of manifestation, you are beyond primordial nature (prakṛti) and unattached to it.

Now, one might ask: how can even one who consists solely of the bliss of experience possess the state of being an experiencer, since from that very state the status of being a Blessed One (Bhagavān) is also observed;
and furthermore, how is it that despite being the Lord (Īśvara) and the presiding controller of primordial nature (prakṛti), he remains unattached to it?
Regarding this, he says: "having cast aside illusion.

By means of its own unerring essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*), it casts that power of appearance (*ābhāsa-śakti*) far away; and likewise, by that same essential power, in the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*)—
"In the highest of the high and low, He dwells, designated as Kaivalya— the mass of the bliss of absolute experience, free from all limiting adjuncts" (BhP 11.9.18).
According to this description from the Eleventh Canto, [He resides] in the Self, His own essential nature, which is called Kaivalya and consists of the bliss of absolute experience.
"Abiding" means that one has experienced the bliss of one's own true nature.
This was stated by the gods in the Sixth Canto: "You are one who has personally realized the experience of your own innate bliss" (BhP 6.9.33).
And by the word *sandoha*, a manifold variety (*vaicitrī*) is shown in the eleventh [chapter];
and that arises precisely from the manifold variety of power (*śakti*). Therefore, the power of essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*) certainly exists.
In this context, what is called "prakṛti" is the threefold nature of māyā;
in this very way, the manifestation of the three powers has been demonstrated by the Master himself.
For it is thus stated in the words of Śrī Devahūti: "The Supreme, the Pradhāna, the Puruṣa, the Mahat..."

"I take refuge in Kapila— the poet, the threefold one, the guardian of the world, who has transcended all conceptual proliferation through self-realization, and whose power is autonomous. Thus [it is said] here.
The Supreme Lord; the reason for this is that His powers are autonomous (*svacchanda*). He states those very powers: *pradhāna*, which is of the nature of *prakṛti*.
The Person who is its presiding controller,
the Great One whose nature is the principle of Mahat.
Time is their agitator;
it consists of the threefold ego-consciousness (ahaṅkāra) and the elements, and it has the nature of both the worlds and their protectors.

Thus, having described [the Self] as having the nature of *pradhāna* and so forth through *māyā*, he now states its state beyond conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcatā*) by means of the power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*):
"In his own self, [the Self] is followed by the power of consciousness through the experience of the Self."

The meaning is: "to that poet (kavi), who is omniscient and the witness to the manifestation of primordial matter (pradhāna) and the rest, in whom all conceptual proliferation (prapañca) has subsided."

In this context, although the Puruṣa is also included within Māyā, he is figuratively designated as its presiding controller; in reality, however, his status is one of transcendence over it. Thus, in the words of the venerable Lord Kapila:

"The self (ātman) is beginningless, the person (puruṣa), devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), beyond primordial nature (prakṛti); it is the inward abode, self-luminous, by whom the universe is pervaded. Thus, through the definition of both name and essential nature, that [self] is clearly distinguished as possessing the three potencies even in the *Mahāsaṃhitā*.
"Śrī, Bhūḥ, and Durgā—these are the distinct forms of the Māyā of the Great Soul (Mahātman) known as Jīva-māyā;
Ātma-māyā is His will, while Guṇa-māyā is of an insentient nature.
This is the meaning [of the verse]. Here, Śrī is the power of protecting the world.
Bhūḥ is the power of its creation, and Durgā is the power of its dissolution;
she who has attained differentiation through those respective forms.
That power of His which has the individual soul as its object is called "jīva-māyā. This is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā:
"I myself, divided into three forms, abide through the three qualities"— immediately after these words were spoken, all those gods, having heard them and being impelled by that speech,
bowed down to Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and Dhārā, being entirely devoted in their worship. Thus [it is said].

And in the eleventh [canto]: "This Māyā of the Blessed One, which effects creation, maintenance, and destruction, has been described by us as having three colors; what more do you wish to hear? [BhP 11.3.16]
The term *ātma-māyā* refers to the power of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*).
By the word *māyā*, even mere power (*śakti-mātra*) is expressed, in the sense that "by this, [something] is measured."
"In that state, as darkness is destroyed by the sun, or as the light of a firefly is eclipsed by day, one who applies himself to the Self destroys the great power of illusion within himself"—
thus the word of Brahmā is likewise consistent.
For what is intended there is merely the gradation of capacity;
indeed, let even a very small capacity be the manifestor of either the false or the true.
For it is understood from that context that [the mind] indeed leads to ruin;
and this is likewise made manifest by the two examples beginning with "like darkness" and so forth.
Likewise, it is heard in the Purāṇas and other texts that in battles many were cut and pierced by weapons and the like consisting of illusion;
from this, it is understood that such illusion is a product of false conceptualization.
For no one becomes wet by the water of a mirage;
[the Self] is joined with its own inherent, eternal power called Māyā.
Therefore, they declare Viṣṇu, who consists of māyā, to be eternal.
Thus says the Śruti, beginning with the Caturvedaśikhā:
"And therefore—her *māyā* would be her will"—here both knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*) are also indicated. Furthermore, in the *Nighaṇṭu*, *māyā*, *vayuna*, and *jñāna* are synonymous terms.
Furthermore, that which consists of the three qualities (triguṇa), as well as knowledge (jñāna) and the power of Viṣṇu (viṣṇu-śakti),
is designated by the word "māyā" by those who know the true meaning of the principles of sound (śabda-tattva).
Thus it is stated in the Trikāṇḍaśeṣa;
"māyā" means deceit and compassion, according to the Viśvaprakāśa;
and so it has been explained by the authors of the commentaries.

In the eleventh [canto], regarding the passage "Time [is] in the jīva consisting of māyā" (BhP 11.24.27), [it refers to Time] as either the activator of māyā or as that which consists of knowledge (*jñānamaya*). In the third [canto] as well, in the passage beginning with "They attained supreme joy" (BhP 3.15.26), having explained the power of the eightfold yoga (*aṣṭāṅga-yoga*) in Sanaka and others by means of the term *yoga-māyā*, [it is stated that] in the case of the Supreme Lord, however, it is *cit*-...
The play of power (*śakti-vilāsa*) has been explained;
therefore, it is established that "self-illusion" (*ātma-māyā*) consists of three divisions.
Or, as it is said: "You are the primordial Person" (*tvam ādyaḥ puruṣaḥ*).
Thus, the original words beginning with [1.7.23] are to be introduced as follows:
although He negates *māyā* in Śrī Vaikuṇṭha, He speaks of that very same thing directly when saying, "You are the primordial one."
He remains as his own partial expansion within the Self, which is characterized by the glorious Vaikuṇṭha and known as liberation (mokṣa) in the state of absolute isolation (kaivalya).
Having done what? Therein—
Having set aside even the distant *māyā* by means of His resplendent power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*), this is the view held by Śrī Śukadeva, who negates *māyā* and the like:
"Wherein *rajas* and *tamas* proceed..."
"Therein there is goodness mixed with passion, yet no influence of time;
there is no illusion, much less others, where the devotees of Hari dwell, who are honored by both gods and demons. [BhP 2.9.10] Thus it is said.
"Liberation, the supreme state, the subtle body, the nectar, and the abode of Viṣṇu"—
these are synonyms for Vaikuṇṭha according to the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa.
Arjuna [speaks] to the Blessed Lord.

[21] [22] From this point forward, until the conclusion of the work, the intrinsic potency (*svarūpa-śakti*) alone is further elaborated, following the summary of the nature of the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth as being identical with the essential nature (*svarūpa*).
[*ENDNOTE 3] In this regard, they say that the qualities (guṇas) constitute his very nature:
"When he lies along with the Unborn through the Unborn, enjoying the qualities..."
Thereafter, having lost his fortune, he partakes in a state of similarity with that [death];
but you, having attained all fortune, cast off that [state] like a snake sheds its skin,
and, possessing immeasurable fortune, you are magnified in glory endowed with eightfold qualities.
And the commentary [states]: "But that *jīva*, because it clings to— that is, embraces— the unborn (*ajā*), which is *māyā* or ignorance (*avidyā*),

and consequently, while enjoying— that is, serving and superimposing as its own self— the *guṇas* such as the body and the senses, thereafter, while enjoying similarity with them and union with their attributes, [it becomes] devoid of..."
Bhaga, though possessing qualities such as concealed bliss and the like, partakes in—that is, reaches—mortality, which is to say, saṃsāra;
but you, indeed, abandon that māyā. [An objection: "But surely it resides in me alone; how can there be its abandonment? To this he replies: "Like a snake its slough."
The meaning is this:
just as a serpent does not regard even its own slough with the notion that it is a virtue, so too you [should not regard] the unborn Māyā.
Indeed, you do not disregard Māyā, thinking that there is no need for her since the Lord of the herd of wish-fulfilling cows is consciousness itself, which consists of uninterrupted bliss;
why is this so? To that he says:
One who has eternally attained sovereignty over one's own self;
in "maha," which is supreme sovereignty endowed with the eightfold qualities, namely the eightfold vibhūtis beginning with *aṇimā*.
You are magnified, you are worshipped, you shine forth; of what nature?
Of immeasurable fortune, that is, of immeasurable sovereignty.
But unlike those of others, your eightfold sovereignty is not limited by space and time;
rather, it is perfectly complete.
The meaning is that it is "immeasurable" because it is inseparable from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Such is this [verse].

And likewise, it was previously stated in that very same place: "You are he by whom all fortune has been gathered together within his own self" (BhP 10.87.14). Or else, in the passage "like a snake shedding its skin," by the word "skin" (*tvak*), [the following is meant].
That which has been cast off is called nothing more than withered skin;
just as one abandons it and does not even go near it, so too you shall not go near Māyā— this is the meaning.
And elsewhere:
"The mass of pure consciousness, complete in its own nature, in whom all purposes are fulfilled, and whose desire is never in vain" (BhP 10.37.22).
Likewise, the Blessed Lord spoke to Uddhava: "Eighteen perfections (siddhis) have been described by those who have reached the further shore of yoga.
Of these, eight are headed by Me; the other ten are causes for the material qualities (guṇas). [BhP 11.15.3] Thus it is said.
And further on it says: "O gentle one, these eight perfections of mine are considered innate" (BhP 11.15.5).
For this very reason, Śrī Prahlāda spoke to the sons of the Daityas:
"The Supreme Lord is whose nature is absolute experiential bliss."
"By means of *māyā*, whose creative manifestation consists of the *guṇas*, His sovereignty is concealed.
And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "Now, if He alone is everywhere, then why is omniscience and so forth not perceived everywhere?
To this he replies: 'By that *māyā*, whose nature is creation consisting of the *guṇas*, His sovereignty is concealed.'"
Thus it is said.

Here, by describing the Lord’s sovereignty as being concealed by *māyā* and by employing *māyā* as an adjective modifying the "creation of the qualities" (*guṇa-sarga*), he makes known that [the Lord] transcends it, just as He transcends His own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Therefore, it should be understood that the qualification "Supreme Lord" (Parameśvara) was also already provided previously by association with that [term]. The Śruti texts state:
"The one unborn, red, white, and black..."
"Creating many offspring of similar form, one unborn (aja) lies beside her, taking delight;
another unborn (aja) leaves her once she has been enjoyed. [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5]
Whatever is the nature of the Blessed One, such is the nature of the manifest individual.
Of what nature is the Blessed One?
He is of the nature of knowledge, of the nature of sovereignty, and of the nature of power.
"Divine self-power, hidden by its own qualities," and so forth [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.3].
Here, the phrase "by its own qualities" means that it is beyond the range of words.
The meaning is: by means of the aforementioned inherent natures.
The Śrutis [speak] of the Blessed Lord:
"All qualities worship me, who am devoid of qualities and independent. [23]
"Friendliness, love for the Self, equanimity, non-attachment, and other such qualities.
And the commentary asks: "Of what nature are they?"
The meaning is that the *aguṇas* do not consist of the transformation of the *guṇas*, but are rather eternal. Such is this [teaching].
And so it is stated in the *Jitaṃ te* hymn of the *Nārada-pañcarātra*:
"Salutation to the primordial piercer who transcends all qualities yet possesses the six divine attributes. Thus it is said in the *Brahmatarka*:
"That Lord Hari, the Supreme Controller, is the possessor of qualities through those qualities which constitute His very nature."
Neither in Viṣṇu nor in the liberated ones is any distinct quality ever admitted.
In the *Kālikā-purāṇa*, within the hymn to Viṣṇu composed by the Goddess:
"How can he be described by me, whose forms even the gods beginning with Brahmā, and the sages whose wealth is asceticism, do not fully reveal?"
"O Lord, what qualities of yours, who are beyond all attributes, can I, a woman, possibly know?
Even the gods and asuras, including Indra himself, do not know your true form. Thus she spoke.
Śrī Haṃsadeva [speaks of] Sanaka and the others.
[24] Elsewhere, having enumerated those many who are embraced by the acceptance of the words of Śrī Haṃsa situated elsewhere, beginning with "truth, purity," and so forth, he says:
O Blessed One, these and other great qualities, which are eternal,
are to be sought by those who desire greatness.
"They never departed" (na viyanti sma karhicit).
And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "These are thirty-nine;
and others, such as devotion to Brahman (*brahmaṇyatva*), seeking refuge (*śaraṇyatva*), and so forth."
"In that [Supreme Being] great qualities are eternal, innate, never departing, and never diminishing"—thus it is said.
Regarding this, the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa* states: "And time consists of units such as *kalās*, *muhūrtas*, and so forth."
"For that which is not the cause of the transformation of one's own power.
[ViP 4.1.84] Thus, Śrī-Pṛthivī [said] to Śrī-Dharma: //24// [25] For this very reason, he said—
Homage to you, the Blessed One, the Brahman, the Supreme Self,
wherein no illusion is heard.
Regarding the conceptualization of the creation of the world:
where [the Lord] manifests in His own essential nature in three ways as the Blessed One and so forth, there Māyā is not heard of;
the meaning is that His manifestation in such various ways does not occur through Māyā.

The reason for this is as follows: she is one whose nature it is to conceptualize at the very moment of the world's creation and to exercise manifold sovereignty through the acts of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
For this very reason, the King also stated [the following] as the reason in response to the question regarding the earth:

"For the mind that has been absorbed into the gross form consisting of the qualities of the Blessed One is indeed capable of being absorbed into the Supreme Brahman, the Lord known as Vāsudeva— the self-luminous, subtlest reality which is beyond the qualities. [BhP 5.16.3]
Varuṇa [praised] the Blessed Lord. 25.
Likewise:
"We meditate upon that Blessed Lord Vāsudeva; we offer salutation to him. 26.
They call me the Teacher of the World by means of an invincible illusion.

Because he is composed of darkness and the other qualities (*tama-ādi*), he is inherently flawed; therefore, those of wicked intellect, being deluded, boast "I am this, I am that," while she, feeling ashamed, cannot even stand within the range of his vision.

We and others of dull intellect are deluded by this Māyā, who, being ashamed to appear before the range of vision of that faultless One who is a mass of existence, consciousness, and bliss, has concealed herself from him. Thus spoke Śrī Brahmā to Śrī Nārada. 26–27.
Thus, having described the sixfold attributes beginning with sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) as being the very nature of His essence,
this section is commenced to explain that the glorious form (*śrī-vigraha*) constitutes the complete essential nature.
In that regard, His eternity— which serves as the accompaniment to His being of such a nature— is already established by His presiding over the aforementioned Vaikuṇṭha of such a character.
Even though he has entered into phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*), he says by way of three [verses]:
"When the world has perished at the end of two *parārdhas*, and the primary elements have merged into the primordial element (*ādibhūta*)."
"When the manifest has passed away by the force of time into the unmanifest,
you alone remain, known as 'the Remainder' (Aśeṣa).
Thus, he is named Śeṣa.
In this regard, the reasoning is as follows: O you whose bonds are unmanifest, they say that this which is time is the activity by which the universe acts.
From a moment to the end of a year, I take refuge in that Great Lord, the abode of peace;
O friend of the unmanifest, You who set Prakṛti in motion by Your mere presence. Action... [is Yours].
[She is] in the form of the closing and opening of the eyes;
and the Śruti says: "All moments (nimeṣas) were born from the Puruṣa, from the Effulgent One" (Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 1.8).
All divisions of time, beginning with the *nimeṣa*,
shine forth distinctly;
"the Person" (*puruṣa*) is the Supreme Self— this is the meaning of the Vedic scripture everywhere.

The meaning is that time alone is the cause of creation and destruction; however, since time consists of the movement of its own limbs (the divisions of time), those two [creation and destruction] are simply not possible therein.
In this context, "kṣemadhāma" serves as another reason. [The word] "tvā" means "you.
Here, by that very manifestation which was her own desired object, she has warded off the fear of Kaṃsa through the logic of *kaimutya* (the principle of "how much more so").
Likewise, he spoke clearly again:
"A mortal, terrified by the serpent of death, fled through all the worlds but did not find a place free from fear."
Having reached your lotus feet by chance today, he sleeps at ease; death departs from him.
Having attained the worlds where there is fearlessness—the absence of fear—[he remains].
The construction is to be understood in both instances as "having attained Your lotus feet";
here, "Your lotus feet" refers specifically to the glorious form (śrī-vigraha). Nevertheless...
She has clearly established this;

for this very reason, she is called "Amṛtavapuḥ" (of immortal form) in the *Sahasranāmastotra*. Furthermore, in the *Śaṅkarabhāṣya*, it is explained: "Death" (*mṛta*) means dying; she whose body (*vapuḥ*) is devoid of that is "Amṛtavapuḥ. [The word] "ādyā" (the primordial one).
The absence of birth has also been demonstrated, because if there were birth, its being beginningless would be established everywhere. Thus it is said:
"He appeared like the full moon in the eastern quarter" (BhP 10.3.8).

And there is a scriptural passage on this point: "He creates by means of Brahmā; He causes dissolution by means of Rudra; that Hari is indeed without origin or dissolution, the Supreme, the Absolute Bliss," as stated in the Mahopaniṣad.
The illustrious Queen Devakī [beheld] the Blessed Lord.
[28] Likewise, in the verse beginning with "utpatti-sthiti-laya," it says: "That form which is eternal, uncreated" (BhP 5.25.9).
The form of that Śrī Saṅkarṣaṇa is eternal, infinite, and uncreated—meaning it is without beginning. Therefore...
In the description of the worship of the Lord of the Year (Varṣādhipa), even Bhava spoke concerning His form:
"Indeed, the vision of Him who beholds is not stained in the slightest by the fluctuations of the mind or the qualities of Māyā" (BhP 5.17.19).
As for that which was said there by Śrī Śuka with reference to that very form— “That which is indeed a portion of the Blessed One,
consisting of *tamas*” (BhP 5.25.1)— and likewise in the prose section by the Lords of Bhavānī— “the *tāmasī* form” (BhP 5.17.16)— it has been stated thus.

This should be understood as being for the benefit of the quality of *tamas* by means of Śiva, who is His own portion (*nijāṃśa*). Immediately after the verse beginning with "creation, maintenance, and dissolution," Śrī Śuka himself [the author] has recorded the words of Śrī Nārada which were not previously mentioned: "Out of great compassion, He assumed a form consisting of pure *sattva*, which is both this [world] and that [the Absolute]."
Wherever it shines forth,
everything there is eternally the very form of the Blessed Lord.
And so, in the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa*, there is praise of Him: "To the one whose body is without beginning, end, or limit, who possesses the universal form.
As for whatever misleading statements appear here in the *Skānda* and other Purāṇas, those are due to the *tāmasa* (dark) nature of those respective Purāṇas.
Because it consists of accounts of the kalpas, and because the Blessed One concealed His own majesty within those various kalpas, that is indeed appropriate.
As it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam: "O royal sage, they speak thus... (BhP 10.77.30).
By such statements as these, that kind of opinion is not accepted;
however, we shall establish this point specifically in the *Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha*.

Our own view, however, is that by the statement of Śrī Pṛthivī beginning with "truth, purity, compassion, and forbearance" (BhP 1.16.27), He demonstrates that even splendor, majesty, vigor, and strength are innate and invariable.
And by the words of Śrī Devakī beginning with "When the world has perished" (BhP 10.3.25),
it is therefore rightly said that His form is eternal.
"It is uncreated," says Śrī Śuka.
[28] He describes His omnipresence:
"Of whom there is neither inside nor outside, neither before nor after... [29]
He who is before and after, outside and inside the world, and he who is the world itself.
Thinking him to be her own son, though he was the unmanifest Adhokṣaja appearing in a mortal form, the cowherd woman bound him with a rope to a mortar as if he were an ordinary child.
And the commentary states: "For binding occurs by means of a rope that is external to one who is enclosed within. Thus it is.

In the case of an object possessing the distinction of front and back, it occurs by holding a cord at the front and wrapping it around from the back; however, this is not the case here, as he says: "nor in between.
Furthermore, [this would require] the pervader [to occupy] the pervaded.

Bondage occurs; however, in this case, that is reversed, as he says: "prior and posterior. Furthermore, because there is no existence apart from that, there is no bondage, as he says: "and that which is the world"—him, the mortal.
"Thinking the linga to be his own son, born of Adhokṣaja, he bound it"—thus is this [verse].

Regarding the phrase "and the world": if, upon the absence of that cause, there were an absence of the effect— the world— then how could there be bondage for that world which is non-different from Him, by means of His power alone, since that power is of the nature of a part of His very self, just as a rope [is the cause of the appearance of a snake]?

For the intention is not that the flames would fail to burn the fire; this is the view of the commentators regarding the passage beginning with "that [body] bearing mortal signs. Now, [one might object]: "But all..."
How did he bind that which is all-pervasive?
For no one can bind even the cosmic egg or similar entities. To this, he says: "The mortal sign," meaning a human form.
If so, how is there all-pervasiveness?
To this he says: *adhokṣajam*, by whom sense-born knowledge has been cast down (*adhaḥkṛtam*).

The meaning is that its nature is inconceivable by means of direct perception and other instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), as it is not within the range of the cognitions of any of the sense faculties (*indriya*).
Therefore, the point is that even though [the cognition] possesses that form, there is indeed omnipresence (*vibhutva*) in that [consciousness],
because it is beyond the senses (*adhokṣaja*).

Thus, the state of being unmanifest has also been explained, and so it has not been further elaborated here. [Objection: Even while possessing a human form, how was it that his omnipresence did not manifest to his mother? To this he says: "considering him to be her own son."
This is the very nature of the specific aesthetic flavor (rasa) of love known as *vatsala* and others:
that it experiences the state of the beloved through its own flood of bliss.
The meaning is that she obstructs the path.
And thus, her lack of skill regarding his virility is itself her greatness; for even though he is bound by ropes, she acts out of love for him.
Because rasa takes the form of an ensuant (anubhāva).
This has been stated [in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa]: "Neither Viriñca nor Bhava... and so forth [BhP 10.9.20].
By the words "as is the natural" and "beyond the senses," [the nature] of the reality...
Furthermore, the objection that [the Lord] possesses a mortal form due to *māyā* while being all-pervasive is also refuted;
for when something falls within the scope of logical reasoning (*tarka*),
it is only there that one might occasionally observe an impossibility.
That which is admitted is accepted;
however, as for that which has already passed away by its own nature,
the acceptance of it therein is exceedingly—
Folly: for example, when the fire named Bāḍava blazes intensely right in the midst of the ocean, to accept it as being a magical illusion;
and the Vedic scripture says: "The gods are on this side of it."
Then, by means of the *visarjana* (concluding rite), there is the verse beginning with "Who knows from whence it has arisen?
(*Ṛgveda 10.129.6*). Furthermore, what is intended is the all-pervasiveness of that very *śrī-vigraha* (the glorious form) which has transcended bondage;
this is because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the pronouns *yat* and *tat*, and because it establishes her lack of expertise therein. In that regard:
The state of having a body (*vigrahatva*) is possible only for that which is limited (*paricchinnā*), because of the arrangement of limbs such as hands and feet.
Therefore, in this very case, limitation and omnipresence (*vibhutva*) exist simultaneously. [Mūla-]
In the Siddhānta itself, it has been shown that He is the repository of hundreds of mutually contradictory powers.
Such a nature is also observed in the world among great medicinal herbs that destroy the three humors (doṣas).
Likewise, His omnipotence is described in the Brahma-saṃhitā:
Yet that path, which is traversed even by the wind, by the mind, and by the preeminent sages for hundreds of millions of years,
exists within the very threshold of his feet— that reality which is inconceivable.
I worship that Govinda, the primordial person. Thus [ends Brahmasūtra 5.40].

And the Śruti, as authenticated by the Madhva-bhāṣya, states: "Hari is neither gross nor subtle, neither intermediate nor middle-sized, neither all-pervasive nor non-pervasive; he is the beginning and yet without beginning, the universe and yet not the universe, possessing qualities and yet devoid of qualities."

Likewise, the *Nṛsiṃhatāpanī* begins with: "The Fourth who is not the Fourth, the Self who is not the non-Self, the Fierce who is not fierce, the Heroic who is not heroic, the Great who is not great, Viṣṇu who is not Viṣṇu, the Blazing who is not blazing, the One whose face is everywhere who is not everywhere-facing" (NTU 2.3).
In the *Brahma-purāṇa*:
"He is neither gross nor subtle, neither the universe nor yet the universe itself;
He is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) because, by virtue of His sovereignty, He possesses the nature of these contradictory attributes."
Likewise, it is seen in the Śrī-Viṣṇudharma: "To Him whose form consists of thousands of minute atoms, down to the very limit of the infinitesimal atom..."
Salutation to the one who holds the universe situated within a ten-thousandth part of the interior of his belly. Thus.
Therefore, from the Śrī Gītā Upaniṣad:
"By Me, whose form is unmanifest, all this world is pervaded."
All beings abide in me,
yet I do not abide in them.
And yet, beings do not dwell in Me;
behold My divine yoga!
I am the sustainer of beings, yet I do not dwell in beings.
"My Self is the creator of all beings" (Gītā 9.4–5).
"With unmanifest form" means that because his nature is such, he possesses a physical body that is beyond the reach of the power of the intellect. — Śrī Śuka. 29/30.

Thus, in order to demonstrate through the experience of the wise and by means of the logic already stated that even that very form which is limited possesses omnipresence (*vibhutva*), this section is commenced.
Therein, [the first] eleven—

He speaks in verse: "Where am I— my body measuring seven spans [of a cubit] within the jar-like cosmic egg, which is enveloped by darkness, the great principle (mahat), egoism (ahaṃkāra), space, wind, fire, water, and earth?"
And what is the greatness of You, whose pores and the pathways of Your breath contain countless cosmic eggs and the movement of atoms?
This is clear. [31]
Is the lifting of the feet of one in the womb possible for the mother in the scripture of Adhokṣaja?
Is it adorned by the designations of "existence" and "non-existence"?
"Within your womb there is some measure of infinity.
The sense is this: since everything has entered your womb, I too am likewise situated therein; therefore, like a mother, you must endure my offense. [32]
Furthermore, he states that which is particularly well-known as your birth:
"Arising from the stalk of the navel of Nārāyaṇa’s abdomen at the time of the deluge of the ocean that bounds the three worlds..."
"The statement that 'I have emerged from You' is certainly not false;
however, O Lord, I have not emerged as something separate from You.
Nevertheless, from You—indeed, from You—I have arisen; I am born from You alone."
The meaning: [33] Now, if I were Nārāyaṇa reclining upon the ocean of dissolution, then you would be from me...
The statement "You have arisen" is also appropriate;
however, suspecting that this might be otherwise, he says:
"You are indeed Nārāyaṇa, not merely for all embodied beings."
The Self is its sovereign, the witness of all the worlds;
Nārāyaṇa is its limb, because He is the refuge of men, the earth, and the waters—
and that too is the truth, not Your own illusion.
He is the sovereign even above Nārāyaṇa, the Lord who is the inner controller of all;
the meaning is "O Blessed One. Indeed, it is certain that you are that very Nārāyaṇa.
You are not [Nārāyaṇa],
but he is Nārāyaṇa, a portion of your own body.
Even if this is so, nevertheless, because I am born from his limb, my origin is from you alone, who are the possessor of that limb; such is the sense.
How is it that he is called Nārāyaṇa?
Or how is my distinctness from that [Self] established? To this he says:
"That which is the Self of embodied beings, the inner controller (antaryāmin) Puruṣa."
Therefore, because He is the refuge (*āśraya*) for this multitude of individual souls (*nāra*), He possesses the nature of Nārāyaṇa;
but that [nature] belongs to You, the direct Lord (*bhagavat*).
The sense is that even in His role as the inner controller (antaryāmin), He maintains indifference.
Furthermore, He is the witness of the entire world;
because He perceives the whole world directly, therefore [He is the witness].
He is called Nārāyaṇa because he knows (ayate) the human being (nara);
you, moreover, are his perceiver by means of that very portion.
But "not directly" means that he is of a different nature than that; therefore,
it would follow for me as well that you are not that Nārāyaṇa.
It is intended by you that the state of being Nārāyaṇa exists; how is that so? He indicates the answer to this very question by means of that same address: "O Sovereign" (adhīśa).

The Lord is the impeller; and because He is the source from which the movement (ayana) or activity of Nara proceeds, He is Nārāyaṇa. Furthermore, due to Your sovereignty even greater than His, You too are Nārāyaṇa.
Just as even a regional king (maṇḍaleśvara) is a monarch,
so too is he a monarch who is their sovereign;
for Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone is the manifest Supreme Lord himself.
For this reason also, He is *para* (the Supreme).
This will be demonstrated at length in the *Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha*.
Now, it may be asked: "The wise know that the principles (*tattva*) born from Nara are *nārāṇi*."
"His [original] abode was *nara*;
therefore he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. Likewise: "The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of *nara*."
Since they were his original abode, he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.

Anticipating the objection that his status as Nārāyaṇa is not well-known among those who are not Manmathas, he says: "And that [status] also [arises] from being the refuge (āyana) of men (nara), the earth (bhū), and the waters (jala).
This means that objects arise for the sake of men, and likewise, the water which was born from man—its...
If that state of being Nārāyaṇa arises from the *ayana* (the path or movement), then how could one explain it otherwise by abandoning the well-established [etymology]? To this he says: "True, not so.
That [state] [arises] from the waters of the ocean of dissolution, and so forth.
The meaning is that being the substratum is not real;
rather, such knowledge belongs to you alone as your *māyā*. Here, *māyā* refers to the power of delusion.
According to the *Viśvaprakāśa*, the word *māyā* signifies both deceit and compassion; thus,
by the very power of Your inconceivable nature, Your form— both limited and unlimited— is [manifested] through water and other elements.
The sense is "because of being undifferentiated.
The intended meaning of these four verses is that since the entire world, beginning with myself, is contained within Nārāyaṇa, he too is included within you.
Regarding Nārāyaṇa’s suchness, there is this Vedic mantra-verse:
"Whatever exists in this entire world, whether it is seen or even heard, Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all of that, both within and without. [34]
To provide proof for his own experience regarding the fact that the form of that [Lord] is not delimited by water and other elements,
he says: "O Blessed One, if that body of yours, which is the world, were present in the water, why was it not seen by me at that very time?"

Or was that form of yours, named Nārāyaṇa, which is the very foundation of the universe, clearly seen by my heart at that very moment, and why did it not appear again immediately? Thus [I thought], as it remained even within the water.

If that which exists were truly real, then why, O Blessed One of inconceivable sovereignty, was it not seen by me even as I entered through the path of the lotus stalk and searched for a hundred years?
And if that form were merely illusion (māyā-mātra), then,

according to the principle of the Trikāṇḍaśeṣa— that "māyā" refers to sorcery (chāmbarī) and cognition (buddhi)— it would be merely what is shown by a specific power (kalā) that manifests the false. In that case...
Or rather, was it seen by me at that very moment in my heart as the solid mass of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānandaghana), through awakening firmly rooted in the yoga of established samādhi;
or was it seen again immediately after the samādhi?
Thus it has been shown to us, yet not [ultimately] seen;
therefore, the meaning is that the illusory nature of your form and its limitation by a specific location are not real.
The introduction to this explanation is to be found in the history (*itihāsa*) in the third *skandha*.
Regarding the phrase "and that too is true" (*tac cāpi satyam*) here:
And that limb is indeed the Truth itself, not the illusory Virāj;
and regarding the phrase "if it were situated in water," if your body, which is of the nature of Existence (Sat), were situated in that water—
They explain that the world would exist as something included within the phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*).
Therefore, in this way, even the entire phenomenal expansion is contained within the divine form whose limbs are Nārāyaṇa; thus [it is] itself—
It was shown by the Blessed One that this was experienced by the illustrious Mother herself; thus he says:
"In this very [work], in the *Māyādhamanāvatāra*."
Indeed, the illusory nature (māyātva) of this entire phenomenal world— manifested externally and within the womb of Your mother— has been revealed by You.

In this very manifestation known as Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which brings about the cessation of māyā, regarding the connection with the entire manifest world seen both externally and within His belly, that which was previously described as its nature of being māyā—
Because it is produced by the five [senses], its being determinable is false;
this has been made manifest— that is, demonstrated— by you to your mother through that [teaching].
Therefore, you are situated within the world, whereas the world is outside of you; such is the nature of māyā.
In reality, however, it is difficult to conceive.
The sense is that, although you are in the middle state by virtue of your own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*), you are nonetheless all-pervasive.

By the phrase "by the nature of *māyā*," it is intended to illuminate that even in the Blessed Lord, who is the object of direct perception through your grace, it has been shown that the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is contained within his glorious form (*śrī-vigraha*), and that this is indeed the truth.
And in order to refute any other [opposed] perception, he establishes the matter at the very outset:
"In whose womb all this shines with its own nature, in whatever manner it may be..."
All that is likewise within you here;
how could this be without *māyā*?
For in your belly, all this world appears together with its self (the individual soul) as being accompanied by you.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "all that [which was previously outside] shines within you exactly as it did there.
This is the meaning: simultaneously with the perception of one's own inclusion within Vraja, Vraja [shines] within oneself.

Demonstrating that [the external world] is included within [the internal], and indicating through the deliberation of Śrī-Jananyā herself—expressed in passages such as *BhP 10.8.40*: "Is this a dream, or is it divine illusion? (*tac cāntar bahir darśanam kim svapna etad uta devamāyā*)—that it cannot be a dream, nor a product of illusion, nor a reflection of an original object, and thus must be one and the same, what [is it]?

In the passage beginning with "svapna" (dream), by the statement "whatever innate union with the Self there may be" (BhP 10.8.40), you yourself— concluding with this final position— simultaneously addressed your mother, thinking that through the very power of your inconceivable essential nature, you were all-pervasive even while remaining within a specific intermediate dimension.
He has demonstrated his own specific nature as possessing both aspects;
therefore, in the second [canto], he was instructed in such passages as "Take whatever is his mother's" (BhP 2.7.30) with the words "you have been awakened."
It has been said: therefore, just as all this appears within your womb, so it is here outside as well;
thus, by means of your own *māyā*, you are both contained within that and yet pervade it.
Without the power that veils reality, what could possibly exist?
The meaning is that nothing at all could exist.
He says, "I too have experienced it exactly like this," as follows: [37]
This very day, without you, what has not been shown to me as your illusory power (*māyā*)?
First you were alone; then all the friends and calves of Vraja appeared. You became that many four-armed forms, and I worshipped you together with all of them.
"Only that much was the universe; that immeasurable non-dual Brahman remains.
"Was it not shown to me, for my sake, this very day by You: 'What is there of this universe apart from You? Apart from You, its nature is *māyā*, and its manifestation occurs through *māyā* alone'?"
Rather, it has already been shown:
the meaning is that this world, which appears to the deluded as being distinct from you who possess a human-like form, is in fact nothing but Māyā.
"How can I, who possess this form of various manifestations, be such [the one and only]? To this he says:

"You are one. Whatever forms, such as those of the friends of Vraja and others, have manifested from You, all of that now remains at the time of concealment solely as this glorious embodied form (śrī-vigraha). That...
The meaning is that both are Brahman alone;
the intention is that this is because all phenomenal objects, being observed to undergo appearance, persistence, and disappearance, are pervaded by those characteristics [of Brahman].
Therefore, the intended meaning is that once his status as Brahman is established, his all-pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) is also established.
Now, one might object: at the beginning of creation, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are indeed distinct entities who serve as the causes. Thus...
Since there are some [beings] established [in their own nature] and others who are incarnations,
how can it be said that I alone am the cause of all?
To this, he says:
But to those who do not know your path, you appear through your own power as the Self within the non-Self, having spread out your illusion—
like the "I" in the creation of the world, like the act of ordaining the universe.
"You are this one, like the three-eyed [Śiva] at the end.
The word "you" (*tvam*) is connected with the word "shining" (*bhāsī*). This is because the connection between the agent and the action is precisely what is intended.
Because of its primacy,
and because the agent here is connected with the second person pronoun "you" (tvam) in the imperative mood,
the word "here" (atra) is not connected with that [pronoun], but rather only with the word "this" (eṣa).
And therefore, this Śrī-vigraha is not to be addressed as the Lord Himself,
because he lacks the status of being a direct incarnation of the Lord's qualities; [this applies] even today.
And because it is contradictory with the immediately preceding statement, "except for you" (*tvad-ṛte*).
Therefore, this is the meaning: [it is said] "toward those who do not know," that is, toward those who do not know your such-and-such nature (*svarūpa*), which is your station (*tvat-padavīm*).
The Self is indeed You Yourself, whose nature consists of those respective parts;
by means of the Self— that is, by means of those respective parts— [You manifest] *māyā*, the power that is the cause of creation and so forth.
The meaning is: having expanded and set in motion the Pradhāna— which is insentient in nature, devoid of self, and the material cause of Mahat and the rest—
it appears as if divided by way of its various distinct effects.
"At the end, 'like the Three-Eyed One'—
the sense is that in reality you alone exist in those various forms, but the deluded perceive them as separate from you."
For in the second [chapter], there is a statement by Brahmā: "Commanded by Him, I create; Hara destroys under His control;
and He who sustains the three powers protects the universe in the form of Puruṣa" (BhP 2.6.30).

Therefore, because he is one with the essential nature of the Blessed One, he is not designated as being like Brahmā or Viṣṇu. Thus, stating that just as there are incarnations through the qualities (guṇāvatāras), so too are there other incarnations, he says: "O Lord, likewise among the gods, the sages, and also among men."
O Creator, may those births of Yours among animals and even aquatic creatures serve to restrain the wicked and to bestow grace upon the people.
By the phrase "the birth of the unborn," it is made known that "birth" refers merely to manifestation. Now,
O Brahmin, what is being deliberated upon here by you,
given that my single form alone is all-pervasive?
It is impossible for the locus of manifestation to belong to the Truth (satya).
Likewise, in the world, the manner in which insentient objects such as jars become manifest is observed only in that way.
How is that so for other entities of consciousness, such as my own Śrīmūrti and others?
Just as many as there are...

"You have seen my manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) only to such an extent that you were amazed by them; thinking as if there were no others, you have come to perceive their limitation. Likewise, those who were previously my portions (*aṃśāḥ*) in the form of the cowherd boys and so forth, they themselves have become four-armed. Thus [he spoke] to someone.
The manifestation of form occurs for some at one time and for others at another;
furthermore, because its very essence consists of the single flavor of truth, knowledge, infinity, and bliss, every such form exists simultaneously indeed.
But how is it that you do not see everything at all times, and how is there simultaneity in that regard? To this he says:
"O Infinite One, O Blessed One, O Supreme Self, who knows?"
O Lord of Yoga, You display Your sovereign power throughout the three worlds; where, how, how many times, and when do You sport, expanding Your yogic illusion?

Where, how, how many, or when do You sport, expanding Your illusory power (*yoga-māyā*)—the inconceivable energy of consciousness—and manifesting it in various ways? Who in the three worlds knows Your *ūtayaḥ*, Your divine pastimes? The meaning is: no one at all.

The meaning of *Kenopaniṣad* 2.3—"That by whom it is not thought, by him it is thought; that which one knows, he does not know"—is as follows: here, by means of the four vocatives preceded precisely by the fact of its being difficult to know, he states the reasoning regarding these four points.
O Infinite One, whose glorious form consists of infinite manifestations embraced within itself!
This is the meaning: even a single primary form of the Blessed Lord simultaneously becomes composed of infinite forms.
In the same way, it was praised by Akrūra as "the one form appearing in many forms" (BhP 10.40.7).
Likewise, the Śruti says: "Being one, yet appearing in many ways.
Therefore, at whatever time, for whomever, and in whatever manner the stage of abiding occurs upon the arising of the fruit of their worship, then—
In that very way they see.

And likewise, regarding the Brahmasūtra [3.3.50], *prajñāntara-pṛthaktvavad dṛṣṭiś ca tad uktiḥ*, the Madhva-bhāṣya states: "Because of the difference in meditation, there is a difference in vision..."
And "division" is the illustrative example:

just as a single substance, such as a particular piece of fine cloth or a specific part of a peacock's tail, which consists of many colors yet has one color as its primary [quality], [is perceived differently] from a certain position...
To a person whose vision has been specifically directed [toward Him], He appears through a particular variety of color;
here, the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa— which corresponds to a specific uncut silk cloth or similar object— is permeated by various internal forms through His own primary manifestation.
It should be understood that these are other forms corresponding to the respective colors and complexions;
as it is said in the Śrī-Nārada-Pañcarātra:
"Just as a gem, when distinguished by qualities such as blue, yellow, and so forth, undergoes a differentiation of form,
so too does the All-pervading One undergo a differentiation of form through the differentiation of meditative absorption (dhyāna).
In this context, "gem" refers to lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*), while "blue, yellow, and so forth" refer to its qualities.
Thus, this reasoning has been stated as to "where" [the Lord resides]. In the very same way, observing the glorious descent of Vāmana, there is the statement of Śrī Śuka:
"That body which shines with ornaments and weapons..."
Hari, whose movement is divine, assumed the form of the unmanifest consciousness made manifest; by that very means, he became the dwarf boy (Vāmana) while they were looking on, like an actor.

And this is the meaning: that body which is the physical form (*vapuḥ-śarīram*) is not manifested by anything; that consciousness (*cit*) which is full bliss is its very nature (*tat-svarūpam*); and that which shines through ornaments and weapons—that body, at that time, [shines] even within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
He established and fixed it so that it would become manifest;
furthermore, Hari became a dwarf boy once again in that very same body.
By the word "eva" (only), transformation, changing one's dress, and so forth are excluded. When?
While the parents were looking on.
In that very form, there is the cause for that state;
for the scripture states: "The divine [powers] are supremely inconceivable, that which has passed, that which is present, and that which is yet to come," and so forth.
They consist of the manifestation and non-manifestation of various configurations that abide eternally within oneself alone.
He is one whose movements (gati) and gestures (ceṣṭā) [are such].

In that regard, there is a slight illustrative example for the aspect consisting of the mere manifestation of one's own nature (svadharma) when it is unobserved, namely, "like an actor" (naṭa). For even an actor—

He was one whose movement was most wonderful, divine, supremely astonishing, and manifested in the form of hand-gestures; even while assuming such a form and conforming to irregularities and the like, he displayed a variety of appearances.
As it demonstrates:
like a celestial actor or one who possesses a divine mode of movement, there is consequently the imitation of this or that [state].

Its form becomes exactly identical to that [of the Supreme Lord]. In this regard, since nothing other than the Supreme Lord possesses such identity in every respect, one should not elaborate upon the defect of partiality (khaṇḍatva) regarding the illustrative example.
Just as the spider (*ūrṇanābhi*)— which produces threads from saliva that results from the digestion of consumed insects—
is heard of in scripture as an example for the Supreme Lord’s unique capacity to create the world,
as in the passage beginning, "As the spider [creates from] its heart" (BhP 11.9.21), so it is here.

Thus, even the venerable Brahmā, intent on ascertaining the true nature of all forms, has said: "O Lord, you indeed abide within the lotus-heart of men purified by the yoga of devotion, appearing to them through the path of hearing and seeing."
"Whatever form Your devotees manifest through their intellect, O wide-striding Lord, You assume that very form for the sake of bestowing grace upon them.
(BhP 3.9.11) Here, "You assume" (*praṇayase*) means You lead forth preeminently; You reveal Yourself.

Since conceptual construction has been refuted by the phrase "the path seen in scripture," even though [the Lord] possesses all forms, there is an exception regarding those forms that are not desired by the devotees.
By the words of Śrī Kardama:
"O Blessed One, those very forms of yours are suitable for you, whatever forms please your own people, even though you are formless. [BhP 3.24.30]
Whatever forms are pleasing to Your own devotees, those alone are Your forms; they are Your beautiful and fitting forms,
and no others— this is the meaning.
And other such [manifestations] are to be understood as being like the contemptible form displayed to Rantideva;
and such a form is indeed merely illusory (*māyika*).
For it is said there: "To him who desired fruit, the lords of the three worlds, created by Viṣṇu’s māyā, revealed themselves as the givers of fruit" (BhP 9.21.15).

And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "The lords of the three worlds," namely Brahmā and the others, "by means of their *māyā*"; the meaning is that they first appeared in the form of outcastes (*vṛṣala*) and so forth for the purpose of testing his fortitude. Thus ends this [section].
The reason for their being unattractive is that they are "formless" (*arūpin*), meaning they are devoid of ordinary form (*prākṛta-rūpa*). And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
The sense is that because [the subject] is non-ordinary (aprākṛta), it is impossible for it to be censurable.
Now, regarding the position under discussion, the remaining three vocatives are explained in connection with the triad beginning with "how" (kathaṃ vā).

O Blessed One of inconceivable power! Since the manifestation of the Blessed One’s form and so forth cannot otherwise be accounted for, it follows that his own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*) alone is the cause— indeed, an inconceivable power.
This is the state of being; the reasoning for how this is so is as follows:
O Supreme Self, O You who descend into Yourself, even though each of the other incarnations—such as Puruṣa and the rest—possesses infinite power.
But in your case, because they are infinitely more so,
the thought is this: how could the manifestations of their appearance ever fall beyond the range of speech and mind?
The reasoning for this is: "How many are these?
O Lord of Yoga!
Even in a single form, there is the yoga characterized by the application of manifold forms.
[The Lord] whose nature is to rule by means of that power of His own essential nature (svarūpa-śakti) which is named [Māyā].
The intended meaning is this: just as Your primary form contains within it infinite forms, so too does Your partial form (aṃśa-rūpa). And therefore—

Whenever you have the desire to manifest a particular form of the fruit of a specific worship within a particular portion of yourself, at that very moment you manifest that form there; this is the reasoning for the question "When? [41]
Therefore, he concludes that even all those various things are included within that very form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; thus, the intended meaning here is summarized as follows:
consequently, this entire world is unreal by its very nature.
That which appears like a dream, devoid of intellect and filled with manifold suffering,
though it arises from Māyā within You— the infinite one whose body is eternal bliss and consciousness— appears as if it were real.
Since you are thus the embodiment of the reality of all things, whether they belong to the realm of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) or non-proliferation (*aprapañca*),

therefore this entire world appears as a remainder within you alone— who are infinite and whose very nature is the body characterized by eternal bliss and awakening; such is the logical connection (*anvaya*).
Being of what nature?
That which, though arising, repeatedly undergoes both manifestation and disappearance; for whatever is born and dissolved repeatedly in this, it [is said to be] in that.

The sense is that it appears thus on earth as if it were a modification of That. If one asks, "In that case, do I not possess the nature of being subject to modification? he says: "No, because of Māyā"—that is, by means of Māyā, which is a particular inconceivable power belonging to You, for it is heard in scripture that [the world] is indeed a modification of That alone.
Because of the phrase "since it has the word as its root" (Vs. 2.1.17), transformation is accepted at the outset;
therefore, it is like a dream precisely because of its repeated appearance and disappearance, and not merely because it is imagined through ignorance alone.

And by the principle stated in *Nyāyasūtra* 2.2.29, "And because of its dissimilarity, it is not like dreams and so forth," as well as because it is an effect of *māyā* whose function is ignorance (*avidyā*), it possesses eight faculties and acts to obscure the knowledge of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
For both of these reasons, it is a source of manifold suffering, even for that which appears as its semblance of happiness.
Because an object is of the nature of suffering, in the absence of Your existence it is non-existent by its very essence, like the horn of a hare;
yet, even though it is such, it appears as if real and as if eternal to the deluded—this is the remainder [of the sense].
And this is an illustration, because [the world] consists of the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth, which are composed of worldly activity and cognition.
It is like that which awakens knowledge because its nature consists of heaven and so forth, and it is like a face.
Thus, because it is delimited by another through the delimitation of its own form and power, this "Thy" [nature] is both delimited and undelimited.
"The body" (vapuḥ) is the meaning of the context. // 10/14//
Brahmā [said] to the Blessed Lord: //41// [42] Thus, in this way, omnipresence has been established because the very form of the Middle Way is the support of all;
it is also established because of its being all-pervading.
How wonderful it is that,
with a single body,
you appear simultaneously and separately in sixteen thousand homes!
"One woman married Him alone. [BhP 10.69.2] "This is indeed wonderful! What is it?
That Śrī-Kṛṣṇa, being truly one, should have married sixteen thousand women.
"Udāvahat" means he married her.
[The opponent asks: "Is there not something wonderful here? To this, he says: "In the houses," and so forth.
The phrase "in all numbers" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
To the question, "Let that be so; what follows from it?", he says:
"Each one separately."
Having stood [there], he performed the marriage rites beginning with the grasping of the hand;
for one might object that this is impossible in a sequential marriage, so he says "simultaneously" (yugapat) in response.

Now, one might object: "Even a master of yoga (yogeśvara), having assumed various bodies simultaneously, is able to perform such a feat; what is so extraordinary about this for you, whose feet are worshipped by masters of yoga?
To that, he says:
Regarding the phrase "with a single body":
if that is so, how did he create it with a single pervasive body possessing many arms and other limbs? Do not say such a thing.
In a single moment, he took the hands of these women in their various dwellings while in their presence.
This is because, as stated at the beginning of the words of the venerable Uddhava, "He is conformable by his own *māyā*," such conformity is well-established in each respective case;
having this in mind.
He refutes this with the introduction of the first word, "separately" (*pṛthak*).
He acted in such a way that he was seen as distinct and separate from each other by means of a single human-shaped body.
Therefore, since a single human body simultaneously pervades all places and all activities, it is a great marvel; such is the meaning of the sentence.

In this very way, the venerable Svāmī-carana has explained the nature of the fifth [form], the glorious form of the Blessed Lord who presides over the worlds, as taught in the prose passage beginning with "of them," and so forth—
[the form] of great opulence.
Because he was the lord of supreme sovereignty, he remained present everywhere through his single form alone; thus,
in a single moment,
those women were in various houses.
"Just as the immutable Lord, assuming such a form, married her... (BhP 10.59.42).
Here too, "assuming such a form" means precisely the illumination of that many locations simultaneously.
This is to be explained;
however, there is no difference in form as there is in the case of Nārāyaṇa and others. As it has been said:
"Manifestation in many places..."
When a single form is manifested at one time, that manifestation is said to be of the very nature of that [form] in every respect. (LBhāg 1.1.21)
This alone should be understood as the distinction between the aspect (ākāra) and the illumination (prakāśa) in other cases.
Śrī Nārada said: //42// [43] He spoke thus to him who was practicing the true dharmas in that very manner.
He beheld that very same One, the purifier of householders, present as the single reality within every house.
In all houses, it is that very same [Self] which is perceived, and not its parts;
it is one alone, and not manifold through a display of bodies, according to the Vedic scripture: "Being one, it is seen as many."
And because its omnipresence is established by the passage beginning with "Neither within nor without" (BhP 10.9.11), he clearly saw it; indeed,
through the power granted by the Blessed One, he experienced it directly.
But it is not merely that Nārada inferred this; such is the implied sense.
Therefore—
Having repeatedly witnessed the great manifestation of the yoga-māyā of Kṛṣṇa, whose prowess is infinite, the sage became [filled with wonder].

He became astonished and filled with curiosity. And in that context, *yogamāyā* is the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) which accomplishes the impossible; as for the Supreme Lord, He is referred to by the term *yogamāyā* in the third book [of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*], verse 3.16.37, regarding the departure of Sanaka and the others to Vaikuṇṭha.

It has also been explained by the Master himself that "the power of consciousness (cic-chakti) is spoken of by one who is engaged [in yoga]. Having seen this, the Sage, his curiosity aroused, was repeatedly struck with wonder;
for such a manifestation of bodily arrays (kāya-vyūha) occurs even among those [beings].
It occurs only in many [instances];
even without that, since its pervasiveness over all things is unprecedented even in its middling form, it is clear that this too is a cause for wonder and not otherwise.
This should be understood as it has been stated;
by this, the description "with hands and feet on all sides" is explained as referring precisely to such a glorious form (śrī-mūrti).

Therefore, the sūtra "Nor even on account of place does the Supreme have both characteristics, for everywhere" (Brahma Sūtra 3.2.11) has been interpreted by the proponents of reality (*tattva-vādins*) as follows:
even with respect to its locus...

For the form of the Supreme Self is indeed not different [from all things], since its nature is present everywhere; for the Śruti declares, "In this very way, Brahman exists in all beings. Viṣṇu, the Supreme, is one alone everywhere, without a doubt.
And by virtue of his sovereignty, one form of his shines forth like the sun.
Thus, from the *Mātsya Purāṇa*:
"Having shaken off the delusion of duality, I have attained that one Sun which, though appearing as many in every reflection, is truly one."

And thus from the *Bhāgavata* [BhP 1.9.42]. Likewise, regarding the sūtra "If it be said that [the whole is not one] because of difference, we say no, because each [part] is not spoken of as such" (VS 3.2.12), and also the sūtra "But in this way, it is one" (VS 3.2.13), their commentary (*bhāṣya*) is to be seen in that [work].
I behold this unborn one, who dwells in the heart of every embodied being that conceives of a self— like the single sun appearing manifold in every reflection.
"I have entered into samādhi, with the delusion of differentiation shaken off.

[BhP 1.9.42] This very Śrī Kṛṣṇa, seated right before me, is established in the heart of every embodied being as His own partial expansion (aṃśa) in the form of the inner controller (antaryāmī) of individual manifestations.
Some [meditate] on the Person, the size of a thumb, dwelling within the space of the heart inside their own bodies.

In accordance with the direction thus stated, although He appears as many distinct forms bound by various individual bodies, I have attained meditative absorption (*samādhi*) upon Him who is truly one and of undivided form;
this very embodiment of supreme bliss is all-pervading.
I am one who possesses consciousness, for I manifest here and there as the inner controller (antaryāmin) by means of my own specific forms inherent within me; hence,
I am one whose delusion regarding duality has been dispelled.
By His very grace, my delusion regarding duality has been dispelled;
that is, I am one whose delusion— characterized by the cognition of multiplicity arising from the impossibility of conceiving the Lord’s form as all-pervading— has been removed.
Regarding their pervasiveness, the reason is that they are perceived within the Self alone—
the supreme substratum— just as the single sun, appearing above trees, walls, and so forth, is seen there without obstruction and in its entirety.
The meaning is that [the manifestation] is seen in many ways as being obstructed and incomplete;
this illustration applies only to the aspect of the mere arising of the one [reality] in various places.
In reality, however, Śrī-...
The form of the Blessed One appears in such a way through inconceivable power;
however, the sun appears with its own nature as something distant and vast— this is the distinction.
Or rather, I have attained that very one whose nature was previously described— him who is seated right before me, though he dwells in the heart of every embodied being.
Although the form of the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) is of a different nature than this form,
nevertheless, I now perceive this very form here and there everywhere as the Great One.

This description of His splendor should be understood as intended to demonstrate that there is no difference in Him despite the difference in location; it is not meant to suggest a distinction between fullness and incompleteness.
Thus, Kṛṣṇa alone was perceived by her with eyes that did not blink.

In this context, through the opening and concluding statements such as "toward the Blessed One by means of the activities of mind, speech, and body," it is the glorious form (śrī-vigraha) itself that is introduced;
therefore, this verse should not be interpreted as referring to the Absolute Brahman. Thus...
Thus, because the states of being delimited and undelimited exist simultaneously, it is perfectly consistent here that the immobile is indeed mobile;
therefore, even though [the Lord] is all-pervasive, his true nature is established through his divine play (līlā).
Bhīṣma [speaks] to the Blessed Lord.
[45] [46] Thus, having established His eternity and omnipresence,
it has been explained in the same manner by the venerable Svāmī.
In the sixth [verse] of the eighth [chapter],
by saying "this [body] was not manifest, now it has become manifest; it did not exist,
now it exists," Brahmā intends to express the eternity and omnipresence of the Blessed One’s body.
For instance, there are two verses and their commentary: "To [the Lord] who is unborn, whose birth, maintenance, and dissolution..."
Homage, repeated homage to you, the one of great majesty, whose nature is beyond calculation, who is subtler than the subtlest, and who possesses the ocean of the bliss of nirvāṇa as your quality.
O Creator, O bull among men, this form of yours is to be worshipped by those seeking the highest good through both Vedic and Tantric yoga; may you,
together with us, [protect] the three worlds.
"I behold Him in that Universal Form"—this refers to the manifestation of the Śrī-mūrti (the Blessed Form), and not to birth and so forth as they exist for those like us; thus he says:
"He whose birth and other states do not exist."

Why? Because it is free from qualities (*aguṇa*); therefore, it means for the ocean of the bliss of *nirvāṇa*, which has the nature of the bliss of liberation beyond all others. Nevertheless, it is subtler than the subtle (*aṇor aṇimna*), meaning extremely minute.
Because it is difficult to know;
but in reality, it refers to Him whose form (*mūrti*) is a state (*dhāma*) that cannot be enumerated and which transcends all measure. Nor is this impossible.
Because its power is great and inconceivable, the word "form" (rūpa) establishes both the eternity and the immeasurability of that embodiment;
O bull among men!
"O Creator!

This form of Yours is always to be sacrificed to and worshipped by means of both the Vedic and Tantric methods for the sake of the highest good; therefore, the sense is that this has not arisen as something unprecedented."
Now, you gods are indeed renowned as objects of worship; it is true that all [gods] are included within this very one.
Thus he says: "O! Indeed, clearly, in you I behold us and the three worlds together. The reason for this is as follows:
The meaning is that since the universe is contained within Your form, this form of Yours does not become limited. This is the point.
