Here, by means of the metaphor of the "ocean" in the phrase "to the ocean of the bliss of nirvāṇa," the state of being solely the bliss of nirvāṇa is expressed.
Thereby, it is shown that even greater than that is the bliss of *sahaja* (innate joy).
As the venerable Dhruva said: "That bliss which belongs to embodied beings from the lotus-feet of You..."

"O Lord, may that [desire for liberation] not arise even while one is in Brahmā’s own glory through meditation or by hearing stories of worldly existence; rather, let it arise for those falling from their celestial chariot, shaken by the sword of Death. (BhP 4.9.10)

Likewise, by first saying "of the subtle, subtler" (*aṇor aṇimne*) and then stating "of immeasurable splendor" (*aparimeya-dhāmnaḥ*), it should be understood that Your state as the substratum of all transformations has been shown through Your great majesty, which consists in inconceivable power.
[47] Now, with two verses, He declares Your transcendence over both the gross and the subtle.
He is indeed neither god, asura, mortal, nor animal;
neither female, nor neuter, nor male; neither a living being, nor a quality, nor action; neither existent nor non-existent.

"May the remainder of the negation, which is without remainder, be victorious! Thus, Brahmā and the other gods— who possess the conceit of various distinctions of marks— beheld Gajendra, who was described as being without distinction.
"When these [demons] did not approach [him], because he is the soul of all, Hari appeared there as the embodiment of all the immortals"—
this is according to the two preceding verses beginning with "Of whom Brahmā and the other gods... and so forth.

Since the state of being the cause of all causes has been manifested, therefore He is none among the gods and so forth. His distinctiveness consists precisely in the absence of qualities such as being characterized by *sattva* or being material, as well as the absence of femininity and masculinity; that is, the lack of those various attributes belonging to *prakṛti*.

Therefore, it is said that he is not a eunuch (*ṣaṇḍa*). Consequently, there is no living being whatsoever; nor is there any quality such as *sattva* (purity) and so forth that serves as a cause for merit or demerit.
He says that it is neither a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) nor an action (*karman*);
this [self] is not a quality (*guṇa*) nor an action,
because those two [characteristics and actions] are also what set [the self] in motion.
This is the intended meaning. What need is there for more?
The point is that whatever exists here, whether gross or subtle, does not exist even as a single thing, because its nature is self-luminous.
However, that which remains as the limit for the negation of everything is called the "residue" (śeṣa);
and through Māyā, it consists of all those various things without exception.
"May he be victorious; may he manifest for my liberation.
And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "By whom [is manifested] that supreme reality which, as thus described, is devoid of distinctions such as the forms of gods and so forth."
That lordly elephant;
those who possess pride regarding the various distinctions of gender;
that which is both "various" and "distinction of gender."

And because they possess the conceit that He is distinct from the forms of the gods and others, those beings such as Brahmā and the rest did not approach Him at that time; for, being the Self of all, He consists of the bliss of the Supreme Self of all, and yet, by His Māyā, Hari— who is the essence of all the immortals— is distinct from them, as He is the Self of everything without exception.
"Thus it appeared.
When Śrī Gajendra thus prayed for manifestation, that which appeared in a form must indeed have been exactly like that; therefore it was well said: "Thou art beyond both gross and subtle objects."
Regarding the term "śrī-vigraha" (the glorious form):
otherwise, if it were devoid of hands and feet, that [form] would manifest in the mind and perform those [actions] merely as such; thus it is said, "consisting of His own will."
Although these two verses are separated by other verses, we have presented them as a pair because they are not separated in meaning.
First, Gajendra [worshipped] Śrī Hari;
second, Śrī Śuka. [48] Now, he also speaks of the reality of the nature of the inner self (pratyag-rūpa-tattva):
O Lord, how can You— the Supreme Self, the Transcendent One who is to be contemplated within the pure hearts of those whose vision is the Vedas by the masters of yoga— be directly perceived by me,
whose intellect is blinded by vast worldly calamities?

"May that one, for whom there is liberation from worldly existence, be visible here to me. And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "O All-pervading Lord (*vibho*), it is a marvel that You, who are the Supreme Self (*para ātmā*), have come within the range of my eyes—the path of my vision—even though You are perceived by the masters of yoga (*yogeśvaraiḥ*) through the eye of the Vedas (*śruti-dṛśā*)."

He is to be meditated upon as manifest within the stainless heart; for He is Adhokṣaja, meaning that whose [perception] is below— that is, prior to— akṣaja, which is knowledge born of the senses (aindriyaka).
For one who might attain liberation from worldly existence, worldly life would be something to be observed;
but for me, whose intellect is blinded by vast calamities and the suffering of existence like that of a chameleon, this is a marvel—such is the meaning. Thus ends this [verse].
The cause for such vision is stated in the *Nārāyaṇādhyātma*: "Although the Blessed Lord is eternally unmanifest, He is perceived through His own power;
apart from that, who could behold the immortal Lord, the Supreme Self? Thus it is said.
Even for the manifestation of such power, His grace alone is the cause.
Thus it is said in the Śruti: "One does not see His form with the eye."
"He is obtained by him alone whom He chooses;
to him this Self reveals His own form.
His form does not stand within the range of vision.
And such [passages] appear in some places.
Likewise, in the *Mokṣadharma*’s *Nārāyaṇīya* section, the Lord of Śveta-dvīpa spoke thus to Nārada:
This should not be understood by you: that I am seen as "possessing form. If I so desired, I could vanish in an instant; I am the Lord, the Teacher of the world.
"O Nārada, this which you see me as is indeed an illusion created by me;
you ought not to understand me as being thus endowed with the qualities of all beings.
Just as another person is seen because he possesses a form, so too is this [me]; this is what must not be understood by you."

And thus, even though he has manifested his own form, by stating its invisibility, he demonstrates that his true nature is indeed non-material (*aprākṛta*). Furthermore, regarding the vision of that [form], he says: "The sole cause is my own unimpeded will, which consists of supreme compassion. (i)
"Desiring thus": "May I perish," meaning may I attain invisibility;
therein lies one's sovereignty over the world.
And he states the reason for this distinctness with the words "O Lord," and so forth:
"Nevertheless, that you see me joined with the hosts of all beings— that which you perceive as being thus joined— is an illusion created by me alone."

The meaning is that such an appearance occurs solely through my own *māyā*. Regarding the passage beginning with "In that [case], it is not so," and so forth, it means that here I possess the power of deception.
For thus it is said in the Śrībhāṣya on that very point:
"Thereupon the eternal Lord of gods, the Blessed One, being pleased with him, revealed himself directly to him—he who is visible to no one else. [MBh 12.323.11]
With respect to that Uparicara Vasu, the word "himself" (svātmānam) is to be understood as the ellipsis; and following that, there is the speech beginning with "Vasu," etc.
"O Bṛhaspati, He cannot be seen by you or by us;
only he upon whom He bestows His grace is truly worthy to see Him.
Thus, even in the Śruti, attributes such as invisibility and so forth are stated to belong specifically to the Śrī-vigraha (the divine form).
And another scriptural passage states: "One does not see its form with the eye."
The king [addressed] the Blessed Lord. [48] [49] For this very reason, having negated ordinary forms and so forth, others are now established;
for Him, neither birth nor action exists.
Indeed, there is neither name-and-form nor even merit and defect;
nevertheless, He, by His own māyā, approaches them in due time for the sake of the dissolution and origination of the worlds.
This is the meaning:
transformation (*vikāra*) is the attainment of another state;
therein, the first transformation is birth (*janman*).
Action (*karman*) is the effort of one who is incomplete toward the purpose of fulfilling oneself.
A name (*nāman*) is a word designated by someone for the sake of conventional usage regarding an object perceivable by the mind.

"Color is the quality (guṇa) perceivable by the eye. In common worldly usage, a "quality" is seen as a specific property (dharma-viśeṣa) that is the cause of a substance's excellence and is based upon primordial qualities (prakṛti-guṇa) such as sattva and the rest.
And for that [Self], because it is always established in its own nature,
because it is full, because it is beyond the reach of even the mind, because it is self-luminous, and because it transcends primordial nature (prakṛti), those [defects] do not exist.
Nevertheless, the connection with the following verse is as follows: "Salutation to him who seeks and attains them" (BhP 8.3.9).
For this very reason, even the Śruti says: "Partless, actionless, peaceful," and so forth (ŚvetU).

Although that [nature] is negated in passages such as "soundless, touchless, formless, and imperishable" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.15), it is nevertheless enjoined in passages such as "possessing all actions, possessing all desires, possessing all odors, and possessing all tastes" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.4).

Regarding the phrase "virtue-fault" (*guṇa-doṣa*), since it is not ultimately real, the meaning is that virtue itself is the fault. Consequently, as will be explained, an inherently established fault (*rūḍha-doṣa*) is in no way possible. And so it is said in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"By virtue of his sovereignty, the Blessed One is designated by contradictory attributes;
nevertheless, defects can never be attributed to the Supreme in any way, whereas even contradictory qualities may be attributed to him from every perspective. Thus it is said.
And there are scriptural passages such as, "This self is free from evil" (ChāU 8.7.1), and:
"They call him Saṃyadvāma; he leads all things desirable; he is indeed this very one."
And because of such passages as, "He shines in all the Vedas" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.2), the word *bhāmaṇī* is used;
for this very reason, in expressions such as "possessing all fragrances," the words *gandha* and so forth denote specifically sweet fragrance (*saugandhya*) and the like. However, when...

However, the connection of the root *ṛch* (to reach/attain) with the quality as a defect is intended as a metaphorical identification (*rūpaka*), because it would contradict the literal sense and because [the defect] is intended to be established as being ultimately real.

Now, one might object that there is a contradiction between the existence and non-existence of those [states], such as birth and so forth, in a single locus; anticipating this, [the author] says: *tad-*...
He states the reason for this contradiction with the words "by His own māyā.

The cause therein is none other than His intrinsic power (svarūpa-śakti), which is difficult to conceive through fallacious reasoning and is known through the principle of "impossibility otherwise" (anyathānupapatti).

Therefore, the intended meaning is that because they are identical with his essential nature (*svarūpa*), they are distinct from those material elements; thus, it can also be said that even those [elements] do not exist. As in the *Śāṅkara-śārīraka* (Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya) at [Sūtra 1.4.15], "Because of the drawing back" (*samākarṣāt*), where the name—
It has been stated that because the object of a formal determination (*vyākṛta*) consisting of form is generally well-known to be independent,
with respect to the absence of such a determination prior to its arising, Brahman— which is indeed existent— is called "non-existent" in the Vedic revelation;
this should be understood in exactly the same way.

Therefore, in the *Śrī-Viṣṇu Purāṇa*, after stating, "O Sage, he has transcended both qualities and defects" (ViP 6.5.83), it further says, "For he is the embodiment of all auspicious qualities" (ViP 6.5.84). Likewise:
"Knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor, in their entirety... (ViP 6.5.85).
"Those things denoted by the word 'Bhagavat' are devoid of qualities and the like that are to be abandoned"—
thus it is stated in the *Pādma-Uttara-khaṇḍa*:
"He who is called 'devoid of qualities' (*nirguṇa*) in the scriptures is the Lord of the World."
"By the qualities (guṇas) associated with what is to be abandoned, which are natural (prākṛta), inferiority is expressed.
Nor should it be thought that the phrase "by its own māyā" implies a different meaning;
for [the Lord] is a mass of pure consciousness by His own nature.
We take refuge in the Blessed One, who consists of all accomplished purposes, whose desired ends are fulfilled, and by whose own splendor the flow of the qualities of *māyā* is eternally stilled.
Thus, from the words of the venerable Nārada:
"One who is intent upon one's own happiness," and so forth.
And because it contradicts the intention of the speaker,
the meaning is therefore that [it arises] in every way from the power of consciousness (cic-chakti).
Hence, even by the Masters, it is referred to by the term "yoga-māyā" as consciousness—
Power has been explained.
[Objection: But does it not follow that occasional occurrence is also perceived?
To this he says: "at all times, it is indeed eternal."
The meaning is that it attains [this state] and never abandons it;
furthermore, one should understand that the manifestation of the power of its own nature and [the attainment itself] stand in a relationship of mutual causality.

Now, how can birth and action be eternal? For they are indeed activities; and the nature of being an activity is established only through the commencement and completion of each respective part, [and thus they cannot exist] without their own essential form.
There is the fault of diminution;
this is not a defect,
because the Blessed One possesses infinite forms of excellence.

This is because of the infinity of His manifestation, and because of the infinity of His births, activities, and characteristic pastimes; and because of the infinity of the manifestations and appearances of those various places for His pastimes and those various associates of His pastimes, which exist within the infinite Vaikuṇṭhas of the infinite material world.

Since this is so, even though the commencement and completion of those respective manifestations of form occur simultaneously, as long as the portions of those births and activities are not fully completed—
or rather, while they are being completed— another [birth] is already commenced elsewhere; such is the case with the Śrī Bhagavān.
Because there is no interruption, those births and karmas exist as truly eternal;

it should be understood that among them, some are commenced with certain distinctive characteristics, while others are commenced with uniformity. [The remainder of the sentence regarding] the qualification—

Due to the difference [in functions] and the unity of the qualifier, there is only a single form which, through a distinction in its manifestations (*prakāśa*), becomes the locus for separate actions. This has been explained in such passages as, "How wonderful! By means of a single body... and so forth.

Then, due to the differentiation of activities, a differentiation of conceit (*abhimāna*) is perceived within the various manifestations of light (*prakāśa*) that consist of those respective activities. This being so, in each instance, there arises an awakening of aesthetic relish (*rasa*) produced by the sequence of divine play (*līlā*).
Now, one might ask: "How is it that those very same [entities] undergo birth and activity? It has been stated that they are distinct because they have begun separately.
To this it is replied:
even for actions that are identical in form, there is unity despite their being manifested at different times,
as in the case of Śaṅkara’s *Śārīraka*.
The word "cow" was uttered twice, but not two "cow" words;
likewise, cooking was performed by him twice, but not a twofold cooking was performed by him.
Since [the world] will come into being through dependence,

it follows that the eternality of birth and karma is indeed logical. For this very reason, even in the scriptures and other sources, the injunction to worship past divine sports (līlā) is appropriate.

And so it has been stated in the Madhva-bhāṣya: "Because they are eternal by virtue of their relationship with the Supreme Self, it is appropriate that qualities such as being Trivikrama and so forth are to be combined [in meditative worship] even when they pertain to those forms."
And this is authorized by the Śruti through this very [passage], "that which has passed and that which is to come," meaning that they are to be subsumed within meditation as objects to be grasped.

The meaning is as follows: therein, that birth is distinct from ordinary birth; it is a mere manifestation either by imitating an ordinary birth or, in some cases, without such imitation, according to the Vedic scripture: "Though unborn, he is born in many ways."
It is as follows:
"Just as the full moon appears in the eastern quarter, so did Viṣṇu, who dwells in the heart of all, manifest from Devakī, who was like a goddess" (BhP 10.3.8).
And so it is said:
"In order to make true the words spoken by his own servant, and to demonstrate the all-pervasiveness of the Self within all beings,"
"Bearing an exceedingly wonderful form that was neither animal nor human, he remained invisible within the pillar in the assembly hall" (BhP 7.8.17);
and regarding the phrase "having entered the potency of Kardama" (BhP 3.24.6), this refers to the descent of Śrī Kapiladeva.
In this context, it should be explained that [the Lord] was brought under the power of the potency of devotion by the mud;

however, the application of the word *vīrya* (potency/semen) is intended to imply, through a pun (*śliṣṭa*), His well-known status as a son. Likewise, the distinction of His action is that it consists solely of the play of the bliss of His own essential nature (*svarūpa*). That...
As it is said: "But as in the world, his activity is mere sport" (VS 2.1.33). And this has been explained by the proponents of reality (tattvavādins):
just as in the world, the playful activity of one who is intoxicated—such as dancing and so forth—proceeds solely from an overflow of bliss and not out of regard for any external purpose.
The same applies to Īśvara;
and in the Nārāyaṇa-saṃhitā it is said:
"Hari does not indeed depend upon any purpose for the creation and so forth."
It performs a dance out of sheer bliss, like that of one who is intoxicated.
"How could one who is full of bliss have any desire for worldly purpose here? Even those who are liberated might still have unfulfilled desires; how much more so the case of Him, the Self of all?
Thus, one should not suggest His lack of omniscience by using the analogy of a madman.
Because [the Lord] sports solely by virtue of the overflow of the bliss of His own nature, without even considering His own purpose;
and because, even in the illustration of inhalation and exhalation, that same fault would arise in states such as deep sleep. Therefore:
His pastimes are inherent to His own nature as the bliss of His essential form;
and the Śruti says: "This is indeed the very nature of the Divine; what desire can there be for one whose every wish is fulfilled?"

In this context, since the activities such as glancing— which consist of the direct movements of the Lord— occurring during the creation of the material world and so forth are in reality of that very nature, it follows by the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutya*) that the same applies to those occurring in Vaikuṇṭha and other realms.
As it was said by the wives of the Nāgas: "For the sake of dwelling in the indeterminate" (BhP 10.16.47).
For this very reason, it is appropriate that even Śrī Śuka and others were impelled by passion (*rāga*) toward hearing those pastimes.
And therefore—
"And thus the poets describe the births and activities of the unborn and non-acting Lord of the heart, who are secrets of the Vedas" (BhP 1.3.35). Here,
this very same explanation should be applied to the verse from the Janma-guhyādhyāya as well.

By the two immediately preceding verses beginning with "yatreme sad-asad-rūpe" (BhP 1.3.33–34), there is the negation of the nature of both the existent and the non-existent— which are superimpositions upon the Self produced by ignorance— precisely through the correct knowledge of the true nature [of reality].
From this cause, the vision of Brahman arises;
and as it has been stated— that the perfection of one's true nature occurs only upon the cessation of illusion (māyā).
In this very way, the seers who delight in the Self describe the births and deeds of the Supreme Self, the Lord of the heart,
for the purpose of negating each of those [worldly pursuits] so that one may find rest in Him.

The meaning is that when [this] is indeed present, there occurs the perfection of experiencing the births and activities associated with that; here, "perfection" (*sampatti*) refers to direct perception.
Therefore, [there is] the bliss of the Blessed One, which surpasses the bliss of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
The meaning is that those very things are of the nature of playful manifestation (vilāsa).
For this very reason, because of their distinction from the ordinary (prākṛta), it is said to belong to the "non-doer" (akartṛ) and the "unborn" (ajana).
Therefore, it is said, "even those secrets of the Vedas.
For instance, regarding the two verses beginning with "As you have been declared by me in the praise of Akrūra" (BhP 10.48.23–24), they were raised in this manner within the commentary itself.

[An objection: "In that case, are my incarnations and their deeds merely imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*), like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell? [Reply: Certainly not, certainly not; rather, this is Your sport (*līlā*. Thus he says in two verses: "By You it was said... and so forth. And in the same way, it is stated in the *Vaiṣṇava* [Purāṇa] with reference to the identity of the Lord's own nature:
"He whose names, actions, and essential natures are not within the scope of any means of valid cognition—that Viṣṇu is the one dwelling in your womb. (ViP 5.2.19).
Alternatively, there is a variant reading: "rūpa-karma" (form and action) instead of "nāma-karma" (name and action).
This very point is intended by the Śrī Gītā Upaniṣads: "He who thus knows in truth my divine birth and action... (Gītā 4.9).
Likewise, the distinctiveness of the Name consists in its being self-established by virtue of resting upon a multitude of qualities that are beyond the reach of speech and mind;
as it is said in the *Vāsudevādhyātma*: "Because its qualities are not well-known [in the world]."
"He is proclaimed as Anāmā (Nameless)"—in the Brāhma [Upaniṣad]: "He is Nameless because he is not well-known; he is Formless because he is devoid of the elements."
O Lord, that wherein conceptual constructions such as name, genus, and so forth do not exist—that is the supreme, eternal, and unchanging Brahman; you, O Unborn One, are that.
"Since there is no comprehension of any object whatsoever without conceptual construction (kalpanā),
you are therefore praised by the names Kṛṣṇa, Acyuta, Ananta, and Viṣṇu.
This statement from the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa is not contradictory even following the preceding [verse].
For in this case, if the meaning were understood merely at first sight, the word "conceptualization" (kalpanā) would be redundant.
Names, genus, and so forth do not exist;
for by this very [statement], the intended meaning is established,
since the words "Brahman," "unborn" (aja), and so on, [function] by themselves.
And it is accepted as being a name that expresses the ultimate reality; furthermore, in passages such as "the one unborn, red, white,
and black" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5), the genus characterized by non-birth is indeed clearly observed.

Thus, since it has been stated that conceptual constructions such as "name" and so forth do not exist, the statement regarding the conceptual construction of names like "Kṛṣṇa" would be contradictory; or else, how could there be such praise through conceptual construction, given that conceptual construction is unrestricted?
Furthermore, because conceptual construction is unrestricted, why is the non-restriction of names such as "Kṛṣṇa" asserted?
Therefore, this meaning follows from the fact that they are the very nature of name and action;
just as, for example, "Kṛṣṇa" and so forth are names within the category of names.
Births—such as the divine state, the human state, the kṣatriya state, and so forth—are merely playful manifestations; for Him and others, such conceptualizations do not exist.
Rather, as stated in the direction of the teaching that "all purposes are fulfilled by His own inherent nature," He is eternally established in His true essence.

The meaning is that those very things are the manifestations (*vilāsa*) of power (*śakti*). And therefore, because the comprehension of every perceived object— apart from mental construction (*kalpanā*), which is the arrangement of names and so forth— is merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*).
Cognition does not arise.

Therefore, for that very reason, having disregarded everything consisting of conceptual construction— both the name and the object denoted by that name— as being beyond the scope of determination by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [it exists] by virtue of its nature as Veda.
You alone, who are self-established, are worshipped by the sages and the Vedas through well-known names such as Kṛṣṇa and others which are themselves self-established and indicative of You;
you are not praised by means of names consisting of mere mental constructs.
But you too are praised by others for those very same qualities of greatness; thus, it is through them alone that your own greatness becomes manifest.
Or rather:
"You are worshipped by those very ones whose greatness is made manifest.
Here, by those names which are extremely well-known in the scriptures, the Blessed Lord himself is immediately recognized;
and it is heard that even in their conventional usage and so forth, such power is attributed to them.
It should be understood that these [qualities] are established by themselves, whereas for others they are merely conceptual constructs.
Or else, O Lord:
That in which the conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) of name, genus, and so forth do not exist— that is You, the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is the specific totality (*kavalaviśeṣarūpa*).
The reason for its being beyond the scope of those various conceptual constructions is as follows:
It is called "vikāri" (subject to modification) because it performs its play (*līlā*) with particularity; it is called "avikāri" (unchanging) because it does not become so [in that way].
It is called "aja" (unborn) because it is not born—that is, it does not manifest—in that form.

The sense is: therefore, depending on what indeed could conceptual constructions (kalpanā) such as name, genus, and so forth be made there? And without those respective conceptual constructions, there would not even be the mere apprehension of any object whatsoever in its state as a mere thing (vastu-mātra), let alone of such a nature as yours, which is Brahman.
However, conceptual constructs such as names, universals, and so forth, do not constitute the intrinsic nature or properties of anything; for this reason,
even when cultivated through convention and other means, they— like you— bestow all human goals (puruṣārtha) in their respective ways.

The meaning is that you are praised by the eternally established Śrutis, Purāṇas, and other texts through names such as Kṛṣṇa which express specific qualities; you are not, however, extolled by those [texts] which propound a featureless reality and are entirely composed of mere conceptual construction.
However, it should be understood that the names of the four [deities], Kṛṣṇa and the others, are merely illustrative (upalakṣaṇa),

because the power of names such as Nārāyaṇa and others is likewise heard in the context of conventional usage (sāṅketika) and so forth; this is established by the statement "the Lord Upavarṣa says that sound is indeed phoneme" and by the statement "and because of its eternity."
By logical reasoning, the eternity of this name—which consists of letters that are the very essence of the Veda—is established by its nature as phonemes (*varṇa*).
Likewise, in the *Gopālatāpanī-śruti*, in the context of the eighteen-syllable name composed of phonemes, there is a statement of Brahmā:
"In those syllables, he reveals the form of the future world" (GTU 1.26).

In this regard, because it is distinct from the world—which consists of sound and so forth and arises at the time of its manifestation—it possesses self-established existence; likewise, its distinction from that [world] consists in its non-difference from the essential nature of the Blessed One. As it is said in the Śruti:
Oṃ! O Viṣṇu, we partake of your benevolence—your great splendor which is known by name as "the Distinct"—even though we do not fully comprehend it. Oṃ Tat Sat, and so forth.
This is the meaning.
O Viṣṇu! Your name is indeed *cit*, the very nature of consciousness; therefore, it is *mahaḥ*, whose form is self-luminous.
Therefore, those who know even a little of this name— but not by way of correctly reciting its greatness and so forth—
nevertheless, while speaking it, [they utter] only that.
By merely practicing the repetition of the syllables, we cultivate and attain the wisdom that has that [Reality] as its object;
for that very Reality, manifested by the *praṇava*, is itself inherently established.

Therefore, just as there is a manifestation of the Śrīmūrti [the Divine Form] even when fear, hatred, and so forth arise, it is likewise present in conventional designations (*sāṅketika*) and the like.
The granting of liberation is heard [in scripture].
Thus it is said in the Pādma:
"Even one whose mind is elsewhere, or who is angry, who should always glorify Hari..."
"He too shall attain liberation through the destruction of bondage, just like the Lord of Cedi.
Likewise, even a single direct perception of his name brings about the destruction of saṃsāra, just as it does for the illustrious Blessed One.
As it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa: "By whomsoever the two syllables 'Ha-ri' are uttered even once,
by him the girdle has been fastened for the journey toward liberation."
Thus, in the Śruti, with reference to the Praṇava, it is said:
"Om—this is the name of Brahman nearest to it;
because as soon as it is uttered, it delivers one from the fear of saṃsāra, therefore it is called Tāra," and so forth.

It is more so; nor should its status as an *arthavāda* (eulogistic statement) be questioned, for according to the *Padma Purāṇa*, such an *arthavāda* would result in the commission of an offense regarding the name of Hari, as it states:
"He who, out of delusion, does not follow [the path] even after having taken the Name, undergoes rebirth."
"Even one whose karma has been burnt by the fire of knowledge becomes a Brahma-rākṣasa if he goes [to the forest] toward the Supreme Lord"—
as stated in Purāṇic passages authenticated by such works as the *Śrī-Viṣṇu-bhakti-candrodaya*.
One should understand that the conceptualization of great offenses, their exegesis, and so forth, constitutes an obstacle.
For this very reason, its nature as bliss— which is witnessed by the Great Heart (Mahā-hṛdaya)— should be understood as an obstacle [to such conceptualizations],
just as the nature of bliss belonging to the Śrī-vigraha is witnessed by the Great Heart.
Thus it was said by the venerable Śaunaka: "Alas, this heart is as hard as stone, since it is not shattered even when seized by the names of Hari."
When there is no transformation— neither tears in the eyes nor horripilation on the body— then [one has not attained it].
For this very reason, according to the reasons explicitly stated in the *Prabhāsa Purāṇa*, it is described as the fruit of all the Vedas.
And thus, the very nature of the Blessed One has been established:
this most sweet auspiciousness of all auspicious things, the true fruit of the creeper of all the Vedas, is the essence of consciousness.
O best of the Bhṛgus, the name of Kṛṣṇa, even if chanted but once—whether with faith or even playfully—can deliver even a mere human being. Thus it is said.
Therefore, the name is indeed the very nature of the Blessed One.
This has been clearly stated in the Śrī Nārada-pañcarātra with reference to the eighteen-syllable mantra:
"For it is evident that the Blessed One himself is indeed Nārāyaṇa manifest, revolving within [our] mouths in the form of the eight-syllabled [mantra].
And in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, with reference to the Praṇava: "The syllable 'Om'—this is all."
[Maṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 1] / "The syllable *oṃ* is indeed all this" [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.3].
For the *praṇava* is the lower Brahman, and the *praṇava* is remembered as the higher.
The *praṇava* is without prior, without interior, without exterior, without posterior, and imperishable.
For the *praṇava* is indeed the beginning of everything, as well as its middle and its end;
having thus known the *praṇava*, one attains that immediately thereafter.
One should know the Praṇava as the Lord, situated in the heart of all;
having realized the all-pervading Oṃkāra, the wise man does not grieve.
He by whom the syllable Om is known— that which is measureless, of infinite measure, and the auspicious cessation of duality— is a sage, and no other person.
Thus, according to [Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 26–29],
it should not be thought that this statement regarding the mere phoneme is merely a form of praise, based on the impossibility of such respective capacities existing in the Supreme Lord alone.

Just like other incarnations, this [manifestation] is an incarnation of the Supreme Lord Himself in the form of a caste; for when this point is accepted on the basis of that very scriptural authority, its possibility follows from His non-difference [from the Lord].
Therefore, there is indeed non-difference between the name and the named.
As it is said in the Pādma [Purāṇa]:
"Kṛṣṇa is the wish-fulfilling gem, whose form is the essence of consciousness."
It is full, pure, and eternally liberated, because name and the named are non-different. Thus it is said.
The meaning of this is as follows: His very name is a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) because it bestows all objects of desire.
Not only is He like that, but Kṛṣṇa, who is characterized by consciousness and other such qualities, is Himself directly [the wish-fulfilling gem].

In that regard, the reason is "because of non-difference. Now, one might ask: how can such things as names and so forth be produced by the sense organ of the Person (puruṣendriya)? It is not so, because the Veda alone manifests within the sense organs of the Person and the like belonging to the Blessed One. As it has been said:

In the eleventh book, the Śrī Bhagavān Himself begins with the verse, "The Word-Brahman is very difficult to understand" (BhP 11.21.36), and continues: "It has been extensively augmented by Me, the Brahman of infinite power."
"Among all beings, she is perceived as if filled with distinctions through the form of sound. [BhP 11.21.37] Thus it is said.
In the sixth chapter of the twelfth book, regarding the context of the Vedas being lost and the exhaustion of lifespans (BhP 12.6.47), the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states:
"One might then object that, because they originate from human intellect, they would not be worthy of respect; anticipating this, [the author] says: 'Impelled by Acyuta residing in the heart.'"
In passages such as "For whom and by what was this manifested? (BhP 12.13.19), it is understood to be by means of that very form, just as in the phrase "in that form" (*tad-rūpeṇa*).
Having all this in mind, it is stated in the *Garbha-stuti*:
"Neither name nor form [exist] through qualities, births, or actions."
"O Lord, although the path of that witness is to be inferred through mind and speech when it is to be described, people nevertheless perceive his activity. [BhP 10.2.36]
Even for that which is of such a nature, its distinctness consists in its being manifested by the very power of its own essential nature, characterized by self-luminosity;
and this has been shown previously.

Therefore, in the second [skandha], for the sake of purifying the reality of the self (*ātma-tattva*), the Blessed One spoke of *ṛta*, as in this passage: "Displaying his form to Brahmā, he who is established in truth (*ṛta*) because of his unswerving vow. [BhP 2.9.4]

And the commentary [states]: As for what was said in the eighth chapter—that since even the Supreme Lord is no different from others in having a connection with a body, how could liberation come about through devotion to Him?—[the answer is:
"That which existed from His belly..."

Regarding the verse beginning with "padmam" (BhP 2.8.8), he says: "for the sake of purifying the reality of the self. This means that for the sake of purifying the reality of the self—that is, for the sake of knowledge of reality—it must indeed be so. What is that which the Blessed One spoke to Brahmā as his own worship through austerity and other means?
Doing what? Manifesting the form of *ṛta*, which is truth and a mass of consciousness;
the reason for this manifestation is that he was sustained by unswerving austerity.
Being thus served,
this is the meaning:
the soul's connection with a falsely conceived body arises through ignorance (avidyā).

However, there is a great distinction in that the manifestation of the Lord’s form as a mass of consciousness occurs through His yogamāyā; therefore, the attainment of liberation (mokṣa) is possible through worshiping Him. Such is this [teaching].
Therefore, even by the venerable Ānakadundubhi, it was established in the two verses beginning with "He, for the sake of the stability of the three worlds" (*BhP* 10.3.17–18);
for here is the meaning: he...

O Creator of the manifestation’s creation, maintenance, and dissolution, when you desire its preservation for the sake of the stability of the three worlds, then— having employed your own *māyā*, the power of *māyā* residing within yourself— you assume your own white color and sustain (protect) the caste of Brahmins and others created by yourself, who are devoted to *dharma*. In this regard:
One's own *māyā* should be understood as consisting of *sattva* alone, because it has been extracted [from the primordial state] and because it is employed [for manifestation].
Then, when you desire creation, you assume the form of the *vipra* and other castes— red and full of desire— having augmented it with *rajas* through your own *māyā*, which consists of *rajas*.
And when you desire dissolution,

then you assume that form which is composed of darkness— black, soiled, and devoted to sin; or else, when you desire stability for yourself in the form of Śrī Viṣṇu, [you assume] the white and pure [form].
The meaning is that he is free from the confusion of qualities (*guṇa-saṅkara*).
This is because, like Śiva-Brahman, there is an absence of association with those qualities for him.
In this very way, it was established by the venerable Śukadeva: "Śiva, endowed with Śakti, is eternally possessed of the three genders."
In passages such as "He is concealed by the qualities" (BhP 10.88.3),
and "For Hari is indeed devoid of qualities, the direct Puruṣa, beyond primordial nature" (BhP 10.88.5), and so forth; for this very reason—
With smiles as bright as moonlight and glances from reddish-cornered eyes,
[she appeared] as if [to scatter] the dust of her own desires.
"From the two *sattvas*, the creators and protectors [arose]" (BhP 10.13.50).
Here, the *sāttvika* and *rājasattva* natures are merely figuratively imagined (*utprekṣita*), and not established as actual realities. Regarding the color (*varṇa*)...

It is form (*rūpa*), not mere luster; for even if one accepts that it consists of qualities (*guṇa-mayatva*), the specific shape (*ākāra*) that manifests those qualities must also be taken into account, and thus it should not be explained as merely "white color. [Śrī-]

This is because Viṣṇu, who is the embodiment of the Supreme Self (paramātman) appearing through the modes of nature (guṇāvatāra), is established in the *Paramātma-sandarbha* as reclining upon the Ocean of Milk (*kṣīroda-śāyin*), where he is universally renowned for his dark complexion; whereas Rudra, the cause of the destruction of people, is universally renowned for his white complexion, which constitutes a direct contradiction to that.

For likewise, in the Sandhyopāsana as taught by Gobhila, there is no intention here for Brahman to be of a red color; nor is there a fixed rule that specific qualities must correspond to specific colors,
especially in the case of those who are supremely tamasic.
Because it is heard that Baka and others were dark-complexioned;
the meaning is that by Your own *māyā*, out of compassion for Your devotees, You bear, maintain, and manifest [Yourself] in the world.

"Red" means being full of passion (*rajas*), characterized by an abundance of desire for creation and so forth; "black" means being full of darkness (*tamas*), meaning it is devoid of the manifestation of its own true nature.
Smoke is more violent than that which is earthly.
Therefore, fire consists of the three qualities (*trayīmaya*).
For it is said: "From darkness (*tamas*) comes passion (*rajas*), and from that, goodness (*sattva*), which is the vision of Brahman" (BhP 1.2.24).
Now, how can you describe that which deludes the world by means of a sentence with another meaning?
For from this, the sense also arises: "At this time, for the sake of the destruction of people, this black color has been assumed by me through the quality of darkness (tamas)."
Anticipating this objection, he offers a rebuttal by saying, "You are his" (BhP 10.3.21). "Being carried away" means being moved here and there.
The underlying sense is this: let alone the case of Brahman...
There is another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that demonstrates [the self] consists of dense and pure sattva;
for even if one accepts forms corresponding to the qualities (guṇas), dissolution is a cause of mere suffering and is of the nature of deep sleep.

In that regard, there is an occasion for that purpose; however, for this time, because it is the cause of the world's happiness through protection not yet performed by you, and because it is the fitness for the destruction of the demons composed of darkness (*tamas*), there is no occasion for that purpose [of liberation] until those demons themselves obtain grace consisting of liberation— which transcends all qualities— under the pretext of their own slaughter.
It occurs, like the case of the Saindhava man; thus it has been said:
"At the time of the victory of *sattva*, [one sees] the celestial sages; at that of *rajas*, the asuras."
"Yakṣas and rākṣasas partook of that [tamas], according to the nature of that time" (BhP 7.1.8).
Therefore, this color is not produced by *tamas*; rather, through *rajas* and *sattva*, they become red and white respectively—this is the position of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*).

And thus, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya-pramāṇa*), the conclusion reached here is that it is precisely the manifestation of the power of its own nature (*svarūpa-śakti-vyañjitatva*); such is the intended meaning.
In the same way, the venerable [text]—with regard to that very same point—[states]:
Queen Devakī also, out of agitation, had already revealed it previously: "That form which they call unmanifest and primordial" (BhP 10.3.24).
Now, let us return to the subject at hand.
Likewise, there is a distinction in quality: even for those who delight in the Self, there is the state of being composed of the elements, which is accessible through the signs of attraction.
As it is said in the words of Śrī Sūta:

In passages such as "The sages who delight in the Self" (BhP 1.7.10) and "Whose mind is captivated by the qualities of Hari" (BhP 1.7.11), and for this very reason it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
Indeed, all virtues are joined with the Supreme Person by virtue of His sovereignty;
faults are never joined to Him in any way, for He is the Supreme.
Some unwise people claim that both virtue and fault exist through illusion alone;
yet neither illusion nor the master of illusion exists therein, so how could those two belong to him?

Therefore, everything is not produced by illusion, nor does everything arise from the power of illusion; for the Lord is indeed free from illusion, and therefore they know him as the Supreme. Thus it is said.

Now, this is the remainder of the explanation for the present verse, "If [it] does not exist. Thus, their distinction from the material world has been established by way of their being the manifestation of the play of the power of their own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Regarding that, an objection is raised:

[Objection: Let it be that these [powers] are indeed identical with His own essential nature; nevertheless, since the essential nature itself is already complete, what purpose is served by attaining each of them? To this, He says: "for the emergence and dissolution of the world.
Here, "the world" refers to the devotee.
For that person as well, "destruction" (apya-ya) means the destruction of saṃsāra, and "arising" (sambhava) preceded by that means the attainment of the bliss of devotion.

Since the root *bhū* signifies "attainment," this [term] is also an elliptical indication for the sake of attaining that; it is also for the purpose of the excellence of the bliss of devotion even for those who are eternal associates.

Thus it was said by the illustrious Arjuna in the first book: "Likewise, this incarnation of Yours is for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth and for the constant remembrance of Your own devotees who possess undivided devotion" (BhP 1.7.25).

The meaning of this is as follows: just as other incarnations such as those of Nara-Nārāyaṇa and others are, so too is this incarnation the direct manifestation of you yourself, the Supreme Lord known as Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
for the sake of the earth who is your supreme devotee.
Although born with the desire to remove the burden [of worldly existence],
he repeatedly and constantly meditates upon his own kinsmen and devotees for the sake of the bliss of his own worship.
[Objection: In that case, since the very happiness of the devotees would have become the sole purpose, how could it be justified that Pūrṇānanda still possesses the notion of a purpose here?
To this, he says: "of those whose state is non-dual" (ananyabhāvānām).

Thus [it is said]. Otherwise, the fault of lack of compassion (*akāruṇya*) would attach to Him—the crown jewel of the omniscient, who is free from defects—on account of His indifference toward those who depend solely upon Him; such is the sense.
Even though He delights in the Self (*ātmārāma*),...

Because it is remembered that "the scope for the quality of compassion exists, and even qualities that are contradictory are all brought together," this [compassion] is possible only in the Blessed Lord, who is a treasury of diverse qualities;
but elsewhere than Him, it is not so.
That very portion of his qualities consisting of his conduct— which is sung aloud with wonder at every step by the Vedas and other scriptures—
and which continues to attract everyone from Brahmā down to the common folk; that...
It has been said by Him Himself:
"Even those who worship Me do not truly worship; how much less so those who do not worship?
For they delight only in themselves, their desires are already fulfilled, they are ungrateful, and they are betrayers of their gurus."
"But I, O friends, do not favor even those beings who worship Me for the sake of following after them," and so forth [BhP 10.32.19–20].
Therefore, for Him who is supremely capable, His compassion— characterized by the happiness of His devotees— [is manifest].

That which is called "having a purpose" (prayojanakatva) is a specific excellence of His own nature, consisting of the supreme wonder that is the manifestation of the bliss of His essential form; this is shown by the very words of the root verse [BhP 8.3.8], "He attains [this] at every moment. Therefore, the notion of having some other external purpose simply does not exist in Him. That—
And its purpose is nothing other than the playful manifestation of bliss for that Supreme Being who is all-capable; this is the general direction. As it has been said:
"The compassion of one who is compassionate but incapable leads only to suffering;
but the compassion of one who is both capable and compassionate leads only to bliss."
The Lord of Elephants [worships] Śrī Hari.

// 49 // [50] Therefore, they establish that even from the scriptural passage regarding Him being "without hands or feet," the intended meaning (tātparya) refers only to the Blessed One whose very form is infinite, self-luminous bliss, and nothing else.
You are the non-agent, the self-ruling sovereign who possesses the power of all causal agents; the gods, together with the immortals, bring you tribute and enjoy it,
just as the subjects of an entire emperor serve the creator of the universe.
"Those who are appointed therein are struck with awe"—
this is the meaning.
Here, "instrument" (*karaṇa*) refers to something like an axe or similar tool, by virtue of being impelled by the power of the agent (*kartṛ*).
An entity that performs an action is accepted as being entirely distinct from the agent, having attained the status of a mere instrument (*karaṇa*) alone,
and not even as having attained the status of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*);
just as, for example, the power (*śakti*) and so forth of fire and the like [are distinct from the fire itself].

Because it has a secondary (gauṇa) meaning, and because in the etymological derivation of the word *svarāṭ*, the instrumental case-ending in the word *svena* culminates precisely in its own inherent power (*svarūpa-śakti*), [the self-luminosity] belongs to the Self. Therefore,
since the individual soul (*jīva*) is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), the hands and other limbs [are luminous] by their own nature.
Because they are insentient, those various instruments, whose powers are dependent upon Him, possess instrumentality in its primary sense.
Therefore, because He is intent upon them, He is "with instruments" (sakaraṇa), whereas You are the inner controller of them.
Because You are unattached to that [world], You are independent of it; since You are self-sovereign (*svarāṭ*), You shine by Your own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*) alone.
Likewise, at the conclusion of the time of dissolution, women whose minds are fixed upon the coils of Your mighty arms as their seat of enjoyment—
"We too are equal to them, for we are those for whom the nectar of his lotus feet is the goal.

Thus, even though he is described by us— who are the teachers of the assembly of the wise— as possessing a multitude of most divine instruments that serve as our own support, he is in fact devoid of instruments (akaraṇa).

Why [is He called] *svarāṭ*? Because by His very nature—which is established through the particularity of His own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*)—He shines forth as the sovereign (*rājase*) by means of those very natures acting as the respective instruments. The sense is that since those [powers] are His very essence, it is impossible for them to function as primary instruments [independent of Him].

Furthermore, if even for you [the opponent] manifestation occurs through objects conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), how indeed could your status as the self-sovereign (*svarāṭ*) be established?
Herein, there exists nothing but bliss— undecaying, ancient, one, though appearing as many.
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "There is no diversity whatsoever" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19),
and such traditional texts as, "He whose hands, feet, face, belly, and so forth consist of nothing but bliss" (Nārada Pañcarātra).
[Objection: But what is the proof for the existence of such intrinsic powers (svarūpa-śakti) within me? To this they reply:
"He who possesses the power of all causal factors" (akhila-kāraka-śakti-dhara).
From all living beings (akhilebhyaḥ prāṇibhyaḥ), [there arise] the causal factors (kārakāṇi), that is, the instruments (karaṇāni).

You hold and bestow the powers that constitute the sense organs within the spheres of the eyes and so forth; thus [you are called the "Holder of the Senses"]. This is because you sustain each of those respective powers within them all.
Yet these powers exist in you inherently, as imperishable and perfectly full.
This is the state of being. And thus says the Śruti: "The life-breath of the life-breath, and the sight of the sight," etc.
(Kenopaniṣad 1.2); and also, "Natural knowledge, power, and action," etc. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8).
This has been stated in the Eleventh [Book]:

"Of whomsoever among embodied beings there are the two types of senses, knowledge arises from itself; for the wind, strength and movement arise from eating. Thus [BhP 11.4.4]. If it is argued that [the Lord is not the agent] because He is devoid of organs (*vikaraṇatvāt*), that has already been answered by the Sūtra-kāra himself in the rule: "That has been explained" (VS 2.1.32). Here, he [the author of the commentary] also states that...

By the phrase "it has been stated," he has established—precisely according to the method already mentioned under [VS 2.1.27], *śruter tu śabda-mūlatvāt*—that its state of being without organs (*vikaraṇatva*) and its state of having organs (*sakaraṇatva*) are to be understood solely through scripture and are beyond the reach of logic. And the scripture is: "For him there exists neither effect nor instrument" (ŚvetU 6.8), and so forth.
Alternatively, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Even though You possess the power of all causal agents, You are indeed without instruments. Why?
Because [the text says] "Self-ruling" (*svarāṭ*) and so forth.
Therefore, because Your majesty is distinct from everything else, the gods are "unblinking" (*animiṣāḥ*).
Indra and the other gods, as well as Brahmā and the creators of the universe, carry out offerings and tributes to You with their heads held high;
they do so even while accompanied by *māyā*, the unvanquished power that governs them.

The meaning is that she too, whose nature is the power of manifestation (*ābhāsa-śakti*), offers an oblation (*bali*) to You— who consist of the power of the bliss of Your own essential nature (*svarūpānanda-śakti*)— for the sake of manifesting the perfection of the Self.
And they consume the sacrificial offering (*havya*) given by humans.
They consume the sacrificial offering (bali) characterized by *kavya* and so forth.
Here, the illustration is "one who enjoys the rain" (*varṣa-bhuj*).
"Rain" (*varṣa*) refers to a circular region (*khaṇḍa-maṇḍala*).
How do they carry out the *bali* offering?
Regarding this, they say: "They perform it.
Indeed, the observance of your command is itself the *bali*.
The meaning is "seizing.
This is according to the Śruti [Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.3.3]: "From fear of him the wind blows; from fear the sun rises; from fear of him Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, run forth."
Alternatively, [the opponent might ask]: "Does he not state a reason for the hands and other organs being the very nature of the Self?

To this they say: "The gods who preside over the organs, being unblinking, carry your offering. Because they are deities of pure knowledge, they are the "creators of the universe," meaning the causes of the creation of all things.

Others are able to manifest objects through their instruments only by relying upon their respective presiding deities; you, however, are the very support for even those [deities]. Therefore, since your instruments would result in being self-luminous, they must be of the nature of your own essential form.
Thus [it is said].
Now, let the great power (*mahā-śakti*) be set aside; [if one argues] that *māyā* alone is the substratum, to this they reply: "by the unconquered" (*ajayā*).
But surely the individual souls (*jīva*) also...
They become the substrata for the presiding deities of their respective sense organs.

Regarding this, they say: "vidadhati" (they perform). This refers to the gods who have been granted authority by You, the Lord of the Universe, over these sense organs which serve as the gateways for the enjoyment of objects.
The meaning is this: living beings are not the substrata [of those powers], as they are merely like the inhabitants of a few villages who hold office;
rather, you alone are their substratum because you are their sovereign authority.

10/87// The Śrutis [speak] of the Blessed Lord. //50// [51] Therefore, by virtue of having hands, feet, and so forth that are distinct [from those of ordinary beings], He is indeed "without hands, feet, and so forth. As it is said:
"Internally covered with skin, beard, body hair, nails, and hair..."
That woman who does not inhale the nectar of your lotus feet is utterly deluded; she clings to a living corpse composed of flesh, bone, blood, worms, feces, phlegm, bile, and wind.
Now, regarding the Blessed Lord, the distinction is indeed clear: while the hair and other features are heard to be of the very nature of bliss (*ānanda*), others are simply non-existent.
For this very reason, [it was said] to Hiraṇyakaśipu:
Even the granting of the boon of Brahmanhood, characterized by the prohibition against people who would kill him, is consistent with this; as it is said:
"By those with life-force or without life-force, by gods, asuras, and great serpents" (BhP 7.3.37). Nor is this intended to prohibit the act of killing itself.
But it belongs to the agent alone;

because this is a section concerning the agent, and since it has been stated that [the action is performed] "by means of non-living things or by living things," it is understood to apply to him alone.
For even though the killer is equal to a living body, he has departed from his portion of vital breath, and because the tip of his nail— which was to be cut off— has been deprived of life.
Therefore, the scriptural passages, "For us, he is indeed breathless and mindless, the Pure One" and "This is the breath of this Great Being," are not inconsistent.
Therefore, it is said in the Vārāha Purāṇa: "He whose form is not composed of the material elements— flesh, marrow, and bone—
is the infallible, all-pervading Lord, whose nature is truth, due to his state as the Yogin and the Supreme Lord."
And that non-ordinary form of his is not something produced by will due to his being a great yogi; rather, the meaning is that it is eternal because of his being the Lord (Īśvara).
And thus is the formal argument (prayoga):
The Lord possesses a body,
because he is an agent endowed with knowledge, will, and effort, like a potter and others;
and that body of the Lord is eternal.
Because it possesses ears, like that [person] who possesses knowledge and so forth;
for this very reason, there is also a difference in character between the living being and the corpse.
By virtue of its association with consciousness, that which possesses it is living, whereas by itself it is a corpse; therefore,

because the form of the glorious Lord consists of the singular essence of consciousness, it is logical that it is eternally alive, as it is of the nature of eternal bliss and consciousness— this constitutes its distinction [from other bodies].
And the sense is that it is logical for [the Buddha] to be worthy of veneration.

// 10.60 // Śrī-Rukmiṇī to the Blessed Lord //51// [52] At the occasion of the dispute among those who argue with the scriptural injunctions and prohibitions regarding His possession of name and form, He indeed establishes that very point.

In both Yoga and Sāṅkhya, some [entity] is observed that resides in a single substratum, yet possesses distinct and contradictory properties, such as "it exists" and "it does not exist," which are established with respect to the object itself.
For that which is equal, supreme, favorable, and vast is Yoga;
it is the scripture of gross meditation (*sthūlopāsanā*),
for therein lies the Lord’s possession of name and form.

It is heard [in scripture]; and because the postulation of that [single cause] is simpler than the postulation of [multiple causes], it is established that [the One] possesses all names and designations such as "pot" and "cloth," and that its feet and so forth are the netherworld (pātāla) and so on.
Thus, the Sāṅkhya knowledge [concludes]: "It does not exist [as a separate entity]."

For in that regard, the scripture— by means of prohibitive texts— determines that the possession of name and form which is negated therein does not exist at all, because that phenomenal name and form is merely imagined. This was already stated previously regarding both views.
"He is named all things and he is of universal form," and so forth;
and by the passage beginning "whatever has been defined by speech" and so on (BhP 6.4.28–29),
[it is shown that] those two have their respective conclusions regarding the reality as "it exists" and "it does not exist."
He clarifies that very dispute:
[it concerns] those two things which possess two such contradictory properties as "existence" and "non-existence," which are distinct.
[An objection: "Let it be that these two have different objects"; [the author] says "no," for they reside in one [locus], having a common object.

Thus, when there is a dispute, whatever object is perceived and recognized as being consistent and appropriate becomes great and highly favorable for both parties. What is that which is appropriate? That which—
The meaning is that there exists some entity characterized by name-and-form (nāma-rūpa) which is distinct from name-and-form itself and from its absolute absence.
This is what is being said:
With respect to a single object, the scriptural passages would have mutually contradictory meanings through the simultaneous affirmation and negation of name-and-form;
however, in this case, both [statements] are supreme.

Since the intended meaning of the scriptural injunctions and prohibitions establishes, through the aforementioned reasoning, that [the Lord] possesses a non-material name and form (*aprākṛta-nāmarūpitva*) alone, those various opinions are merely matters of dispute.
It is precisely in this way that Śrī Dhruva has stated here that there is no dispute.

O Unborn One, Your most massive form, which consists of the many principles beginning with Mahat, is perceived by animals, serpents, birds, reptiles, gods, demons, mortals, and others, as the distinction between the existent and the non-existent.
"I know nothing higher than this, wherein there is no dispute" (BhP 4.9.13).
Here, the word *rūpa* alone functions as the substantive in both instances;
thus, "the supreme form and the formless."

And furthermore, according to the Vaiṣṇava statement, "and yet another" (cāparam eva ca) [ViP 6.7.47], the meaning is that from this point forward, the form characterized by having four arms and so forth is called the *vapuḥ* (body). This will be demonstrated further on. [52]
The meaning is: "I did not know this until now";
he clarifies that very point:
"He who, for the sake of favoring those who worship at his feet..."
The Blessed One is nameless and formless, infinite;
yet He assumed names and forms through His births and deeds. May that Supreme One be gracious toward me.

The meaning is that he who, though indeed devoid of name-and-form, assumed names and forms—that is, manifested them—along with births and actions. He states the fault in the contrary case [of his being subject to change] as follows: "Ananta..."

Thus [it is said]. If name-and-form (nāma-rūpa) and so forth do not exist in that [state], then it would follow that it possesses only finitude (sāntatva) with respect to its capacity for those things.
This has been stated by the Wise Ones (pracetasaḥ): "For there is no end to You..."
"He is sung of as the Infinite among all manifestations" (BhP 4.30.31); this is the reason for his manifestation in various ways. The Blessed One is the possessor of power whose essence is *bhaga*.
The Supreme Lord negates the illusory nature (*māyātva*) of that power, [stating] that "Mā" (Lakṣmī), who is the form of the power called Parā, resides in Him;
otherwise, His status as the Supreme would not be possible.
The sense is that there would be a contradiction.
Therefore, it is not the case that everything arises from the sovereignty of Māyā, because the Lord is indeed free from Māyā; for this reason, they know him to be supreme. Thus it has been said.
Now, one might object: "If [the Lord] possesses the form of all names and is yet devoid of them, there are indeed those who worship Him in His various aspects who serve as proof;
but who could possibly be the witnesses here? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For the sake of bestowing grace upon those who resort to the soles of His feet."
That reality does not shine forth correctly through Yoga or Sāṅkhya, but only through devotion;
for such is the Vedic revelation: "Devotion alone reveals Him," and so forth.
Therefore, the sense is that it is logical for those two to be mere dispute;
for this very reason, it will be stated immediately thereafter:
O best of the Kurus, as he was thus offering praise during that Aghamarṣaṇa rite, the Blessed One, who is affectionate toward His devotees, appeared before him.

By the statement "Having placed His feet upon the shoulders of Suparṇa" (BhP 6.4.35–6) and so forth, ending with "to those who resort to the soles of His feet," it is indicated that the form exists even prior to its manifestation for their sake.

From the Śruti passage beginning with "The foot is pure, spread out, ancient," and so forth; the past-tense reference "he resorted" (bheje) serves to establish the firmness of its authority by indicating its beginninglessness. Regarding the word "infinite" (ananta):
The meaning is that names and forms are indeed infinite;
and here the commentary states: "even though he is devoid of ordinary name and form."
// 6.4 // Dakṣa [worships] Śrī-Puruṣottama.

//52// [53] Thus, because He is eternal, all-pervading, the substratum of all, distinct from gross, subtle, and non-material entities, the counter-form (pratirūpa), self-luminous, and established by the harmony of all the Vedas—
Thus it is established that its form is indeed the form of the supreme reality (paramatattva). For, having experienced it through supreme wisdom, he clearly states this very point in three verses:

This very form, which was first assumed as the sole seed of hundreds of incarnations for the sake of constant grace toward those from whom darkness has forever departed through the arising of the essence of awakening—
I have manifested from the abode of the lotus at the navel.
Beyond this, O Supreme One, I behold Your own nature— which is pure bliss, free from conceptual construction, and of unblemished luster—
as the one creator of the universe, who, though within the self, is not the universe itself.
I have resorted to that intoxication which consists of the elements and the senses.
Indeed, this auspiciousness of the world was shown by you in meditation for the sake of our welfare as your devotees;
we pay homage to that Blessed One, and let us follow after you.

"He who is disregarded by those destined for hell due to their attachment to what is unreal"—and the commentary says: "Now, you too do not understand correctly; even this form which has been seen by you consists of the *guṇas* alone, whereas the Brahman devoid of *guṇas* is the reality. To that, he replies with two verses beginning with "rūpam" (the form).
Because darkness is perpetually and completely suppressed by the arising of the essence of awakening, this form of Yours—

which has been assumed and manifested by You alone through Your own sovereignty for the sake of favoring the virtuous devotees— is the single seed and root of the hundred incarnations whose nature consists of pure being (*śuddhasattva*).

To demonstrate that it is the seed for the descent of qualities (*guṇāvatāra*) for the purpose of manifesting that [nature], he says: "That which does not shine forth. O Supreme One, whose splendor is unobstructed! Your essential nature—which is unobscured light, free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*), and without division, and therefore pure bliss—I do not perceive as being separate or distinct from this form.
But this very thing is that;
for this reason, I have resorted to this form of yours.
He says it is also because of its fitness: "That which is the sole creator of the universe, the foremost among those worthy of worship. For this very reason—
The non-universal is that which is other than the universal.
Furthermore, "consisting of the elements and the senses" means being the self, that is, the cause, of both the elements and the senses.
One might object: "Even so, this [vision] is still conditioned (*sopādhika*) and merely recent. Anticipating this, he says:

"O Bhuvanamaṅgala, that very same [form] is this one which was shown by you (*te*) to us, your worshippers, for the sake of our auspiciousness during meditation. For it is not something conditioned for us, whose minds are intent upon the path of the Unmanifest (*avyakta*)."
The sense is that [your] vision is appropriate.
Therefore, let us pay homage to you; we shall perform it through our devoted service. If so, why is it that some do not honor me?
Regarding this, he says: "He who is disregarded," meaning [disregarded] by those whose fallacious arguments are based on atheistic sophistry; such is the verse.
Here, it is suggested that even a different, imagined meaning is simply impossible for him, due to the weight of his qualities as a learned man;
for he does not follow an unmanifest path.
And this was stated previously by way of praise: "Those whose souls are intent on the path of the unmanifest" (BhP 3.8.33).
"They do not honor me" refers to me in my manifested form.
This is precisely the meaning;
for [the deity] has been established as the Supreme Brahman precisely by means of a formal embodiment (vigraha).
Therefore, those who [regard] the embodiment...
Because they do not believe in such a thing, their views being contrary to the experience of the wise, they do not even believe in Īśvara;
therefore, he says "nirīśvara" (without a Lord). For this very reason—those who [do not perceive] the fragrance of the bud of Your lotus feet...
O Lord, those who have taken refuge in Your feet with supreme devotion smell You through the openings of their ears as You are brought there by the wind of the Vedas;
You never depart from the lotus-heart of Your own people.

In the immediately following verse, however, by the word "tu" (but), those who are distinguished from the outward-looking people mentioned in the passage beginning with "he who is disregarded," and who are solely devoted to such a form of the Blessed Lord,
are indicated as having their feet grasped through devotion, using the phrase "carried by the breeze of the Vedas" as the authoritative proof.
And its excellence has been stated by way of experience. // 3.9 //
Brahmā [worships] Śrī-Nārāyaṇa.

//53// [54] The very form of Śrī-Ṛṣabhadeva, who is recognized as an incarnation by way of direct possession (āveśāvatāra), is also to be applied in this manner: "This body of mine is difficult to conceive."
For my very being is my heart wherein righteousness resides;
since unrighteousness has been cast behind me,
the noble ones therefore call me Ṛṣabha.
Indeed, this human form is certainly difficult to comprehend and difficult to conceptualize; that which is the reality is precisely that.
Wherever there is the Dharma characterized by devotion to the Blessed One, right there my heart and mind reside. For I have cast behind me all that is contrary to it, such as non-dharma and its like.
Therefore, the meaning is that I am turned away;
for this very reason, even the final pastime of this speaker, Ṛṣabha-deva, [is not perceived].

The disappearance was indeed by means of a stratagem; however, it was described in that manner solely in accordance with the common perception of worldly people, for the purpose of demonstrating the manner of delighting in the self.
Thus it has been said: "The rule for the final departure of yogis."
Regarding the phrase "anuśikṣayan" [BhP 5.6.6],
therefore, in the expression "desiring to abandon his own *kalevara*," the word *kalevara* has the meaning of *prapañca* (the phenomenal world) alone.
Because it is well-known as such in the scriptures on spiritual practice (*upāsanā-śāstra*).

Likewise: "Then, a fierce forest fire, born from the friction of bamboo stalks shaken by the force of the wind, licked that forest and burned it along with him" (BhP 5.6.8). However, in its actual meaning (*vāstavārtha*), it is [burned] by Him.
The word "saha" [expresses] the third case in the sense of assistance to the agent (*kartṛ-sāhāyye*),

because according to the principle of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇa-mukhya-nyāya*), the application [of the case ending] occurs primarily with respect to the agent alone. Consequently, the forest fire [consumes] the gross bodies of the living beings, such as the trees, existing in that forest.
He burned [the subtle body]; however, since Lord Ṛṣabha burned only the subtle body, it should be understood that he bestows complete liberation [upon others].
Whosoever has been touched by him, or seen, or has lain down with him, or even followed after him—

"Just as those Kosalas went to the place where yogis go" (BhP 9.11.22). In this manner, having described his similarity to fire, it is also implied that his disappearance was likewise like that of fire. For this very reason, it is stated in the third chapter that there was the manifestation of the god Ṛṣabha, but not his birth.
5/5// Śrī-Ṛṣabhadeva [to his sons] //54// [55] Thus, if even in the physical form of Ṛṣabha there was such a state, how much more so for the Blessed One himself? He says:
"In the midst of a crowd of hosts of sages, excellent kings, and..."
In the assembly at King Yudhiṣṭhira’s Rājasūya sacrifice,
the worship due to them was received; this very Self, visible to my sight and within the range of my vision, has now appeared before me.
And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "This Self of the worlds, being within the range of my vision—the path of sight—is manifest, clearly present.
The sense is: 'Oh, what good fortune! Thus [ends the verse]. (1.9)
Śrī Bhīṣma said to the Blessed Lord:
"And likewise— in the passage beginning with 'That form which...'— you are directly Viṣṇu, the lamp of the supreme self."
Thus [it is said in BhP 10.3.24].
That which the Vedas call "some form" or "the Reality"—
what is that reality?
Regarding this, he says "the unmanifest" and so forth: whatever such entity, resembling an effect, there may be, You alone, Viṣṇu, are that which directly falls within the range of perception.
And likewise, in the Nirmāṇa-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa, the words of Śrī Vedavyāsa to the Blessed Lord are as follows:
"O Madhusūdana, I desire to see you with my own eyes."
"That which is Truth, the Supreme Brahman, the source of the universe and the Lord of the universe—whom the Upaniṣads call the Eye—may He be my Master.
The reason for this is stated: "The Lamp of the Inner Self [is] the aggregate of the body, its causes, and its effects."
The meaning is: "appearing as the illuminator.
The intention is that for one who is thus constituted, there is no fear or apprehension for you.
Thus, this is the essential meaning (bhāvārtha) shown by the venerable Master (Śrī-Svāmī), which is also consistent with the context. Śrī... [text ends]
He is intent solely on conflict, because otherwise there would arise no apprehension of fear.
10.3 Śrī Devakī [speaks] to the Blessed Lord.
[56] [57] Therefore, he states that even those who are portions (*aṃśa*) of Him possess such qualities— truth, knowledge, infinity, and bliss.
For those who perceive through the Upaniṣads, they possess a form consisting of a single essence, even though their vast majesty remains untouched by such limited vision.

And the commentary says "satya-jñāna" etc., stating that there is no distinction even though all possess form: they are real (*satya*), of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna-rūpa*), infinite (*ananta*), and of the nature of bliss (*ānanda-rūpa*).
Even therein, they consist solely of that [one essence], being of a different class from anything else.
They are free from differentiation;

moreover, they are of a single flavor (*ekarasa*) there, their forms being eternally of one nature. Or rather, Brahman—which consists solely of the single flavor of truth, knowledge, and so forth—is itself their form. For this very reason:

The *upaniṣad* is the knowledge of the Self; for those who possess that very vision as their eye, it is certain that they were all seen to be untouched by earthly greatness—that is, those whose vast majesty was not touched by anything fit to be touched by the earth. Such was the case. This is the meaning.
In this context, the word *mātra* indicates that those qualities, such as color and so forth, are internal attributes of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Indeed, neither the Master [Vallabha] nor the venerable Śukadeva holds the view that the word *mūrti* here refers solely to the Self (*ātman*) in some other sense.
Because figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) consists of arduous conceptualization;
[this applies] specifically to the four words: "untouched" (*aspṛṣṭā*), "of vast majesty" (*bhūrimāhātmyā*), "also" (*api*), and "the vision of the Upaniṣads" (*upaniṣaddṛk*).
Because this would entail the destruction of the inherent nature (*svārasya*) of both the individual and the collective [meanings], because it must conform to the manner already described,
because it follows what will be cited later in [BhP 3.15.38]— "they beheld their own fortune of meditative absorption, which was beyond the scope of the eyes"—
and because it contradicts the heart of Śrī Śuka in [BhP 12.12.68] beginning with "their own bliss" (*sva-sukha*).

Therefore, statements such as "the mass of pure consciousness" (BhP 10.37.20), "to the embodiment of pure knowledge" (BhP 10.27.21), and "in You alone, whose body is eternal bliss and awareness" (BhP 10.14.22), should not be subjected to forced interpretation by treating them as figurative.
