In the same way, having embraced the embodiment of bliss— perceived through her vision— as described in the verse beginning with "having obtained the Self" (BhP 10.41.25),
she clasped her beloved, who stood between her breasts, with both arms and cast off her exceedingly long-lasting fever.
And in such passages as [BhP 10.48.6],
the fact that [the union] has any other purpose is excluded by means of seeing and embracing.
And it is said in the Mahāvārāha:
All the bodies of that Supreme Self are eternal and everlasting;
devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted, they are never born of *prakṛti*.
"The masses of supreme bliss and the measures of knowledge exist everywhere;
herein, in the Lord, no distinction between body and embodied ever exists. Thus it is said.
10.13 // Śrī Śuka said:
//57// [58] Having intended exactly this, he said: "Know this Kṛṣṇa to be the Self of all Selves."
"For the welfare of the world, He too appears here as if possessing a body through Māyā" (BhP 10.14.55).

"I bow to this worshipful one whose form is like a cloud" (BhP 10.14.1)—understand that the realization of His form described in such passages occurs only through the wisdom obtained by My grace, and not by means of logic or other forms of inquiry; this is the meaning.
Even though He is thus situated, for the welfare of the world and to draw the hearts of everyone toward His own Self, He appears as if possessing a body and as if living, and He plays;
by the word "as if" (iva), it is implied that Śrī Kṛṣṇa, however—
It is understood that He entered a separate body like a living soul;
for this very reason, the glorious Dhruva described the divine form as being characterized by the supreme goal of human existence.
"O Blessed One, your lotus feet are indeed the source of true blessings for one who worships them in such a manner, for you are the very embodiment of the goals of human life (puruṣārtha).
Regarding this, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "O Blessed One, *puruṣārtha* is supreme bliss; you are he whose very form (*mūrti*) is that."
Therefore, your lotus-feet are the true blessing compared to sovereignty and the like;
for it is certain that the ultimate fruit is the true blessing. In that manner, you alone are the human goal (puruṣārtha) through such desirelessness.
"From experience"—thus [ends] this [verse].
10.14 // Śrī Śuka //58// [59] Therefore, he utters a statement suitable for the conclusion, showing that the Brahman which is expressed by words is indeed the Śrī-vigraha (the glorious form):
O Kṣattṛ, during the Kṛta Yuga, the lotus-eyed Blessed One, being pleased, revealed himself to him.
"Assuming a body that is Śābdabrahman.
Assuming that body and manifesting it, the Lord known as Śukla exists in the Kṛta Yuga;
that very Supreme Reality, Brahman, which is to be established by the Word (Śabda), [manifests] toward that Kardama.
The meaning is that he caused [it] to be seen.

// 3.21 // Śrī-Maitreya //59// [60] Thus, since such a distinction of the Blessed One is established, the initial faulty inference that [the Blessed One] exists because he is visible, like a jar, is not possible, because it is stated at a time when its application has passed.
Intending this very point, he establishes the absence of the six modifications of being and so forth in that [Self], prioritizing its reality, and thus accepts its nature as complete.
You alone are the one Self, the ancient Person, the Truth, self-luminous, infinite, and primordial;
eternal, imperishable, ever-blissful, and stainless.
"Full, non-dual, liberated from limiting adjuncts, and immortal.

[BhP 10.14.20] With the words "I bow to You, O Praiseworthy One," [BhP 10.14.1] and so forth, this declaration of His being worthy of praise establishes that He alone—characterized by the cloud-body and other such forms—is the Self of all and the supreme refuge. As it has been said:
And it is said: "You were alone in the beginning" (BhP 10.14.18),
and "Know this Kṛṣṇa to be the Self of all selves" (BhP 10.14.55).

Since you are the Self, you alone are the Truth; for other things possess truth only by depending upon the truth of the supreme substratum. Thus, the sense is that the primary resting place of truthfulness lies in you alone.
Thus it has been said: "He whose vow is truth, who is devoted to truth," and so forth (BhP 10.2.26). Kṛṣṇa is established in truth; truth is established in Him.
Govinda is truth from truth; therefore, he is indeed "Satya" by name.
And thus in the Udyoga Parvan [MBh 5.68.12]:
"Furthermore, since modifications such as birth and so forth do not exist in you, he says: 'You are the primordial cause; you are one.'"
In the passage beginning with "First" (BhP 10.14.18), because suchness is perceived,
there is therefore no birth; rather,
the birth of Hari is merely His becoming perceptible, and in no way is it a modification— this is precisely the tradition of the Padma Purāṇa.
Therefore, it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Failing to recognize the supreme body, which is the immutable self consisting of bliss,
they superimpose [upon it] that which is born, composed of the five elements, and insentient."
This is the reason for being "primordial" (ādyatva):
the Person (puruṣa), while indeed having the form of a person, is "ancient" (purāṇa) in the sense that he is "new even from of old" (purāpi navaḥ), meaning he exists even prior to any effect.
And scripture says: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, in the form of a person" (AitU 1.1.1).
For this very reason, it precludes any modification characterized by the existence of another birth.
"Being eternal" means having an everlasting form (*sanātana-mūrti*).

Likewise, "full" means that even in its intermediate state, it remains as it was before; this refers to its growth. "Constant bliss" means that it is eternally of the nature of happiness; this refers to its transformation (*pariṇāma*) into bliss. Regarding bliss...
The masculine gender is Vedic, just as in the passage "Knowledge, bliss, Brahman" (BAU 3.9.28), where bliss (*ānanda*) is neuter;
likewise, the term *akṣara* should be understood as neuter.
"Amṛta" means non-perishing; it is the cause of fullness. "Ananta-advaya" means devoid of limitation by space and time.
Even though it is devoid of the determination of a real entity (*vastu-pariccheda*), because another possesses that capacity and cannot exist without it,
there are four kinds [of arguments] to establish its immortality (*amṛtatva*).
And it precludes [the view] that [liberation] is the fruit of ritual action (*kriyā-phala*).

Among those [objections], "origination" is already refuted by the phrase "the first. The remaining three—namely, "self-luminous," "stainless," and "liberated from limiting adjuncts"—are [refuted] by the three words [of the verse]. And therein:
Attainment may occur either through action or through knowledge.
Attainment through action has already been refuted by the very term "Self," because [the Self] is the innermost essence of all.
Likewise, He precludes attainment through mere knowledge, stating, "He is self-luminous. This was said by the Blessed Lord to Brahmā: "This is My power of will."
Regarding the phrase "the surveying of the worlds" (lokāvalokanam) [BhP 2.9.22], the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "And he says that this was obtained by you solely through my grace;
*manīṣitam* means desire."
"This is the power of that desire of mine which was, 'It must be given to you. What is that? He says:
it is my beholding of the world."
Thus it is said:
"The Lord, though eternally unmanifest, is perceived through His own power. [Note 16]

Now, one might object: in the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, Vāsudeva, when addressing Uddhava, enumerated himself among the manifestations (*vibhūtis*) in the passage beginning with "I am the Lord of the blessed ones" (11.16.29), yet at the very end he stated, "All these are merely modifications of the mind" (11.16.41).
This is true.
That enumeration is intended to express abundance, as in the expression "the kṣatriyas go.
For it is said in that very same [text]:
"Earth, wind, ether, water, light, I, and the Great One..."
"In the transformation, the person, the unmanifest, rajas, sattva, and tamas— the Supreme"— in this passage from BhP 11.16.37, even Brahman is included among them by the word "Supreme" (para).
Thus, in this manner, attainment [of that state] is prohibited.

Now, one might argue that even if there were a transformation, it would occur through the removal of adventitious attributes (*upādhi*), just as rice is transformed by the removal of its husk through threshing;
however, because [the Self] is non-conjoined (*asaṅga*), such a thing is impossible. Thus he says: "liberated from attributes" (*mukta upādhitaḥ*). As it has been said:
"To Him whose form is pure knowledge" (BhP 10.27.21), and "a mass of pure consciousness" (BhP).
And so on in such passages as these. Therefore, verses such as "my skin being pierced by his sharpened arrows" (BhP 1.9.34) are merely descriptions of His illusory pastimes (māyika-līlā).
Thus say certain sages who are well-versed in this matter, O royal sage.
"Since that which contradicts one's own words certainly does not conform [to reason]," and so forth—
according to this principle (*nyāya*), because it contradicts reality;
for it is said thus in the *Skānda*:
Though unattached, imperishable, indivisible, ungraspable, and indeed incapable of being dried up,
Viṣṇu appears as if pierced, drenched in blood, and bound.
"Deluding the Asuras, this God plays even among the Suras;
he regards humans with a neutral gaze, but never those who are liberated. Thus it is said.
It is entirely appropriate that Śrī Bhīṣma appeared in such a manner at the time of battle because he was possessed by a demon;
however, it should be understood that his report is now being made like the distress of a bad dream.
Furthermore, does purification consist in the addition of some excellence or in the removal of impurity?
In that regard, the imparting of excellence has already been refuted by [the doctrine of] fullness; furthermore,
the [state of being] "stainless" (nirañjana) precludes the removal of impurities, as it is inherently pure (nirmala).
The meaning is that he is the embodiment of pure knowledge.
10.14 // Śrī Brahmā //60// [61] Thus,
it has been established that sovereignty and the other qualities are, in this way, constitutive of His very nature; and this is logical because they are internal attributes of that nature.
Just as light is the very nature of its internal qualities, such as its white color and other attributes, and not of the nature of darkness or the like, so it is in this case.
Now, the fact that the glorious form possesses the characteristics of the perfect essential nature is likewise established; thus,
the fact that the glorious form possesses the characteristics of the perfect essential nature has been proven.
And that is logical,
because it has the singular nature of the supreme reality endowed with all powers.

In this regard, that which is the eternally inherent internal nature— the scriptural tradition of the glorious form (śrī-vigraha)— is the very reality characterized by those various configurations and defined by supreme bliss; that alone is the glorious form.
He alone is the Lord Himself, because He is the eternal substratum even for other internal attributes such as sovereignty (aiśvarya) and the rest,
just like pure sugar-candy.

Regarding *laḍḍuka*: just as people recognize and employ the term *laḍḍuka* for a piece of sugar-candy specifically characterized by a shape that indicates its nature as a *laḍḍuka*, and which possesses the natural fragrance and other qualities inherent to that candy;
in the same way, in passages such as [BhP 3.9.2], "That which is this form... and so forth, the Supreme Reality itself is the Śrī-...
And that very form (vigraha) is understood by the wise to be the Blessed Lord himself, and it is so employed [in scripture].
Thus, having established that the glorious form possesses the nature of the complete reality,
for the purpose of nourishing that [conviction]:
Another section is commenced,
extending as far as the description of the retinue;
therein, regarding the attendants:

Regarding the fact that [the vision] is of the very nature of that [divine form], he states the inferential mark (*liṅga*)— consisting in the manifestation of the vision accompanied by its constituent parts— in two verses:
"That wonderful child with lotus-eyes..."
"Four-armed, with weapons such as the conch and mace," and so forth.
This is clear. 10.3. Śrī Śuka said: 61/62. With this very intention, he spoke as follows:
Just as for those who experience oneness,
[the deity] is itself free from conceptual construction,
though designated by the names of ornaments, weapons, and physical forms.
By means of its own māyā, it assumes various powers.
By that very power of truth,
may the omniscient Lord Hari protect us with all his own forms.
He is always, everywhere, and all-pervading.

Although He manifests as the supreme essential nature whose sole flavor is supreme bliss, being free from conceptual construction for those who experience oneness and are intent upon perceiving the absolute supreme form, He does so in such a manner that—
By means of that compassion which I bestow upon my own [devotees] as they relate to Me through their respective lordship,

and by My very own nature consisting of manifold powers acting as the cause, I assume— through the manifestation of those powers— the powers known as the ornaments and so forth, and bring them within the range of perception.
By that very means of valid cognition characterized by the experience of the wise;
by that very means of valid cognition characterized by the experience of the wise, that...
"If it should be true"— this is the meaning.
May He protect us with those very ornaments and other characteristics, in all His forms, through the manifestation of various diverse forms.
Therefore, in the *Śrī-Viṣṇudharma*, within the hymn to the Discus offered by Bali, it is said: "Whose form is indescribable even by the most excellent yogis," and so forth.
And immediately after that— O Lord of the Earth, as that wheel was revolving, the Daitya beheld the entire triple world, beginning with Bhūḥ and Bhuvaḥ, within the center of its hub. Thus it is said.
Thus, in this very way, this *cakra* was also praised by the illustrious Ambarīṣa in the ninth [chapter]. The *liṅgas* are the Garuda-shaped banner and so forth.
By this, even that which is heard in some places as if it were accidental is also [explained].
It should be understood as being like the manifestation of the Śrī Bhagavān;
here, in this third verse, the statement "the stainless jewel, the reality of the Caitya, is upon his neck" (BhP 3.28.28) also serves as supporting evidence.

Therefore, even in the twelfth book, passages such as "The Unborn One bears His own self-effulgence under the designation of the Kaustubha gem" (BhP 12.11.10) are shown through the vision of non-difference for the purpose of meditation upon [the Lord] as residing in the Virāṭ, as far as possible directly.
It should also be contemplated as having a divine form (*śrīvigraha*).
For it is said in the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*:
"The Self of this world is untainted, free from qualities, and stainless..."
"The Blessed Lord Hari bears the form of the Kaustubha gem. (ViP 1.22.68)

// 6.8 // Viśvarūpa [assumed the form of] Mahendra. //62// [63] Furthermore, that the world of Śrī-Vaikuntha is likewise of such a nature has already been established for him in the passage: "The Blessed One, being honored, revealed his own world" (BhP 2.9.9). Moreover...
It is established for the sake of those of dull intellect,
because it cannot be attained through action and so forth,
and is heard as being beyond all conceptual proliferation (prapañca).
For those who have attained that [state], it is praised by virtue of its quality of being free from stumbling; it is obtained precisely in the state of freedom from qualities (*nairguṇya*).
Even for that [attainment] in the worldly sense of "Lord" (*bhagavannike*), there is that same...

Because its freedom from the gunas is extended by analogy through this absorption (āveśa), it is therefore understood all the more clearly as being of that very nature. It is heard directly in scripture as being beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), proclaimed as eternal, and attainable only through devotion— which even surpasses the bliss of liberation— [revealing] the reality of existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda).
"It is designated as a density.
In that regard, it is unattainable by means of karma and so forth; for example:
"There was one [Lord] of the gods who have become celestial beings, and of the earth-dwellers."
The earthly realm (bhūrloka) belongs to mortals and others, while for the perfected ones (siddhas), it is beyond the triad [of lower worlds].
Below, the Lord created the Asuras and the Nāgas of the earth;
thus he established all the destinies within the three worlds for those whose nature consists of the three *guṇas* according to their actions.

The stainless destinations of yoga, austerity, and renunciation are Maharloka, Janarloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka; the destination of the yoga of devotion is My own state. Beyond these three worlds attained by the perfected ones through yoga and other means are Maharloka and the others.
Below the earth are the netherworlds such as Atala;
within the three worlds are the realms of Pātāla and so forth, namely Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ; and [the sphere] of domestic duties (gārhasthya) pertains to karmas.

The austerity (*tapas*) of all dharmas is practiced by the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), as is the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). In that regard, through the distinction between the temporary student (*upakurvāṇa*) and the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*), one should know that *mahas* is attained through celibacy; *jana* through the stage of the forest-dweller; and *tapaḥ* through renunciation (*nyāsa*). Furthermore, everything is attained according to the gradations of yoga.

My destination is the realm of Śrī Vaikuṇṭhaloka, which—as will be described—is attainable through *bhakti-yoga*, as supported by such statements as "those who do not go there" (BhP 3.15.23) and by the context of the section concerning the worlds. And it was stated in the Third Canto by Brahmā himself to the gods regarding that very place: "The multitude of Hari’s abodes... (*saṅkulaṃ hari-padān*).
"By those seen in excessive measure," and so forth [BhP 3.15.20].
And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "By the celestial chariots (*vimāna*) of the devotees seen to that extent, and not by those obtained through karma and the like. Such is this [explanation].

In the same way, the Śruti says: "Having examined the worlds acquired through action, let the Brāhmaṇa attain detachment; there is nothing uncreated that can be attained by means of what is created" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12).
Here too, regarding the word *akṛta*...
The qualificand is simply "the world," because that is what is implied;
as in [passages] such as "The Lord of all beings."
"Go to Him alone for refuge with your whole being, O Bhārata;
by His grace you shall attain supreme peace and the eternal abode. Thus [ends the verse from] the Śrī-Gītā 18.62.
In the Bhagavad-upaniṣads, Chapter 11, Verse 14:
The Blessed Lord said: [64] Transcendence of phenomenal manifestation (prapañca).
A person devoted to his own duty for a hundred births attains the state of Viriñca; beyond that,
he becomes a Bhāgavata, and then indeed a Vaiṣṇava, who is unmanifest.
"O wise ones, just as [the sun reaches] its station at the end of the kalās;

even beyond that, by means of the excellence of merit, the devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata) comes to Me at the end of the body— Me who am beyond the unevolved (avyākṛta), beyond the phenomenal world (prapañca), and the object of the manifestation (vyākaraṇa) well-known from the Śruti, which says, 'Let me manifest names and forms.'"
He goes to the Vaiṣṇava station, Vaikuṇṭha.
Just as I, having become Rudra, exist by virtue of my office, so too do the wise gods exist as office-holders; at the end of their office, when the period [of their office] has passed, [their] liṅga—
Since they will exist until the dissolution [of the world], it is according to the principle that "the abiding of those who hold office lasts as long as their office."
4.24 Śrī Rudra [spoke] to Pracetas. [64] [65] From that follows non-stumbling; furthermore, that manifestation of mine, who am possessed of illusory power (māyā).
They do not crave the eightfold sovereignty that has come to them,
nor do they long for the auspicious fortune of the Lord;
rather, they attain it in this world for the sake of another.
Those who are devoted to me shall never perish in this world of tranquil form; my unblinking weapon does not lick them up, for to them I am as dear as their own self and their son.

He is my friend, teacher, well-wisher, and beloved deity. Furthermore, immediately upon the cessation of ignorance, through my Māyā— specifically through the compassion directed toward my devotees— I manifest for their sake my divine power (*vibhūti*), which is the perfection of enjoyments.
Likewise, they do not even desire the divine fortune (*śrī*) directly related to the Lord, known as *sārṣṭi*— that is, the attainment of equal power;
the meaning is that although they do not long for those things because they desire only the bliss of devotion, nevertheless...
The phrase "tu me" means "indeed in my world," namely that which is called Vaikuṇṭha; they surely attain it— thus His particular affection (*vātsalya*) is demonstrated,
as was the case with Sudāmā, the excellent florist.
He too chose unwavering devotion to Him alone, the Soul of all,
as well as friendliness toward His devotees and supreme compassion for all living beings.
Having granted him these boons, as well as the goddess Śrī who increases one's lineage— thus [it is said in BhP 10.41.52].
Thus, their lack of attachment to those [defilements] is illuminated;
and by the words "immediately after ignorance" and "solicited through my compassion," the fact that they are of the nature of misfortune is refuted.

Or rather, even the prosperity attained in the Brahma-world and other realms requested through illusion— this demonstrates their power over all things, but not their enjoyment thereof; for because such [prosperity] is utterly insignificant, it is unworthy of them.
And there is a scriptural passage on this point:
"Just as here the world won by action perishes, even so there the world won by merit perishes" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.6).
Immediately following that, it says: "But those who depart from here having realized the Self and these truths... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.6).
"For them, there is freedom of movement according to their desires in all worlds.

But if that is so, then because there is no distinction in their being "worlds," the enjoyers and the objects of enjoyment might at some point perish, just as in the case of heaven and other such realms.

Regarding this, he says: In that Vaikuṇṭha, whose form is peaceful— that is, whose nature is tranquil and unchanging— the worlds residing there, being devoted to Me, shall never perish, nor shall they ever be deprived of objects of enjoyment.
My unblinking weapon—my wheel of time (kālacakra)—does not lick them;
it does not swallow them, for according to the Śruti [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1], "he does not return again. All worlds, up to the realm of Brahmā, [are subject to this].
O Arjuna, those who return;
but for one who has reached Me, O Kaunteya,
there is no further birth.
Thus from the Śrī Gītā Upaniṣads.
It is also stated in the *Sahasranāma-bhāṣya*: "The supreme, most excellent abode or place, free from any suspicion of return, is the *parāyaṇa*."
In the masculine gender, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. He says "of whom" (*yeṣām*) to show that their greatness is not merely this much;
[namely,] those for whom there is nothing without me.
The meaning is that there is another who is a recipient of love;
or else, it was said thus with reference to Goloka and other realms.
For in that [realm], the glorious gopīs exist eternally in such a state;
or rather, what kind of state do those people attain immediately after ignorance?
To this, he says: "Of whom..."

Thus, those who— whether they be the hosts of sages shown in the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa* along with their latent impressions (*savāsanā*), or others besides them— who meditate upon me with the thought, "This Self is indeed Brahman itself,
manifest," they alone [attain this].
The meaning is "they attain.
The plural number in the word *suhṛdaḥ* (friends) is used with reference to the various different types of friendship.
Thus, in the fourth [chapter], in the words of Śrī Nārada—
"Peaceful, possessing equal vision, pure, and pleasing to all beings—those who are dear kinsmen of the Infallible go directly to the abode of the Infallible. [BhP 4.12.37]
// 3.25 // Śrī Kapila //65// [66] He then states simultaneously that [the Lord] is beyond all phenomenal expansion and is unswerving:
"O twice-born ones, Vaikuṇṭha is the parasol, the abode from which there is no fear on any side" (BhP 12.11.19).
"Of that which has the nature of conceptual proliferation (prapañca)" is [stated] because of the context;
"O twice-born ones" is an address.

// 12.11 // Śrī-sutaḥ // 66 // [67] Men who are absorbed in goodness (sattva) go to the heavenly realm; those absorbed in passion (rajas) go to the world of men; but those absorbed in darkness (tamas) go to hell, while those devoid of all qualities (nirguṇa) go to Me alone. [BhP 11.25.22]

Since the world is attached [to him], one ought to say "my world"; however, intending his own non-difference from that by stating that "attaining him" is indeed "attaining me," he says "me alone. (11.25)
The Blessed Lord said: 67–68. To dwell in the forest is the highest refuge of freedom from the qualities (nirguṇya); the forest is said to be sattvic, while the village is said to be rājasic.
"The gambling hall is characterized by tamas, but my abode is devoid of the gunas.
The intended meaning is that it is designated as "devoid of the gunas" precisely because of his (the Lord's) pervasive presence therein.
// 11.25 // He himself: [69] As for his transcendence of primordial nature (*prakṛti*): "From there he went to the radiant Vaikuṇṭha, beyond darkness."
Where Nārāyaṇa himself is present, the supreme goal of those who have renounced all worldly ties.

"For those who are peaceful and have laid down the rod of punishment, from which [state] there is no returning once gone"—the word "śiva" (auspicious) is to be supplied as the object of "agamat" (he went). He went to that auspicious state.
// 10.88 // Śrī Śuka said: //69// [70] Regarding its permanence:
Janaloka is located upon its neck.
From her two breasts came the world of austerity (tapoloka),
and from her heads came the eternal world of Brahmā, the world of truth (satyaloka).

And the commentary states: "The world of Brahman (brahma-loka) is that which is named Vaikuṇṭha; it is eternal and constant, and not something contained within the created phenomenal universe. It is called 'Brahma-loka' because it is a world that has become Brahman."
2.5 Śrī Brahmā to Śrī Nārada:
[70] [71] The state of being attainable solely through devotion, which transcends the happiness of liberation—
[that state] which those who do not engage in the composition or narration of the deeds of the Destroyer of Evil (Viṣṇu) do not reach.
Alas! Those whose minds are destroyed by wicked stories concerning other realms listen to them;
yet when those very stories are heard by men whose fortune is ruined, they cast those men into various shelterless darknesses from which their essence has been snatched away.
And those who, following the lead of the Bull among Sages, go to the realm of the Unblinking One— those whose conduct is truly enviable even by us who are far below them—
are filled with mutual passion for recounting the excellent fame of their Lord.
With their limbs covered in horripilation due to the flow of tears of agitation, they departed—
those for whom Vaikuṇṭha was [as if] above them, or who were of a nature desirable to us,
or from whom Yama was far removed, having set aside the constraints of Yama through their perfection as Siddhas.
By the phrase "of her husband, the illustrious one," it is indicated that such devotion is renowned for its power to set aside even the bliss of liberation;
as in the verse beginning with "They do not disregard [it] even though it is ultimate," O dear one.
"Those who have taken refuge at Your feet are experts in the nectar of Your stories, whose fame is a sacred bathing place," according to the words of Sanaka and others.
(3.15) Śrī Brahmā [spoke] to the gods. (71) [72]
The nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss;
thus, do these whom I have instructed indeed remain upon my path?
Those who abide in Me find security;
they know that to be the supreme Brahman.
My paths—characterized by knowledge, action, and devotion—are the means for attaining Me. Knowledge...

Because even among those devoted to ritual action (*karman*), devotion (*bhakti*) provides some assistance at some time and in some place from the very outset; and because they know— that is, they understand— that the supreme Brahman is that secure state consisting of the auspiciousness of devotion to Me, as will be illustrated in this very way— having thus reflected, the Blessed One, who is possessed of great compassion, [acted].
The All-pervading Lord revealed to the cowherds His own world, which is beyond darkness—
that eternal light of Brahman, which is truth, knowledge, and infinite.
"For that which the sages, being composed, perceive as the cessation of the qualities" (BhP 10.28.14–15).
In both cases, however, any alternative interpretation would result from the forced insertion (*adhyāhāra*) of words such as "and" (*ca*), and would thus be strained.
Furthermore, by those very same commentators, this has been explained as an epithet of Vaikuṇṭha as well, in the phrase "beyond the darkness of primordial nature" (*tamaso 'prakṛteḥ param*).
Thus it is said.
11.20 // The Blessed Lord //72// [73] Likewise— where Time, the supreme lord of the unblinking ones, does not exist.

From where indeed [did they come], those gods who rule over the worlds— a place where there is neither being (sattva), nor passion (rajas), nor darkness (tamas); neither modification (vikāra), nor the Great One (mahat), nor primordial matter (pradhāna)?
Desiring to cast off that which is not the Self by saying "not this, not this," they abandon their own wickedness and, with undivided affection, declare the supreme state of Viṣṇu.
At every step, they conceal within their hearts that state which is worthy of being sought;
desiring to cast off that which is other than consciousness— thinking "not this, not this"— they abandon their own wickedness.
Having abandoned the view of non-difference between the Lord and the self, [one should take refuge in] the station—
the lotus-like foot— of the venerable Blessed One.
At every step and at every moment, having embraced and clung to it with their hearts, those who possess no affection for anything else—
being such as they are— whatever they perceive or know,
that indeed is the station of Viṣṇu.

The intended meaning is that Śrī-Vaikuṇṭha is indeed the very nature of Brahman. By this, through the indicative mark of the means characterized by divine love (prema), any other interpretation suggesting a formless nature is refuted. Herein—
Even for the author of the *Muktāphala-ṭīkā*, who was devoted to the formless [Brahman], his speech, manifested by destiny, was as follows:
"They declare that supreme Vaiṣṇava state to be like a kingdom presided over by a sovereign who is himself presided over by a higher authority."
It is said that even the positions of Brahmā and the others are "supreme" because they are presided over by Viṣṇu;
the meaning is that they are presided over by Viṣṇu alone.
Therefore, even in the Śruti, its being established solely in its own majesty is stated: "O Blessed One, in what is He established? In His own majesty" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1).
For this very reason, it is said: "Who indeed knows where He is? (Rig Veda 8.77.3).
2.2 // Śrī Śuka said:
//73// [74] He clearly stated, as the meaning of the Vedic passage beginning with "Who indeed [knows thus]," that they do not know their own world.
Where Janārdana is the Lord,
those of smoky intellect who do not know Him declare the Veda to be accompanied by ritual action.

Those of smoky intellect who claim that the Veda, along with its ritual injunctions, teaches only ritual action, do not know the true nature and realm of Janārdana; rather, they know only heaven and such.
In that realm—[as described in 4.29]—Śrī Nārada [taught this] to Prācīnabarhis. [74] [75]
And thus—

in the prose passage beginning with "Oṃ, salutations to you, O Blessed One"— the wandering mendicants who are supreme *paramahaṃsas* have, through the highest meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of self-yoga, fully cultivated and clearly manifested the state of a *paramahaṃsa*.

When the door of the heart, its panels of darkness opened by means of the Dharma, was flung open, you experienced for yourself the realization of your own innate bliss within the world of the Self. Here, *tamas* refers to material nature (*prakṛti*) or ignorance (*ajñāna*).
"In the world of the self" means in the world that is one's own true nature;
"this is the world of the self, this is the world of Brahman."

For in the Śruti it is said: "In the divine city of Brahman, this Supreme Self is established," and so forth; that which they declare to be the subtle, supreme, eternal state of all-pervading majesty is to be known.
"Ordinary people do not know this essence of the world; the sages established in yoga know it"—thus in the Pippalāda recension.
"That which is placed beyond the firmament, hidden in the secret cave, shines forth—that which the ascetics enter"—thus in the other [recension].
This indeed is the supreme abode of the teacher of the King of Mantras, where there is no suffering and the like, where the sun does not shine,

where death does not enter, and where no defect exists; it is that eternal bliss, the peaceful, the ever-auspicious Brahman, worshipped by Brahmā and others, meditated upon by yogis, having gone to which they do not return.
For the yogin, this very point is expressed by a Rigvedic verse: "The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, like an eye stretched across the sky; the inspired poets, full of praise..."
"The watchful ones kindle it,
that which is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu"— thus it is stated in the *Śrī-Nṛsiṃha-Tāpanīya-Upaniṣad* (5.10).
Yet even this [verse] should not be explained as referring to the city of Brahman (*brahma-pura*).
By the phrase "having gone there" [in the verse], he does not accept that [the world] is merely a place of worship;
for this *ṛc* was recollected with reference to the realm of Śrī Viṣṇu in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*, as follows:
Above and beyond the Ṛṣis is Dhruva, where he is firmly established.
O Brahmin, that is the supreme abode for ascetics who have shaken off the mire of defects and whose selves are fully restrained, once their merit and demerit have been exhausted.
Where, upon the cessation of both demerit and merit, the causes for exhaustion and decay are destroyed,
and having gone there one does not grieve— that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
That supreme abode of Viṣṇu, where Dhruva and the others who are witnesses of the world abide in accordance with Dharma, is illumined by the yoga produced from attaining equality with Him.

"That wherein this entire universe— the past, the moving and the non-moving, and that which is yet to be— is woven like warp and woof, O Maitreya, that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. And in the *Tāpanī-śruti*, there is the passage beginning with "where the wind does not blow," which describes the state beyond material nature (*aprākṛta*).
Even there, it consists of the negation of each respective [object], because those very things are heard in that context;
however, one who has been pierced in the heart by the word-arrows of a co-wife or a stepmother, remembering them—
"He did not desire liberation from the Lord of Liberation, having subsequently fallen into remorse" (BhP 4.9.29). Likewise:
"Alas! What a lack of self-knowledge on my part!"
Behold the misfortune of one who,
having gone to the feet of the Destroyer of Existence, begs for that which is finite!
Thus, the humility of Śrī Dhruva is heard [in BhP 4.9.31].

It is fitting that even though he had obtained a boon exceeding his desires, he spoke in such a way merely to set aside his own ambition, having prayed for that high station solely out of a desire for it.
For it was said there indeed by the venerable Vidura: "That supreme state of Hari is very difficult to attain" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.9.28);
and by the venerable Dhruva himself, who is dear to Him:
Then you shall go to my abode,
which is honored by all the worlds,
situated above the rishis.
"From which, once gone, one does not return" (BhP 4.9.25);

thus it was said by the two Śrī-Pārṣadas as well: "Abide in that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, which is worshiped by the worlds" (BhP 4.12.26). And by the son of Śrī [Śukadeva], regarding Dhruva’s Vaikuṇṭha—

Regarding "ascending to the foot" (padādhirohaṇam) [BhP 4.10.1], and in the description of the wheel of light in the fifth book: "They circumambulate that which is the supreme foot of Viṣṇu" [BhP 5.22.17]. That which belongs to Viṣṇu...

And because it says, "They proclaim the supreme state" (BhP 5.23.1); for even though it is included within phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*), its nature as that which is spoken of as a quality remains unchanging, according to the principle: "It likewise states its abiding condition by way of not participating in modification. Therefore, in this...
In this world, it should be understood that only the external, phenomenal portion undergoes dissolution;
at that time, however,
there is merely its disappearance.
Taking this very point as his basis, Hiraṇyakaśipu said: "What is the use of others, such as the Vaiṣṇavas and so forth, who have been swept away by Time at the end of the aeon? (BhP 7.3.11).
Therefore, even today, those who speak in such a manner [are following his example].
The meaning is that they too are equal to that.
Furthermore, the nature of Śrī Mahāvaikuṇṭha as being such is all the more evident,
just as [is described] in various Vedic scriptures.
In the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa* as well, following the description of the manifestations (*vibhūti*) included within *prakṛti*, Śrī Śiva has manifested that very nature through the raising of the path:
"Such is the supreme form of the manifestation whose nature is *prakṛta*."
But hear now, O daughter of the mountain, of the form of the three-quartered manifestation.
Between Pradhāna and the supreme ether flows the auspicious Virajā river, made to flow by the waters produced from the perspiration of the Vedāṅgas.
Beyond that is the supreme ether, consisting of three-quarters,
eternal, immortal, perpetual, constant, infinite, and the highest state.
It is composed of pure sattva, divine, imperishable, the station of Brahman,
possessing a splendor equal to many millions of suns and fires, and immutable.
Consisting of all the Vedas, pure, and devoid of all dissolution;
golden, the state of liberation, called the bliss of Brahman.
It is free from equality or excess, devoid of beginning or end, and auspicious.
That supreme abode of Viṣṇu is endowed with such qualities as being most wonderful in its splendor, delightful, and an eternal ocean of bliss.
Neither the sun, nor the moon,
nor fire illumines that supreme abode of Hari, reaching which they do not return.
That supreme abode of Viṣṇu is eternal, constant, and infallible;
indeed, it cannot be described even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. (PadmaP 6.227.57–hareḥ padaṃ varṇayituṃ na śakyam)
Whether it be by me, by the Creator, or by the most excellent lords of sages— that immutable Lord who resides in that state—
He alone knows it, or perhaps He does not know it at all.
That syllable which is the secret of the Vedas, in which all the gods are seated—what will he do with the Rigveda who does not know it? But those who know it, they sit together here.
The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu—
the imperishable, eternal, and constant, like an eye stretched out in the sky.
It is impossible for deities such as Brahmā and Rudra to enter;
it is perceived by the foremost of yogis through knowledge according to the path of the scriptures.
Neither I, nor Brahmā, nor the gods, nor the great sages know the meaning of all the Upaniṣads; having seen it, O lady of virtuous vows, I shall speak.
In the supreme station of Viṣṇu, however, is the fountain called Śubha in the midst;
there the cows with many-horned heads, the progeny, dwell in their own happiness.
For here shines that supreme abode of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow as he is being sung;
that supreme abode shines through the rays of his songs, which bear auspicious names.
The world of Brahman, radiant as the sun, beyond darkness, the supreme light, is the support; it is pure and indeed eternal.
In this eternal state, far from the undifferentiated generality,
the two youths Śrī and Sanātana remain awake, steadfast and alert.
Since you, O sister Bhūlīlā, beloved of Viṣṇu, are young;
and here are the ancient Sādhyas and Viśvedevas who existed in the past.
Those great ones, of auspicious appearance, having attained the celestial realm,
the wise Brahmins who have realized it kindle that station through their knowledge.
That supreme abode of Viṣṇu is designated as liberation;
in that state, those freed from bondage attain their own true, blissful station.
Having attained which they do not return, therefore it is called liberation (mokṣa).
Liberation is the supreme state, the subtle body (liṅga), the immortal, and the abode of Viṣṇu.
The imperishable, the supreme abode, Vaikuṇṭha, the eternal and highest,
the perpetual, the supreme ether, the most excellent, and the ancient.
"Indeed, these are synonyms for that supreme abode of the Infallible One;
now I shall describe in detail the form of His three-quarter manifestation," and so forth.

These scriptural citations from the Rītikas are generally well-known among Vedic scholars and thus are not cited here. Furthermore, in the *Śrī-Nārada-Pañcarātra*, within the dialogue between Śrī Brahmā and Nārada and in the hymn *Jitaṃ te*, it is said:
"The world named Vaikuṇṭha, endowed with the six divine qualities..."
It is unattainable for those who are not Vaiṣṇavas, and it is devoid of the three qualities (guṇas).
It was eternally established and filled with those devoted to the five-fold ritual times;
it was graced with assembly halls, palaces, groves, and auspicious pleasure gardens.
It was beautifully adorned with ponds, wells, lakes, and groves of trees;
it was extraordinary, worthy of worship by the gods, and possessed a radiance equal to ten thousand suns. Thus [it was described].
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Him, the abode of infinite qualities, the great splendor difficult to approach, imperceptible, incomparable, supreme bliss beyond the senses. Thus it is said.
In the *Mudgalopākhyāna* within the *Itihāsa-samuccaya*:
"Above the abode of Brahmā is that supreme station of Viṣṇu,
the pure, eternal light which they know as the Supreme Brahman."
Those virtuous ones who are free from possessiveness, free from egoism, free from the pairs of opposites, who have conquered their senses, and who are devoted to meditation and yoga— they go there.
Those who worship Hari, Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, the Victorious, the Eternal,
the unborn god Nārāyaṇa, Viṣvaksena, the four-armed one;
"Those who meditate upon the divine Person and remember the Infallible attain the station of the Infallible; this is the eternal Vedic revelation. Thus [it is said].
In the *Skānda Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śrī Sanat-kumāra and Mārkaṇḍeya:

"O best of Brahmins, he who is a devotee of Viṣṇu and is marked with the pure signs of the discus and so forth, indeed goes to the world of Viṣṇu, which is free from burning and dissolution. Thus it is said.

In this context, if someone somehow interprets the word "pada," "dhāma," and so forth— which denote location— as denoting the essential nature (*svarūpa*) itself because it is not conventionally established as such,
then that same [fault] would apply elsewhere as well.
This [objection] must be refuted by the explicit mention of the word "place" (*sthāna*) in such passages as, "They go to that place which they know as the supreme Brahman," and so forth;
for even there, one would have to resort to supplying ellipses such as the word "and" (*ca*).

If, out of dejection, one accepts a split in the sentence— contrary to the qualification "that which they know as the Supreme Brahman" found in the aforementioned collection of Itihāsas— then one must rely upon the word *loka* as it is used in various places within one's own school of thought.

And thus, because those words—*pada*, *dhāman*, *sthāna*, *loka*, and *rūpa*—are employed together for a single object while mutually excluding other meanings, what [meaning] do they not make known of their own referent?
For example: "This is the Blessed Lord Hari Viṣṇu."

Now, if it is argued that even there [the word "Brahman"] seeks to denote its own essential nature alone, then the opponent must clearly be put to shame by the statements of the *Padma Purāṇa*, the *Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa*, and other such texts.

However, it must be stated that there certainly exist specific scriptural passages— such as those depicting Him with a cane in His hand— that establish His unattainability by karma and other such factors;
therefore, the verse beginning with "oṃ namas te" (BhP 6.9.33) has also been correctly explained.
// 6.9 // The gods [worship] Śrī-Hari //75// [76] Thus, the nature of Śrī-Vaikuntha has been described; and that is exactly as the Blessed Lord Himself.
It exists in some places in its entirety and in others as a partial portion; likewise,
its many subdivisions should be observed in the *Pādmottarakhaṇḍa* and other such texts.
It indicates that very point— that even the footprints of Śrī, Matsya, Deva, and others will be described therein:
Thus, having destroyed Hiraṇyākṣa of unbearable prowess, Hari, the primordial Boar,
returned to his own world of unimpeded festivities.
"Propitiated by means of the *puṣkaraviṣṭara* and other offerings.
Having placed and having struck [the vessel],
Bodhāyana says this in the context of the *pavitrāropaṇa*:
"Thus, the wise man who performs this every year undoubtedly goes to the supreme abode where the Lord, the Man-lion, resides.
In the *Vāyu Purāṇa*, however, Śiva’s city is likewise heard of, as follows:
But surrounding the edge of the inner ocean on all sides is the Ghanodadhi ocean;
supported on all sides by its waters, it remains stable.
On the outside, it stands encircling the mass of water on all sides— horizontally and upwards—
sustaining it with its intense radiance.
The fire, resembling a glowing iron ball and circular in shape,
remains there, supported on all sides by a dense wind.
The origin of the elements and likewise space, as well as the origin of the elements and the Great One (mahat),
are supported by the Great One, which is pervaded by the infinite Unmanifest (avyakta).
It is infinite, unmanifest, and without beginning or end;
it is mere darkness, devoid of light, boundless, and without a guide.
"At the end of darkness and at the end of space, it is renowned and radiant;
because it extends to the furthest limit, that great abode of Śiva is a divine place inaccessible even to the thirty gods— so says the Śruti."

// 3.19 // Śrī Maitreya //76// [77] And thus, just as the body of the illustrious Blessed One manifests in the world, so too is it heard that in some place, for someone, the manifestation of that very state occurs.
Vikuṇṭhā was the wife of Śubhra; by her and through the Vaikuṇṭhas, the best of the gods, the Lord Vaikuṇṭha himself was born from their own portions.
By him, desiring to please the Goddess and being entreated by her, Vaikuṇṭha— the world honored by all the worlds— was fashioned.
Just as the mere manifestation of the Blessed Lord is called his "birth," so too...

Even the conceptualization and manifestation of Vaikuṇṭha is not artificial like that of material things; rather, because both are eternal, he says "he was born" (jajñe) to indicate their similarity. Śrī—
This Vaikuṇṭha belongs to the son of Vikuṇṭha alone;
however, it is well known from the Second Canto that the primordial Vaikuṇṭha was seen by Śrī Brahmā prior to creation.
It is said: "Having searched that dwelling and seeing it empty, he roared in anger" (BhP 8.19.11). That place, however, should be understood as being located in heaven and so forth.
// 8.5 // Śrī Śuka said: //77// [78] For those who dwell in the city of Vaikuṇṭha, who are devoid of body, senses, and life-force... [BhP 7.1.34]
The meaning is: for those who are devoid of the material body, senses, and vital breaths which constitute the cause of birth, and who possess bodies composed of pure *sattva*.
// 7.1 // Yudhiṣṭhira [spoke] to the venerable Nārada // 78 // [79] Likewise—
by means of sixteen [attendants] equal to himself—
[He saw him] being attended by those whose eyes were like blossoming autumn lotuses, though he was without the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem.
[He was accompanied] by sixteen [attendants], beginning with Śrī-Sunanda. Śrī Śuka said:
[80] For this very reason, they have transcended time and are in close proximity to the supreme human goal even for those who are supremely devoted;
thus he says: "Therefore, I know those blessings of embodied beings—longevity, prosperity, power..."
"From Indra up to Brahmā,
I do not desire those who have been agitated by You, whose nature is Time and whose strides are vast; lead me instead to the side of Your own servants."
This is clear. 7.9. Prahlāda [worships] Śrī-Nṛsiṃha. 80. [81] And likewise in the Pādma-Uttara-khaṇḍa:
"The worlds of the three-quarters of the manifestation are proclaimed to be innumerable."
All of them consist of pure sattva and are designated by the bliss of Brahman-ānanda.
All are eternal and changeless, free from the passion for that which is to be abandoned;
all are golden, pure, and possess a radiance equal to ten million suns.
All were divine, consisting of the Vedas, free from desire, anger, and other such passions,
and devoted solely to the singular essence of devotion for the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa.
"Resorting to the constant bliss of the complete chanting of the Sāman,
they all possess the splendor of the Vedas through their very nature as the five Upaniṣads," and so forth.

In this context, by the term "three-quarter manifestation" (tripād-vibhūti), the world beyond phenomenal expansion (prapañca) is denoted, whereas by the term "quarter manifestation" (pāda-vibhūti), phenomenal expansion itself is denoted.
As it has been stated in that very same place:
The three-quarters are pervasion in the supreme abode; one quarter of this [Being] came into existence here again.
Of that fourfold manifestation, the three-quarters are eternal, while the divine quarter is transient.
That form of the Lord is eternal, auspicious, and situated in the supreme abode;
it is infallible, everlasting, divine, and always endowed with youth.
It is eternally endowed with enjoyment, sovereignty, glory, and the earth. Thus it is said.
Therefore, the second book should also be interpreted accordingly. In that regard:
"He is the Lord of immortality and fearlessness, who has transcended mortal food."
Therefore, O Brahmin, this majesty of the Puruṣa is difficult to surpass.
The pair beginning with "immortality" (amṛta) is also an elliptical reference to "security" (kṣema), which will be mentioned as the third.

And in the Śruti: "Moreover, he is the Lord of immortality"—here, "immortality" is indicative of that pair. In this [text], there is a mention of the substratum (dharmin) as the primary element, whereas in the Śruti, there is also a mention of the mere attribute (dharma).
The intended meaning lies precisely there:
"Amṛta" (the nectar) refers to that which is praised by those persons who have seen their own Self;
and according to the statement beginning with "That which is beyond the highest" (*BhP* 2.9.9), it is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).

For this very reason, its synonym is "Amṛta Viṣṇu-mandira" (the Immortal Abode of Viṣṇu). "Fearlessness" refers to the total absence of even the slightest fear, as expressed in passages such as, "And there is no dread of the onset of Time" (BhP 2.9.10).

Therefore, it is said: "O twice-born ones, the abode is fearless from all sides" (BhP 12.11.19). According to such statements as "Where there is no security, there is Māyā" (BhP 2.9.10), there is an absence of any connection with qualities that cause one to turn away from the Blessed Lord.
It should be understood that the worship of the Blessed Lord is the locus of all auspiciousness.
Thus it is said in the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"She who is the crest-jewel of all auspicious things, eternally composed of perfect bliss..."
"O best of the twice-born, may you possess unwavering devotion toward me. Thus [he spoke].
"Only there do they find security, my own abode," so it is said.

In that context, by means of various words and through the difficult interpretation of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), he establishes the reason for negating the denotation of Janaloka and the other worlds: "Even for Brahmā, there is fear of me, the mortal one, for two *parārdhas*."
By the principle expressed in *parāyuṣa* (BhP 11.10.30) and other such passages, he is subject to the nature of death;
yet, because he has transcended—having gone beyond—the food that is the fruit of karma and so forth, as well as the three worlds and the rest, he shines resplendent therein. This is he.
His nature consists of sovereignty over immortality and other such powers;
he is difficult to overcome—incapable of being restrained even by the mind of anyone, despite their practice of celibacy and other disciplines. [82]
Thus, having stated that immortal sovereignty consists of three quarters and mortal [sovereignty] of one quarter, he further elucidates his fourfold sovereignty.
Those who abide in the state of the Supreme Person know that all beings reside in His feet; there,
immortality, security, and fearlessness are found.
[The threefold power] was placed upon the heads of the Three-headed One.

"Sthitayaḥ" refers to the sovereign powers of mortals and others, in which all beings abide; He whose feet are such supports—He of the Staying-Foot—is the Lord of sovereignty within His four feet alone.

Within the parts [of the body], he displays all beings, down to the attendants (*pārṣada*). The "head" (*mūrdhan*) is the very summit—the active manifestation—of the three categories of objects, beginning with the *sāttvika*. Of those three, [he displays them].
Upon those crowns, which shine resplendently above, the immortal, secure, and fearless state of Śrī-Vaikuṇṭha-loka is established; the meaning is that it remains eternally sustained there.
Consequently, because the former consists merely of mortal food, it possesses only one foot.
The sense is that because the northern quarter consists of the triad beginning with Amṛta, it possesses three quarters; thus,
by this, [it is shown that] "all beings are one quarter of Him."
The meaning of the verse "Three-quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven" has been shown.
Its "quarter" is likewise in that very direction, in Vaikuṇṭha; and that which consists of the immortal and so forth, being three-quarters, is the meaning of "all beings."
Here, there is a statement of the identity between the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and that which is supported (*adhiṣṭheya*).
Now, regarding its fourfold nature, he shows another alternative view, similar to the arrangement of the three worlds:
"The three feet were outside. [83]
The stages of life for those lacking progeny end within the three worlds; however, the householder’s life, though its vows are not extensive, is superior to them.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of a cumulative conjunction (*samuccaya*).
The three feet were indeed situated outside of *prapañca*;
however, as for the division that is the opposite of the fourth foot—which is of the nature of *prapañca*—it is situated outside the triple world (*trilokī*).
And there were three other quarters; thus the mantra also speaks likewise with the word "punaḥ" (again). Which are they?

They are the worlds to be attained by those in the stages of life (*āśrama*) who do not procreate—namely, the celibate student (*brahmacārī*), the forest-dweller (*vanastha*), and the ascetic (*yatī*).
Therefore, because all four are attainable through the three-fold dharma, they possess the status of being "three-quarters."
But the fourth quarter is "within" the three worlds; therefore, the householder is to attain that. For this very reason, he says that the person is four-quartered in both ways.
He has traversed both paths— the one that consumes and the one that does not consume—
namely, ignorance and knowledge.
But the Puruṣa is the support of both;
he is Viṣvaṅ, the all-pervading,
the Puruṣa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
These two paths, characterized as the manifold (prapañca) and the non-manifold (aprapañca), are the two courses of the individual soul (jīva).
He has stepped across them— he stands having traversed them.
Of what nature?
It is characterized by both the consumption and non-consumption [of karma], being joined with the experience of the fruits of karma and so forth, as well as the transcendence thereof;
this belongs to that very [soul].
The cause for the invasion is as follows:
the meaning is that ignorance and illusion (*māyā*) are the substratum in one stream, while knowledge (*vidyā*) and the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) are the substratum in the other.

But Puruṣottama is the substratum of both of these; and this will be stated by the passage beginning with "From whom Virāṭ was born as Daṇḍa" (BhP 2.6.21). Therefore, the sense is that the fourfold nature [of dharma] exists through both universal sovereignty and partial sovereignty.

// 2.6 // Śrī-Brahmā to Śrī-Nārada // 84 // [85] Thus, because the Blessed One— who possesses the majesty of peaceful inner nature— is manifested by His very power which constitutes His own essential nature (*svarūpa*), that power is of the nature of His essential nature.

And since that [power] is the very nature of that which is qualified by power, even while falling within its own nature, it undergoes a function characterized by differentiation; therein, it manifests a particularity of illumination and a multitude of variegations.

In each such case, regarding that very state, our authority is precisely those gurus who have attained perfection through the practice of *bhrama-upāsanā*. This very point he expresses in fourteen [verses]:
Thus, at that very moment, the Blessed One, whose navel is like a lotus and whose heart is dear to the noble ones, having perceived the transgression of his own people,
went to that place of the great sages who are supreme swans.
Moving his feet, which were worthy of being sought after, together with Śrī;
they beheld him who had arrived with the necessary offerings brought by their own men—
him who was the object of their eyes and the fortunate fruit of their own meditative concentration.
He held two fans of the splendor of swans, and a white parasol— like the moon with its filaments of light— shaken by the auspicious breeze;
he whose face was gracious with complete favor, and whose abode was desirable.
He touched his heart with a glance full of affection,
as if beautifying his own abode by adorning his crest-jewel with the splendor gracing his broad, dark chest.
Upon her broad hips, clad in yellow garments, she shone with a girdle of many tinkling bells and a forest garland;
and upon the shoulder of the son of Vinatā, he saw his own beautiful bracelets.
With one hand placed [on his hip] and shaking a lotus with the other,
his high cheekbones and face were worthy of adornment by makara-shaped earrings flashing like lightning; he wore a crown set with jewels.
With a priceless necklace moving through the space between his arms and the Kaustubha gem resting upon his neck,
he was accompanied by the gentle smile of Indirā, which was directed toward him.

Whose eyes, never satiated with joy upon beholding Him, did not bow down in delight— He who was fashioned by the intellect of His own people, who is enriched with manifold beauty, and who honors me, Śiva, as well as all of you? [BhP 3.15.42]
The breeze, carrying the nectar of *tulasī* mixed with the filaments of the lotus feet of that lotus-eyed one,
entered through their own openings and purified them.
They caused agitation even to the minds and bodies of those who dwell in the imperishable;
for they gazed upon the lotus-bud of his face, with its most beautiful lower lip and jasmine-like smile.
Having received their blessings, they should again gaze upon His pair of feet, which serve as a resting place for the red-jewel-like nails,
for those men who seek the ultimate goal here through the paths of yoga.

They praised him who displayed a masculine form, highly esteemed as the abode of meditation and delightful to the eyes, endowed with innate perfections unattainable by others and possessed of the eightfold sovereign powers.
The Śrī-kumāras said:
You, who remain hidden even though you have entered the hearts of the evil-minded, have this very day been attained by us at the very root of our vision, O Infinite One!
When indeed that secret was described by our father, who was born from you, as it entered the cave of our ears,
we know You, O Blessed One, as the supreme reality of the Self.
Because they now cultivate delight in these [scriptures] with their whole being,
the dispassionate sages, whose knots have been untied, perceive them in their hearts through the application of firm devotion known by remorse.
They do not even reckon Your favor as ultimate, much less anything else that carries fear with the raising of Your eyebrows; O Lord,
those who have taken refuge at Your feet are devoted to Your story.
Those who are skilled in discerning aesthetic flavor find delight in the fame of the holy places worthy of praise.
May Lord Bhava lead us to the hells by our own sins, provided that our hearts may take pleasure in Your feet like bees.
O Puruhūta, if our speech were like the *tulasī* plant, it would be filled with the splendor of Your feet;
and if our ear-cavities were filled with the multitude of Your virtues—
since You have manifested this form.
By that, our eyes have attained complete fulfillment;
let us offer this salutation to the Blessed One, who is recognized as the Lord whose manifestation is difficult for those lacking self-mastery to attain. [BhP 3.15.50]
Now it is explained in sequence:
"In this way, at that very moment. And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says:
"In this way, having immediately recognized a transgression or offense against his own elders at that very instant,"
He went to that place where Sanaka and the others had been obstructed by Jaya and Vijaya; it was a region dear to the hearts of the noble ones (*ārya*),
and he proceeded while setting his feet in motion.
The intention was this: "I shall pacify the anger born from their obstruction of my sight of the feet by demonstrating them [to them]. Thus, under the pretext of haste, he went on foot.
And [the Lord] bestowed the glory of refined literature upon them so that He might satisfy even those free from desire with His opulences and ask for their forgiveness; such is this [account].
Herein, for the sake of granting bliss even to those who delight only in the Self, by means of the sight of His feet—his...
The state of being a mass of existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānandaghana) is intended;
by means of the word "Śrī," it is further intended that even the playful manifestation of His power is non-different from His essential nature.

The plural number in "svānām" (of their own) is used either with the consideration that the fault of even two [individuals] falls upon all members of the retinue, or out of great respect for those two;
by the word "sva" (own), it is intended to show that the sages do not possess such a sense of personal ownership.
There, he describes with five verses what was seen by them regarding the Lord:
"But when He had arrived," and so forth; those [sages] beginning with Sanaka, through their own meditative absorption (*samādhi*), [perceived] that Brahman which is fortune, the fruit to be attained.
Or rather,

it is the fortune that consists of the fruit, arising from the manifestation of the supreme reality (para-tattva) in the form of Brahman within one's own heart through one's own meditative absorption (samādhi), which is the object of the senses.

For that which is the object of the senses is now being clearly experienced as it manifests through all the faculties of cognition and action, having been refined by the power of its own self-luminosity.

By this, as before, it has been established that all phenomena— namely those called sound, touch, form, taste, and smell— are essentially a mass of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*sac-cid-ānanda*). Likewise, they are eternally possessed of such ever-arising sweetness.

He was being served by his own personal attendants, who, preceded by the experience of manifold wonders, were serving him with various articles for service brought from the abundance of the highest bliss of supreme love.

At that time, having somehow, somewhere, and only at some rare moment, beheld the Blessed One solely through the dawning of some fortune born of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), they [longed] for even a fraction of the bliss of the Blessed One in those beings of Śrī-Vaikunṭha, who are the objects of longing for those supreme sages.
The nature of Śakti as consisting of playful manifestation (*vilāsa*) has been shown.

Now, because they cause agitation to the mind by acting as excitants (*uddīpana*) for devotion to the Lord, he describes the same quality of their attendants and so forth in three and a half verses beginning with "Haṃsa. [The verse begins: *Keśarā*...
"Long pendants made of pearls" refers to the "entirety of the serene ones," meaning the entire [assembly] of gatekeepers and sages.

"In the grace of the multitude" means "having a pleasant countenance"; thus, it is shown that he is the abode, the locus, of all desirable qualities. "With a glance of affection" indicates his charm; [it is] heavenly bliss—
The places of enjoyment (bhoga-sthānāni) consist of the nature of eternal and infinite bliss;
and their crest-jewel (cūḍāmaṇi)— the abode of the Self, one's own essential form— is the place of Śrī Vaikuṇṭha.

Even though he was of such a nature, he seemed to be making himself fortunate by means of the beauty gracing his chest, as if placing a particular ornament there; "as if" (*iva*) is used here as a poetic figure (*vākyālaṅkāra*).
By this, the glory of Śrī Vaikuṇṭha is described;
and it has been stated in passages such as "He is the preceptor of the universe" (tad-viśva-guru) and "They attained supreme joy" (āpuḥ parāṃ mudam), etc. (BhP 3.16.26).
Furthermore, it will be said later:
Then those sages, having seen Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of that [Lord], which was a vessel for the delight of their eyes, [were filled with wonder].
And having circumambulated, prostrated before, and paid homage to the self-effulgent Lord of Vikuṇṭha, [he departed].
They returned, greatly rejoiced, praising the Vaiṣṇava splendor;
thus [it is said]: "in yellow garments."
In the phrase "with a girdle and a garland of forest flowers," the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of a characteristic (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the word "lightning": it means "by that which is captivating" (*haratā* = *manohareṇa*).
Thus, having described the attire and other such items as being likewise [beautiful], he again [describes] his extreme mental...
The word *hara* means "taking away" when preceded by the prefix *ava*; thus,
*indirāyā utsmitam* refers to the pride of Indirā,
which has been taken away (*ava-upasṛṣṭam*) by the Blessed One.
It was conjectured by their minds that, through the constant acquisition of this beloved one, [his splendor] has become eternally and even more intensely manifest;
the reason for this is— *bahu-*...
[It is] rich in excellence and endowed with the perfection of infinite forms and qualities.
Now, one might ask: "How can there be a manifestation of such a supreme reality, which is even for Lakṣmī herself a great secret treasury? To this, he says: "To me."
The meaning is: for the sake of devotees such as Madhu and others, He assumes a limb, manifesting a form that accepts us as His own objects of concern.
Your nature of supreme asceticism, which transcends all three types of boundaries and surpasses all expectations,
remains concealed even by you through the power of illusion.
Some, whose being is non-dual with you, behold [you] incessantly.
As it is said in the *Stotra-ratna* (verse 13):
"Devotion alone leads him; devotion alone reveals him," and so forth, according to the Śruti. Such being the case...
They announced him; and having gazed upon him with joy, they bowed their heads,
yet they were not especially satiated.
Those whose eyes are such [as described];

"of him" (tasya) [refers to the Lord]. And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "It is stated that for them, the bliss of worship (*bhajanānanda*) is even greater than the bliss of their own essential nature (*svarūpānanda*). [This refers to] the *tulasī* which is mixed with the filaments (*kiñjalka*), the pollen, of his lotus feet.
The wind joined with *makaranda* [nectar],
through its own aperture— the nostril—
of those who partake of the syllables (*akṣara*).
Even for those who dwell in the bliss of Brahman,
there is agitation in the mind, excessive joy, and horripilation on the body; such is this [state].

In this context, it should be explained that the *tulasī* is mixed with the filaments (*kiñjalka*) of the lotuses (*aravinda*) on the two feet. Furthermore, at that time, both the lotuses and the *tulasī* should be understood as being situated within the forest garland (*vana-mālā*).
Let it be so, for they are of the nature of the Blessed One (*bhagavat*).
The meaning is that the capacity to cause agitation belongs not only to those primary and secondary limbs of the elements, but also to the wind associated with them.
He describes the agitation caused by joy in two verses.
Regarding the phrase "te vā": indeed, they,
having their desires fulfilled upon looking up at that very face— which is like the slightly blossomed bud of a blue lotus, a dark-blue water-lily— [beheld it].
Having again and again beheld with a downward gaze the pair of feet— the very refuge and support for those sun-crystals which are the rays—
[she did so] because she was unable to grasp the beauty of all his limbs simultaneously; and thereafter...
The meaning is that they fixed their gaze and reflected;
simultaneously, with the longing "How might we see all of this?", they reached the state called *cintā* (reflection), which nourishes the underlying emotion (*sthāyibhāva*).
"Of men" (puṃsām): highly esteemed even by Brahmā because it reveals wealth, it is an object of great reverence. "Displaying the male form" (pauṃsnaṃ vapur darśayānam):
the manifestation of the qualities of the Puruṣa who lies within the ocean of the womb (garbhoda-śāyin).
The meaning is that he displays his own body as non-different from that form known as Śrī-Viṣṇu, and not in any other way, as is the case with Brahmā and others;
[he does so] by means of his own, inherently established nature, which is not other [than that].
The meaning is "by the elements" (bhūtaiḥ).
For this very reason, they are "innate" (autpattikaiḥ), which means they are established as beginningless in that same way.
[The body] is endowed with the eightfold sovereignty such as atomization (aṇimā) and so forth; it is distinguished [by these], not merely characterized [by them].

By this, through the specific qualification of being the object of praise for them, their state as such is manifested— that is, they possess all divine attributes (bhaga) characterized by sovereignty.
"Samagṛṇan" means they praised correctly.

Then, the venerable Kumāras confirmed the Lord’s own words— which revealed His such-like state— by means of a hymn of praise that expressed their own inner devotion, saying: "The venerable Kumāras said."
He utters praise with five verses beginning with "yaḥ" (who).
Here, the explanation follows the principle of the verse: "Even for those who take pleasure in the syllables... (BhP 3.15.43).
That you always manifest in the form of Brahmā is not surprising;

but now you are directly perceived in a form that is of one essence with the supreme reality of dense light, manifested through the specific function of your own inherent power (svarūpa-śakti) characterized by pure being (viśuddha-sattva).
"Oh, what great fortune is ours!
they said.
"O Infinite One, You who, though dwelling within the hearts of the wicked, remain hidden and do not manifest Yourself—"
"You are not hidden from us; you have been attained and reached by us right here at the very root of our vision.
And thus, this is the subject matter (*viṣayavākya*) for the sūtra: "Also [the Lord is known] through perception and inference in the process of propitiation" (*api saṃrādhane pratyakṣānumānābhyām*).
"Those things which the Self-existent pierced through so as to be turned away; therefore you see the external, not the inner self.

Only some wise man, desiring immortality, has beheld the inward self with his eyes turned back. This is the reason for the absence of invisibility: when that Brahmā, your father and our own progenitor, [did so].
The very moment the secret was described and the mystery called Brahman was pointed out, at that very instant, through the path of action, I entered the cave of my intellect in the form of That.
Now, it may be argued: "The secret called the reality of the Self, which was taught by our father, is invisible;
but I must be something else, because I am visible."
"It is not so;
because the distinction [between the two] is dispelled by our recognition of you, they say:
'To you, that one...'"
O Blessed One, we know, we understand, and we recognize you as the supreme, absolute reality of the Self, whose nature is Brahman.
By what means do you recognize [this]?
Now, at this moment,
through [your] being— that is, by the manifestation of this form within us—
we have not known [you] for all this time.
The meaning is that we have now ascertained this through direct experience.
You appear to us even in our eyes, like Brahman, within the pure activity of the mind.
The intended meaning is that [the object] is not [established] merely by way of being visible.
They say that it is not merely recognition alone;
[it is that which] produces delight for us.
The sense is that, otherwise, even our love for You would not arise.

By demonstrating through their state of being free from egoism, pride, and so forth, that even other self-delighted ones lack love for anything else, they describe the reality of His nature; therein, by virtue of the excellence of the means, there is something indescribable.
And they say this is its distinction:

that the reality of the Self, manifesting as your very form, is your remorse and compassion; through that alone, those who know perceive it by means of firm yoga of devotion (bhakti-yoga) made known by you.
Or rather, [I know them] through your firm yoga of devotion, made known by your remorse and humility;
of what sort are they? They are those who have untied their knots and are free from egoistic pride.
Therefore, they are free from passion (*virāga*).

Thus, in the passage "the secrets described by the father," it is indicated that the word *rahas* (secret) refers exclusively to the love of devotion (*prema-bhakti*), according to the manner of the four verses.
Now, although previously they possessed non-dualistic minds, their thoughts are now variegated by the playful manifestations of the power of the bliss of one's own essential nature; thus,
once again seeking devotion characterized by duality, they describe the supreme happiness of the devotees:
"Not ultimate" means even that clarity characterized by liberation is not ultimate, let alone other states such as the rank of Indra and so forth.
Now, manifesting their own transgression, they pray with devotion, saying "Kāmam":
"O Blessed One, previously we had no sin; but now, indeed, all [our sins]..."
Since they were born cursed for their lack of devotion to you,
let our birth (bhava) be at will among those sinful ones in the hells.

By this, through the principle that "the non-clinging and destruction [of karma] in the subsequent and prior halves [of life] occur upon the realization of That, because of the designation thereof," even for those knowers of Brahman who are otherwise incapable of such states, there occurs the forgiveness of the fall into manifold sins that cause hell, thereby effecting the non-clinging and destruction of those two.
Just as in the expression "Hari, who possesses such qualities," his state of being the most wondrously great of all is indicated. Alas! Even the hells would surely come to pass;
yet even that is not sufficient.
And we have no fear even of them;
however, the root cause here is the very state of being turned away from the Blessed One, which bears evil fruit,
and that [state] belongs to us.
"They pray with a tone of lamentation, 'May it not be so!'"— here *nu* expresses a deliberation (*vitarke*).
"But if your mind [is set] upon our feet..."
One may take delight even there, but that too is solely in view of tasting its sweetness, and not in view of the experience of Brahman as the Self;
thus it is said, "and so forth regarding speech," and so on.

In this context, it should be understood that the Blessed One’s forgiveness of the offense was due to the fact that their anger was produced merely by his own will, and thus their offense was only an appearance of an offense.

In these two verses, it is naturally implied that for us— who desire nothing but devotion to You— hell itself is superior even to absolute liberation (kaivalya), because it is not incompatible with that devotion;
nevertheless, it is as follows:

They say, "The fulfillment of our purpose is most wonderful," with the words "Prāduḥ" (manifest). To You, who—though unmanifest to those without self-mastery, who lack exclusive devotion to Your Self—are thus perceived; to Him [I offer salutation].
"Let us pay this homage to you.
By this, it is meant that these [are the means] for the knowledge of Brahman.
They are the teachers even of the Siddhas and of the gurus of both the higher and lower paths;
for this very reason, they are called the great sages of the Paramahaṃsas.

I seek You, that mass of knowledge, who are contemplated within the hearts of Sanandana and others, while the delusions regarding the distinctions of the qualities of *māyā* have been destroyed by Your very nature.
