Thus, at the beginning of the words of the illustrious Aṃśumat, he correctly declared the reality of the self; and at the beginning of the words of Brahmā, "O Self, that which the sages have perceived," he spoke to him whose impurities had been washed away.
The Lord Sanatkumāra shows the further shore of darkness; this is likewise well-known in the Śruti.
However, even for one who has already attained experience, there may be obstacles such as the powers of atomization (aṇimā) and so forth.
It is to be cultivated,
but not for one who has already attained realization;
[rather, it is for one] who has ascended to that samādhi along with its conceptual elaborations.
"Yoga does not again resort to the dream-state, for its object is reality as perceived by one who has awakened"— from this statement of Śrī Kapiladeva,
it follows that even anger and other such emotions do not arise in those whose delusion regarding the distinctions of the qualities of māyā has been utterly destroyed.
They have also explained that it arose solely through the will of the illustrious Blessed One, who brings about the impossible;
thus, their state of being constantly immersed in the bliss of Brahman is established. That...
It has been stated: "even for those who enjoy the syllables" (BhP 3.15.43), and "he who has disappeared" (BhP 3.15.46), and so forth;
and elsewhere it is heard that those who enjoy Brahman possess undistracted minds.
As stated in the seventh [chapter] in the words of Śrī Nārada: "That which is unimpeded by desire and the like, wherein all mental fluctuations have become tranquil..."
"The mind touched by the bliss of Brahman shall never arise again" (BhP 7.15.35);
nevertheless, it is said that their minds are drawn toward the bliss of the Blessed Lord.
The same applies to others as well.
Such a state is heard of those who delight in the Self in passages such as:

"With his mind intent on his own bliss, he cast that [desire for liberation] aside; though even non-existence [liberation] does not attract him, his essence is drawn by the charming pastimes of the Unconquered One" (BhP 12.12.68), and so forth.
Is their mode of devotion, characterized by outward dress for the sake of gathering the world, due to the force of ancient impressions?

It is not so; for in both cases, such a dress is merely a formal arrangement, as in the verse "blinded by the intoxication of wine" (BhP 3.28.37), because true absorption (*āveśa*) is impossible therein.
But it is seen elsewhere that there was no such entry [into the womb]: my mental sons, Sanaka and the others, who were born before you,
traveled through the worlds by way of the sky, free from [physical] bodies.
Because of the statement "longing" [BhP 3.15.12],
whereas in the case of the Blessed One, there is absorption (āveśa) for the great sages who are paramahaṃsas, as seen in the passage: "whose feet are to be sought after" [BhP 3.15.37].
Because it is stated that [the goal] is not accidental and must be sought out as something non-contradictory;
whereas in the fifth [chapter], for those whose every impurity has been shaken off by the fire of unattached, sharpened wisdom, and who delight in the Self— the very nature of existence— ...
In the prose passage beginning with "munīnām anavarata-pariguṇita-guṇa-gaṇa" (BhP 5.3.11), his exclusive devotion to Him alone is also stated;
likewise, in the verse "ajita-rucira-līlākṛṣṭa-sāra" (BhP 12.12.69), it is mentioned in that very same context.
And here too, in such passages as "By Him even the eyes attained cessation" (BhP 3.15.50),
the quality of bestowing happiness is explicitly stated.
Furthermore, in this praise, for the reason previously mentioned...

Nor should it be explained that because of the context of the "criticism of what has already occurred" (*pratutopālambha*) and the direct statement, "touching his heart with a fraction of a loving glance" (*snehāvaloka-kalayā hṛdi saṃspṛśantam*— BhP 3.15.39), pleasure arose for the eyes alone, thereby implying non-attachment (*anāsakti*).

Therefore, because He is the locus of delight for those who find pleasure in the Self, the Blessed Lord is indeed the reality of the Self known as Brahman. Furthermore, since it is heard in the scripture [BhP 3.15.43], "He caused agitation even in the mind and body of those who enjoy the Imperishable," He is even more intensely manifest than that.
That very variety of bliss is perceived through the observation of the various attachments to the limbs, minor limbs, and so forth of the glorious Blessed One;
and since it cannot be explained otherwise, it is indeed the manifestation of His own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*).
Now, let it be granted that, due to their abundance of bliss, there is in them a dense manifestation of the very bliss of the undifferentiated nature (svarūpa),
owing to the presence of limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
For, that Brahman which flashes forth within the mental modification (citta-vṛtti) cultivated by the portion of pure being (viśuddha-sattva),
that very same [Brahman] is the solidified, undivided pure being (akhaṇḍa-viśuddha-sattva).
When I, the Blessed One, am manifest through being superimposed upon that [form], having attained identity with it,
it manifests in a particularly distinct manner.
For this very reason, there are scriptural statements regarding the non-difference between the Śrī-vigraha and the Supreme Brahman.
This is indeed with reference to absolute identity;
for this very reason, in each and every limiting adjunct (upādhi), one and the same undivided supreme bliss is perceived.

But there is not even a scent of any particular form; rather, the requirement for this or that limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is rooted in the curiosity of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) on the bliss of each respective stage. Therefore, how could it be that by this means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), those various limiting adjuncts themselves possess the nature of the supreme reality?
"It is established," it is said: "In your own view, the Supreme Brahman manifests within the pure activity of the mind; indeed, it manifests perfectly."
Because it is accepted as the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) precisely through the abandonment of even a trace of the aspect of difference,
and because incorrect knowledge (*asamyagjñāna*) is not admitted to be the reality (*tattva*) by that [means].
And because of the impossibility of liberation (kaivalya),
it is therefore not logical to accept the manifestation of further [divine] powers within the glorious form (śrī-vigraha) and so forth.
Furthermore, what is your intention in asserting that the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) characterized by the body and so forth consist of pure sattva?
Are they transformations of that [sattva], or are they predominantly composed of it?
Not the first, for it has already been stated that transformation is impossible due to the non-existence of *rajas*;
nor the last, because in those [entities] such as the body (*vigraha*) and so forth, that—

Thus, because it is stated that [the Lord] is directly perceived (*gocarīkṛta*), the notion that He is seen through a lineage of tradition is refuted;

They are neither transformations of ordinary *sattva* nor abundant in it;

For the desired goal is accomplished by the mere presence of that which consists of unbroken, pure goodness;

By this statement that [the experience] is born from the gateway of the experience of the syllable (*akṣara*), the view that this is merely a semblance of absorption— similar to the grief for a son experienced by Vaiśiṣṭha and others— is also refuted.

"Variety.

In this context, any alternative resolution based on the word "sarvātman" (the self of all) is refuted in accordance with the subject matter of the section. Thus, it is stated later in the narrative concerning the Kṣatriya:

"For whatever I manifest, I shall indeed become composed of that."

In that very context, regarding the worship of the lunar mansion of the month, its transcendence is clearly stated as follows: "O Acyuta, you are beyond the beyond; you are the supreme Self, higher than that which has become Brahman."
"O Acyuta, likewise grant me my desire and remove my calamity, O Immeasurable One. Thus [he said].

And in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "He is the further shore of Brahman, having become the shore beyond the further shore," according to the Vedic revelation: "Higher than the Imperishable (akṣara), higher than that, is the Supreme."

// 4.24 // Śrī Rudra to Pracetas // 98 // [99] With this very intention, in the passage beginning "Now, this person consists of the essence of food" (TaittU 2.1), after each successive description of the innermost self, it is stated: "This earth is the tail, the support."

That Śruti is recorded by the word *pratiṣṭhā*, which is placed in proximity to the word *brahma*;

And he who serves Me with unswerving devotional yoga— he,

This is intended as the reason for the preceding statement, "He is fit for becoming Brahman" (Gītā 14.26);
therefore, [the state of] being beyond the qualities—

Since "Brahman" is the subject under discussion, it is inappropriate in this statement of the reason for the prior matter to use the word "that" (tat) in a figurative sense to denote another meaning, such as the form of Brahmā or the form of Hiraṇyagarbha; rather, it is appropriate only in its primary sense, as follows.

[Objection: But how can the attainment of the nature of the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahma*) come about through devotion to You? That [attainment] occurs through the exclusive experience of that [Brahman].
To this, he says: "For [it is said] 'the tail, the support, of Brahman'. For (*hi*), because it is stated that "the tail, the support, of Brahman," [devotion leads to that realization].

That which is well-known in the Śruti as being the supreme support is shown in that very Śruti to be a limb of the *ānandamaya*, namely the Brahman characterized as its "tail. Thus, the state of the supreme Brahman—designated as the *ānandamaya*—is the one intended by the author of the Sūtras in the aphorism: "The *ānandamaya* [is Brahman] because of the repetition [of the word 'bliss']."
Just as the sun is characterized by abundant light, so am I, the Blessed Lord, whose nature is abundant bliss; I am your foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Although there is no difference in substance between me, who am Brahman, and the Blessed Lord, nevertheless—[the Blessed Lord...]
The meaning is that by His form alone, He stands as if elevated above me; this is the supreme limit (*parā kāṣṭhā*),
because by the very manifestation of His essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*), even the manifestation of His own nature (*svarūpa*) is rendered more excellent.
For it is heard that even above the manifestation of the undifferentiated Brahman lies the manifestation of the Blessed Lord;
therefore, even of a single reality...

In that same manner, the differentiation of the light of the sun, which destroys the darkness of night, should be conceived as being like the differentiation of the rays contained within the solar orb;
therefore, since even the light of Brahman is dependent upon me, [it is attained] by means of that which is performed with the desire for liberation through me—
The meaning is that one being led toward Brahman by means of worship also attains the attributes of Brahman.
On this point, the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa also speaks in agreement: "He is the auspicious refuge for the mind, for the vital breath, and likewise for the self" (ViP 6.7.76).
And regarding this, the Masters have also explained:
"The support and foundation of the Self, who is identical with the group of deities (savarga), is also the Supreme Brahman.
As it was said by the Blessed One: "For I am the foundation of Brahman."
And regarding this, they have explained:
"I am the foundation of Brahman; I am indeed Brahman itself in its solidified state.
Just as [when] solidified—
The meaning is that the solar orb is indeed light; thus it is said.
Here, the suffix *cvi* is used because the manifestation of Brahman within the hearts of its respective worshippers is figuratively described as having been previously non-existent.

In this very context, the commentary stating that "the image is the installation" is fabricated out of malice;

having made each [basis] the object of observation,

O You who are beyond both the existent and the non-existent, and who are the immortal remnant remaining within these;
if those who bear the vital breath— living beings who are like bellows, appearing merely to breathe— even they become Your conforming devotees, then they truly breathe and live.
The sense is that we consider the life of only those living beings who are devoted to them [to be true life].
How so? Through the grace of You, whose [grace] extends to both the collective (samaṣṭi) and the individual (vyaṣṭi)—

The sense is this: Mahat, Ahaṃkāra, and the others created the body as form, undivided and vast; therefore, it is only fitting that for others who are turned away from You—who are Yourself of such a nature—there is a state of being like a mere skin-bag (dṛti).
They demonstrate their very grace: "In this regard, You have entered into the continuity (anvaya) within Mahat, Ahaṃkāra, and the rest."
Thus [it is asked]:
how could they have such power merely by my designation?
To this, they say: that which...

Since that which is beyond both the existent— the Brahman called "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya)— whose parts are pleasure and so forth, and the non-existent, such as food and so forth, namely the Brahman that is the tail, the foundation of all; indeed,
you [should understand] that very one to be the remainder (avaśeṣa) even there, by virtue of being the remainder of the sentence within these statements regarding the foundation.

For it is well known elsewhere in such passages as "I am indeed the foundation of the established Brahman," and it is also renowned as *ṛta* (Truth) in the words "That which the Blessed One spoke for the sake of purifying the reality of the Self," beginning with the word *ṛtam*. Śrī...

You are indeed the form of the Blessed One; therefore, among the [sheaths] beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*), you are that which is "of the nature of a person" (*puruṣavidha*), having the form of a person, which is the final one among the Brahman-sheaths—consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*)—that possesses as its constituent parts *priya*, *moda*, *pramoda*, and *ānanda*.
You are that.

Therefore, because you are the nature of fundamental supreme bliss (*mūla-paramānanda*), it is entirely logical that they possess such power through entry into you alone; this is the intended meaning.
For who indeed could breathe, and who could live, were it not for this [Self] in space?
"there would be no bliss," according to the Śruti (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7.1).
In this context, the following is stated:
although even a single entity in its own nature possesses various internal distinctions, nevertheless, such...

He grasps it. Thus, in this case, through faith alone, by means of that very [faith], reality is seen correctly;
and since that [reality] is Brahman, its nature is not [grasped] incorrectly.
And in that regard, when there is grasping by way of generality alone—
Because the causal cognition lacks the capacity to investigate the intermediate distinctions contained within it,

that [cognition], remaining entirely external to them, is self-luminous— even though it is variegated by various manifestations established through the experience of the multitude of Bhāgavata paramahaṃsas.
In the case of the ultimate reality characterized by its own nature, that which is apprehended as mere commonality of manifestation is itself conceived as having the form of valid cognition;
and from that, it follows that it possesses the nature of the self.
Its state of being a partial manifestation (*aṃśatva*) and its state of being a divine power (*vibhūtitva*) are thus designated.

Therefore, the Blessed One, whose nature is the indivisible reality (*akhaṇḍa-tattva*), exists as the source of the manifestation of the universal form (*sāmānya-kāra-sphūrti-lakṣaṇatvena*), which is the very mode of His own radiance.
It is indeed logical that he is also the support of Brahmā.

For this very reason, it is said: "He whose body is the earth, whose body is the Self (Ātman), whose body is the unmanifest (avyakta), whose body is the imperishable (akṣara)—he is the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, and godly."
The other scriptural passage, "Nārāyaṇa is one," also reveals that Nārāyaṇa is the Self even of Brahman denoted by the word "Imperishable" (akṣara).
By the evidence of the method of exhaustion regarding the aforementioned words such as "Self" (ātman), the particle "ca" (and) caused their agitation toward the Imperishable.
Moreover, from the perspective of the usage of the term *juṣām api*, it is indeed Brahman alone that is denoted here by the word "syllable" (*akṣara*).
Likewise, in the discourse on Sāṅkhya by the venerable Lord [Kṛṣṇa]: "Time, within the individual soul composed of Māyā... [BhP 11.24.27].

this is declared to be the method of Sāṅkhya.
I have severed the knot of doubt by means of both the reverse and the direct orders of creation, through the vision of the higher and the lower.
In this context, by the phrase "one who perceives the higher and the lower," this is the distinction [intended]:
Sāṅkhya is indeed the teaching (*khyāna*),
that is, the scripture which, having investigated the specific nature of that [reality] as its own essential form, [reveals] that essential form.

At that time, only the *mātra* remains, and it is precisely this that is called Brahman; and because the phenomenal world has dissolved within the final limit demarcated by the phenomenal expansion, it is appropriate to describe it as being indistinguishable from Vaikuṇṭha, due to the manifestation of its own essential particularity (*svarūpa-bhūta-viśeṣa*).
And that [bliss], being merely its own substantive, is experienced there as if distinct from the Śrī Bhagavān residing in Vaikuṇṭha, who is qualified by His essential power (svarūpa-śakti).
Thus, it is characterized by a lack of distinction in terms of touch and form.

Even though He is devoid [of material attributes], His nature as the splendor-form of the Blessed One has not been overlooked; rather, His status as Brahman is designated by virtue of His non-difference from that [splendor].
Consequently, because He possesses the sweetness of His essential nature and other qualities, He is characterized as *saviśeṣa* (possessing distinctions).
This is established all the more clearly by the direct light emanating from the limbs of the Blessed Lord;
as was stated by the Blessed Lord Himself to the illustrious Arjuna in the account of Mahākālapura in the Śrī Harivaṃśa.
O best of the Bharatas, that great, divine, and spiritual splendor which you have seen is I myself; it is my eternal radiance.
That is my supreme nature, eternal, both manifest and unmanifest;
entering into it, the best among those who know yoga become liberated here in this world.
That, O Pārtha, is the goal of the Sāṅkhyas, of the yogins, and of the ascetics;
that is the supreme, the highest Brahman, which differentiates the entire world.
"O Bhārata, you should know that very dense splendor to be me alone. (HV 2.114.9–12).

By the term "prakṛti," its status as his own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*) is also indicated through its being his source of manifestation (*tat-prabhātva*). Thus, the previously cited passage from the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* concerning the Kaustubha gem is also to be understood in this same way.
It should be understood as providing corroboration.
Therefore, the explanation "like leather bags" is also perfectly sound.

And therefore, since that which is the supreme, vast [reality] possesses the status of Brahman by virtue of its greatness— just as the light of the stars is called "vast" (bṛhat) because it shares in the nature of universal existence— it is precisely there that the primary application of the word "Brahman" occurs. Thus it is said in the Brāhma:
"By such terms as 'Ananta,' 'Bhagavān,' 'Brahman,' and 'Ānanda,' Viṣṇu alone is designated; others are so called only by way of metaphor. Thus it is said in the Pādma Purāṇa.
His qualities cannot be described individually because they are immeasurable;
therefore, by means of the word "Brahman," there is the inclusion of them all.
"Therefore, this word 'Brahman' is indeed a qualifier of Viṣṇu alone,
because immeasurable qualities belong to that all-pervading Lord and to no others.
In this [verse], the great purport of the entire treatise is distilled.
Those who know reality declare that nondual gnosis alone is reality;
and that, being perceived even without any qualifying attributes (*vaiśiṣṭya*), is Brahman.
Indeed, the Blessed Lord (Śrī-Bhagavān) is so designated because He possesses distinct attributes;
and that Blessed Lord is essentially composed of the glorious form (śrī-mūrti) characterized by the aforementioned qualities, and is not formless (amūrta).

Furthermore, in the verse from the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* (6.7.47), "O King, it is both embodied and unembodied, supreme and even non-supreme," those who accept its fourfold nature must likewise accept its unembodied state as distinct; otherwise, just like its Brahmanhood, its status as the object of the vision of its worshippers— *Note: The text appears to be cut off.*
Let it be exactly according to the capacity of the practitioner;
for indeed, to one who possesses correct devotion, [the Lord] manifests in His supreme form as Śyāmasundara with four arms and so forth.
For one whose worship is of the proximate (arvācīna) form, it is through the lower form (apara-mūrti), which consists of the conceptualization of the netherworld as its feet and so forth;

for one whose knowledge is dry (rukṣa), it is through the higher form characterized by Brahman; and for one whose devotion is abundant with knowledge, it is through the other form characterized by Īśvara.

In this context, "inferiority" (aparatva) should be understood as being a subordinate step following the manifestation of the supreme form (parama-mūrti), and not as a lack of substantiality like that of Brahman;
it is not intended to imply a state of being non-excellent. Thus it should be known.
Alternatively, "otherness" (paratva) is in relation to the supreme form;

for it is said that "that very [form] is the universal form, while the other form of Hari is the Great One," because [the former] is the substratum of the universe and possesses eternity and omnipresence.

One should contemplate Brahman as the embodied form of the Blessed One, which is free from all dependencies and devoid of desire; this constitutes its state of being without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhitva*).
The phrase "He is the Real" (bhūtaṃ tam) [ViP 6.7.83] indicates his nature as the defining characteristic from the subsequent perspective.

The phrase "beyond the three states of contemplation" (tribhāva-bhāvanātīta) [ViP 6.7.76] refers to his transcendence of the three types of contemplation well-known therein: that consisting of ritual action (*karmamaya*), that consisting of the conjunction of knowledge and action (*jñānakarmasamuccayamaya*), and that consisting of pure knowledge (*kevalajñānamaya*). Thus, he is supreme.
Even though it possesses the characteristic of reality (*tattva*), its perfect manifestation through devotion alone has been indicated as belonging specifically to the Embodied One (*mūrta*).
For this very reason, it is said: "He is the auspicious support for the mind, which is all-pervading and of an immovable nature. (ViP 6.7.76)

Furthermore, it should also be understood that at the conclusion of that passage, the statement regarding withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) from even the presence of that embodied form (*mūrti*) is established as being directed toward the worshiper of the distinct [form]. In this context,
the verse [ViP 6.7.70], "the dissimilarity of that universal form," should be understood as referring exclusively to the embodied form.
O Lord of Men, that Sovereign creates all forms of power known as gods, animals, and humans.

This...

It has been explained precisely as "otherness.

Thus, when it is established that this very reality consists of the nature of Śrī’s form, then the form characterized by hands, feet, and so forth, which is heard of everywhere, is also not distinct from the previously described form of Śrī; this has indeed been indicated at the conclusion of the section on omnipresence (*vibhutva*). in that very context, his own glorious form—

In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, however, with reference directly to the Blessed Lord Śrī, there is this illustration: "The form of that Brahman is twofold: indeed, both embodied (mūrta) and unembodied (amūrta)."

"Therefore, O best of the twice-born, devotion to Adhokṣaja [should be practiced] by men according to the divisions of social class and stage of life," as stated in the opening verse [of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa].
"Perfection of one's own performed dharma is the pleasing of Hari"—
in this manner, with the sole purpose of pleasing the Blessed Lord through pure devotion (*śuddha-bhakti*).
It is indeed supreme because it is defined by its nature as a producer;
for even that [other practice] has completely abandoned the deceit characterized by the expectation of a fruit, since its sole intent is directed toward that [supreme practice].
Being thus,
by the prefix *pra-* even the intention for all types of liberation, such as *sālokya* and so forth,
is excluded; because, through having that alone as his sole purpose, he is the fruit for those who are free from envy.

Envy (*matsara*) is precisely the inability to endure the excellence of others on the part of one who is lustful; it is for those devoid of that [envy] alone that the sacrifice of animals serves as its indicator,
and for compassionate beings alone is their own duty [established].

Since he did not state so clearly that [the practice] "is prescribed for others," his superiority over the *karma-śāstra* and the *upāsanā-śāstra* regarding those respective sections that expound them has been stated;
for the arising of *dharma* occurs in both cases alike.
This being the case, the sense is that even the mention of [practices] such as direct chanting (kīrtana) is far removed from [the goal]; let alone their actual practice.
Now, he declares its superiority even over the branches of the Jñānakāṇḍa, as before, with the words "that which is to be known" (vedyam).

The meaning here is that "the object of knowledge" (vedyam) refers to that which becomes ascertained even among those who are for the most part indifferent to devotion to the Blessed Lord, by means of the principle stated in [BhP 10.14.4]: "casting aside devotion, the path to the highest good," and so forth.
It is so called because it uproots the threefold suffering, cutting away everything down to ignorance (*avidyā*), which is its root;
and likewise, it is so called because it bestows and causes one to experience *śiva*, which is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).
In another [text], regarding liberation:

For if one were to merely contemplate [the Self] as an experience, it would result in the undesirable consequence that it would not be a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*); thus, its distinction [from other contemplations] lies in the fact that it involves contemplation of that [Self].
Nor does this [contemplation] require such a detailed investigation [into the nature of the Self], given that it serves as the means for attaining those various rare objects.
Excellence alone is the cause;
however, he says "in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata" to indicate that its very nature is also [the cause].
This is the state of being the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata.

The state of being the expounder of the Blessed One constitutes "glory" (*śrīmattva*); it is the possession of such an inherent power, as in the case of the name "Śrī-Bhagavān" and so forth. The suffix *matup* is used here in the sense of eternal connection.
Therefore, by designating it as a whole, its status as a name (nāmatva) alone is indicated, just like [the compound] "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*);
otherwise, however, it would be an undifferentiated [referent].
Otherwise, there would be the fault of [the definition] being too narrow (vidheyāṃśa-doṣa).
Therefore, it is stated in the Śrī-Gāruḍa: "The work named Śrīmad-Bhāgavata consists of eighteen thousand verses.
And likewise by the commentators: "The tree of the gods named Śrī-Bhāgavata..."

Therefore, in some places, the name *Kevala-bhāgavata* is used just as *Satyabhāmā* is called simply *Bhāmā*. He also states that the cause for possessing such power is the state of being the supreme and most excellent creator;
thus says the great sage Śrī...
And because the Blessed One was the crest-jewel of that very host of great powers who had reached the further shore of supreme discernment,
it is heard in scripture that, having become a sage (muni), he reflected thus.

Since it was first revealed in brief by him in the form of four verses, it has now been revealed in its entirety, following the lead of the opening question: "To whom and by whom was this expounded? (BhP 12.13.19).

Thus, while such excellence may generally exist elsewhere as well, he says "or rather" (kiṃ vā) to express the supreme power of this [place], stating that the direct realization of the Blessed Lord— the crest-jewel of all knowledge, scriptures, supreme objects of knowledge, and human goals— is easily attainable only there.
Is the Lord, the Blessed One, immediately apprehended— that is, made firm— in the heart by means of other scriptures or the proofs stated therein? The word "vā" (or) is used in a sense of irony.
But that [knowledge] is attained only with great difficulty and after a long delay;
here, however, it is grasped at that very moment by those who are desirous of hearing and truly wish to listen.
Now, one might ask: "Why then do all people not hear this? To that he says, "by the wise" (*kṛtibhiḥ*), which means by those of meritorious deeds (*sukṛtibhiḥ*).

The point is that the desire to hear [this teaching] does not arise without such merit. Alternatively, [it is not heard by others] because they lack the dharma characterized by the worship of the Lord, which aims at liberation as its ultimate goal.
The meaning is: what greatness, or how much greatness, is established here by those goals—whether mentioned or unmentioned—such as the direct realization of Brahman and so forth?
For that Lord is somehow [attained] by the accomplished ones.

Having attained fulfillment through devotion gained by following the sequence of its practice, those who desire to hear it here immediately stabilize that very [reality] in their hearts, pervading it for even a single moment; indeed, from that very moment onward, they do so at all times.

Therefore, because it provides a particularly clear exposition of the secret of the three sections (*kāṇḍatraya*) and specifically takes the form of the *īśvarākarṣi-vidyā*, this alone is superior to all other scriptures.
For this very reason, the word "here" (iti) has been stated three times; for that [repetition] serves the purpose of emphasis (nirdhāraṇa).
Thus, the intended meaning is that this alone must always be heard by everyone.

therefore, even in the context of the *Catuḥślokī*:
The Blessed Lord alone is the ultimate reality;

"Accept this, along with its secret and its constituent parts, as spoken by me.

The meaning is: "Accept what has been spoken," for no one else knows it;
because it is the supreme secret, more hidden even than the unknown, as stated in such passages as: "[It is the secret] even of the liberated and perfected ones" (BhP 6.14.5).

therefore, for that person—

The meaning is "I am characterized by [these].

In the passage beginning with "mayā," it is stated: "Supreme knowledge is the manifestation of my own majesty" (BhP 3.4.13). In that context, by the term *vijñāna*, it is made clear that even form and other qualities are of the nature of its own essence (*svarūpa*).
Herein lies the blessing of *vijñāna*.

It is manifest; and it is secret, because through the experience of the true nature of each respective state—which consists of supreme bliss—there necessarily arises a surge of love. Because it has been employed [in this sense],

Thus, from such scriptural passages as: "In the beginning, this was indeed Vāsudeva; there was neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara;

And he is that Person in whom the maintenance, emergence, and dissolution of the universe reside;
the Lord of Māyā, whose own self is liberated from Māyā.
"He lies within the cave of all," [BhP 2.8.10].

In this regard, who would dwell there, and who indeed would rest upon it? [BhP 3.7.37]
It is also stated in the Śrīdhruvacarita of the Kāśīkhaṇḍa: "Indeed, my devotees do not fall away even in the great calamity of universal dissolution."
"Therefore, he alone is Acyuta (the Unfallen), all-pervading, and immutable in the entire world.
By the word "eva" (alone) in the phrase "I alone," there is the exclusion of any other agent and of such qualities as formlessness. [The phrase] "I indeed was... [is understood].
In that regard, there is the cessation of disbelief.
This is what was stated in the verse beginning with *yad-rūpa-guṇa-karmaka* (BhP 2.9.32).
For this very reason, or rather, because [the Lord] is indeed the object of the knowledge of outsiders such as Brahmā regarding the creation and so forth—*āsam eva*—[He is the cause].
There is indeed the exclusion of other characteristic actions,
but not even of one's own internal play;
just as when it is said, "Now this king performs no action at all," [it is understood that] he performs no action related to the kingdom.
In this way, only that [specific thing] is negated, but not even sleeping, eating, and so forth; it is just like that.
Or rather, from the root *ās*, meaning "to go," "to shine," or "to take," [the term refers to] these present characteristics being seen by you now.
"I stood at the forefront, shining intensely"— by this, there is specifically the exclusion of being formless and so forth.
This has been stated by him in this verse within the *Muktāphala-ṭīkā*, which provides the definition of Viṣṇu as possessing both form and being formless.
Nor is there non-pervasion regarding those [cognitions] that possess forms (*sākāra*), because for them, [the object] is not concealed by a form.
Thus says the Aitareyaka Śruti.
And by the statement, "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, in the form of a person" (BAU 4.1.1),
it is taught that the knowledge of the Blessed Lord alone is superior even to the Puruṣa, because of its existence prior even to the observation of primordial nature (prakṛti).

Now, it might be objected that in some places the Śruti declares that Brahman existed as something entirely devoid of distinctions; to this he replies: "There is nothing else, other than that which is beyond both being and non-being.
"Being" (sat) refers to the effect, and "non-being" (asat) refers to the cause; Brahman is that which is beyond those two, and it is not [devoid of distinctions].

"Other than me": in some case, regarding a qualified person or a scripture that is incapable of producing an understanding of the specific nature that constitutes one's own being, the meaning is: "This very 'I' appears as devoid of distinctions. When that is the case, then...

Because there is an absence of distinctions within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), [Brahman] exists there in the form of pure consciousness devoid of distinctions; however, in Vaikuṇṭha, it exists in the form of the Lord endowed with distinctions. Such is the systematic arrangement of the two scriptures.
And by this, [it is established that] of Brahman indeed...
In the statement "I am the foundation," it is precisely the knowledge of the Blessed One that has been expounded; for this very reason, its supreme secrecy has been declared.
[Objection: But surely you are not perceived immediately after creation?
Regarding that, he says later: "Even after creation,
I alone am present— in Vaikuṇṭha in the form of the Blessed Lord and others, and within the manifested worlds in the form of the Inner Controller (antaryāmī)," this being the implied sense.
By this, it has been established that His cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution is His divine knowledge alone; thus, the Lord’s knowledge itself has been taught.
Now, one might object: "But surely those forms of jars and cloths which are perceived everywhere are not actually of that [divine] nature."
Anticipating the objection that this would entail the consequence of your being incomplete, he says:
"That which is this universe—that too am I alone;
because it is non-different from me, its very essence is myself. This is the meaning.

By this, O dear one, that Blessed Lord, the creator of the universe, has been described to you in brief— He who is Hari, and nothing other than Him exists, whether it be the existent or the non-existent.
Thus, by such statements, the knowledge of the Blessed One alone has been taught;
likewise, he who remains at the time of dissolution is none other than I myself.
By this, it has been stated that you alone remain, designated as the "Residue" (Śeṣa);
thus, the very knowledge of the Blessed Lord has been taught.
Likewise, previously, by way of being made manifest through His grace—
This has been declared as far as it was taught to make known that [Brahman] is not limited by any time or place;
thus, by the statement "there is nothing else beyond being and non-being," and by the declaration "I am indeed the foundation of Brahman," its true nature (yathābhāvatvam) is made known.

That which is the nature [of the Blessed One] is made known through the description of the Blessed One’s form with all its aspects and limbs, by way of making known his possession of infinite forms that are distinct from [all others],
and through the description of all his bases.
The quality of possessing infinite, distinctive attributes is made known by [the text];
and the quality of possessing infinite worldly actions is stated through the description of being the substratum for various activities characterized by creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
And there is also the status of being an object by way of making known.

Now, for the sake of understanding the nature of the self as distinguished by such forms and so forth through the method of negation, he states the definition of illusion (māyā) beginning with "without an object" (BhP 2.9.33).
This has indeed been explained previously [Note 35].
And this is the summary of the meaning:
that which is perceived elsewhere than in the vision of me—who am the supreme goal of human endeavor—is nothing other than that.

That object which cannot be perceived within the self, and for which there is no perception even independently of me— its meaning being that it has no self-manifestation apart from me— one should know that thing to be the *māyā* of me, the Supreme Lord.
Herein is an illustration:
Just as an appearance is a reflection or a ray,
and just as darkness is a visual impairment;
therein, regarding the appearance—
Suchness is indeed evident;
for darkness is perceived only where light is not seen, and it is not perceived without the eye, which consists of light.
The meaning of this use of the third person in "one should know" (vidyāt) is as follows:
this instruction is indeed intended for others; but you—my [disciple]—are...
"By the power granted [to you], you are experiencing Me directly"—
thus, having transcended the illusory perspective,

The meaning of this, expressed by way of exclusion (vyatireka),
is as follows: even though the true nature of existence and so forth is determined by words,
its experience does not occur except through the penetration of the effects of māyā.
Therefore, for that purpose, one must simply abandon illusion (*māyā*).
By this, it is understood that because of its invariable concomitance with that [illusion], love (*preman*) is also experienced. [106]
Now, he makes known the secret nature of that very love:
"Just as the great elements [pervade] all beings, high and low..."
"Whether they have entered or not, I am likewise neither in them nor outside of them"—
just as the great elements, though remaining outside, are said to have entered into all beings even without actually entering.
They shine as abiding within; likewise,

although I have not entered them by virtue of residing in Vaikuṇṭha, which transcends the world, I have nevertheless entered those people who are devoted to me— those renowned for their various virtues— and abide in their hearts.

Bhāmi: Here, while there is entry and non-entry [of the senses] through the differentiation of the portions of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), for that [consciousness] it occurs through the differentiation of its manifestations (*prakāśa*). Thus, despite this difference, the illustration is based on the mere similarity of entry and non-entry.
In this way, it is indicated that their secret is what is called "love-devotion" (*prema-bhakti*), which exercises such mastery over the self.
And so it is said in the Brahma-saṃhitā: "He who, by means of those very potencies which are manifested as the essence of bliss and consciousness, exists as his own essential nature..."
I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person, who dwells in Goloka itself as the self of all beings.
With the eye of devotion anointed with the collyrium of love—

I worship that Govinda, the primordial Person, who is dark-complexioned and beautiful, whose nature and qualities are inconceivable, and whom the saintly always behold within their hearts. [BrahmaS 5.30]
The meaning is: by that eye which is the form of devotion, which shines intensely as if anointed with the collyrium known as love—whose nature consists of inconceivable qualities;
[those] who worship me with such devotion.
And from the Gītā-upaniṣad: "In me they are, and I also am in them" (Gītā 9.29).
Or rather, it is just as those [objects] appear both when situated outside and when situated within.

And [the phrase] "I manifest within the devotees, both in their internal mental functions and in their external sensory functions," suggests that the secret of my nature is a certain self-luminous reality consisting of bliss, called love, which is the cause of the devotees' state of absolute non-duality in every respect. In the same way...
The venerable Brahmā said: "O dear one, my speech is never observed to be false, nor indeed does my mind ever turn toward what is untrue."
"My senses do not fall upon the path of the unreal,
because Hari has been held by my heart which is filled with longing"— thus [it is said].
Although this meaning might have to be set aside according to other commentaries, nevertheless, in this [context]...

If that were not the case, even the phrase "chinna-pada" (cut-off word) would be redundant in those [verses].
For the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is established through the two actions of the example itself.
Moreover, this indeed is what is called a "secret":
that a thing which is extremely difficult to obtain is [kept secret] for the purpose of warding off the gaze of wicked and indifferent people.

It is concealed by another common object, just as a *cintāmaṇi* jewel is by a casket or the like; for this very reason, the sages speak of things being beyond perception, and it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (11.21.35): "That which is beyond perception is dear to me."
And there is the word of the Blessed One:
thus it is made indirect when that which is not to be given, being a great object of rare occurrence, becomes [the subject].

That this very work is difficult to obtain, rare in its critical inquiry, and of great significance is evident in many places, such as in [BhP 5.6.18]: "He never bestows liberation, but rather the yoga of devotion.
This is what is known as the *Bhāgavata*.
"That which was spoken to me by the Blessed One— this summary of manifestations—
you must expand this."
So that men may have devotion for the Blessed Lord Hari,
the Self of all and the support of everything.
Having thus resolved, describe it.

this secret, whose nature is love, belongs to me, the Blessed One, for one who desires to know the reality of the Self.
