Therefore, through the instruction on his own knowledge, wisdom, the secret, and its constituent parts—even within the *Catuḥślokī*—he himself beheld there the Lord of all the Sātvatas, using the very term "Śrī Bhagavān": "There he beheld the Lord of all the Sātvatas" (BhP 2.9.15).
Thus, here, supported by the Tāpanī Śruti and by virtue of being a characteristic mark (liṅga) of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the speaker’s status as the Blessed Lord (Śrī Bhagavān) itself is clearly manifest;
it is certainly not that of Nārāyaṇa, who is merely a partial expansion (aṃśa-bhūta) of Him.
The state of being the Person reclining within the Garbhodaka ocean;
for this very reason, the explanation of this Mahāpurāṇa is indeed "Śrī-Bhāgavata.
It has been stated accordingly:
"To whom and by whom was this incomparable lamp of knowledge taught in the past?"— in such passages as these,

and in the verse beginning "We meditate upon that which is pure, stainless, free from sorrow, immortal, true, and supreme" (BhP 12.13.19), the word "supreme" (*para*) indicates that the Blessed One is the speaker.
The first incarnation is the Supreme Person (Puruṣa), because in the second [verse] there is a mention of a distinction;
therefore, this was previously told by the Blessed One to Brahmā from the lotus of his navel.

The term "Bhagavat" is used here as well in the phrase: "It was revealed out of compassion to one who remained [there] and was afraid of worldly existence. Indeed, at that very place, the venerable Lord himself, having manifested the all-pervading Great Vaikuṇṭha to Brahmā—who was seated upon the lotus-navel of Śrī Nārāyaṇa—revealed this Purāṇa.

This is the meaning. And this is consistent with the *Itihāsa* of the second *Skandha*. [108] Thus, the synthesis of all scriptures (*samanvaya*) is in that very Blessed Lord. Śrī-Bhagavān [speaks] to Brahmā. 102–107.
[108] This is the synthesis of all scriptures in that very Blessed Lord.
And thus, the Supreme Deity alone is to be sought through inquiry by means of all the Vedas; no other can be established by the Vedas.
Therefore, Him—

"Having studied all the Vedas and having reflected upon them, one who desires liberation should wish to know [the Self]," so it is stated in the *Caturvedaśikhā*. "To whom all the gods bow, as well as those seeking liberation and the exponents of Brahman," so it is stated in the *Śrī-nṛsiṃhatāpanīya* (NTU 2.4.10).
"One who knows the Veda does not think of that Great One, the Self experienced by all, at the time of transition;
rather, I ask you about the Person of the Upaniṣads"—this is the beginning of another [passage]. And:
"By all the Vedas, I alone am to be known; I am the author of the Vedānta and the knower of the Vedas"—thus says the Śrī [Bhagavad Gītā 15.15].

In the *Gītā-upaniṣads*, it is stated that in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the Lord Viṣṇu alone is determined as the one [subject] when all the operations of the scriptures have been subjected to analytical investigation; thus it is said in the *Padma-purāṇa*. All—
"He is the name, the denotable object, and he is praised in all the Vedas," so it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa;
"We bow to him in whom the eternal foundation of the words of all the worlds is established," so it is said in the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.14.23).
Having mastered all the Vedas, along with the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, logical treatises,
and the Pañcarātras.
Viṣṇu is to be known, and not otherwise.
Thus it is said in the *Brahma-tarka*.
Therefore, in this way, He Himself declared that all the Vedas are in harmony with Him alone, the Blessed Lord: "The Vedas enjoin Me and describe Me."
"For by conceptualization, the 'I' is indeed discarded.
Thus, the Blessed Lord has demonstrated that He alone is the meaning of all the Vedas.
In that regard, the King’s question:
Śrī Viṣṇurāta said— “O Brahmin, regarding Brahman, which is indefinable...”
How do the Vedic scriptures, which describe the functions of the qualities, directly apply to that which is devoid of qualities and transcends both being and non-being?

The meaning of this is as follows: first, the scriptural passages (śruti) are seen to apply to qualities such as *sattva* and so forth, because they are common to all that consists of mere sound (*śabdamātra*).
However, Brahman is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), transcending qualities such as *sattva* and the rest; therefore—
It is likewise indefinable,

because it is the locus for the absence of other qualities— namely those called genus, quality, and action— which are the effects of various specific qualities; and because such a substance is itself unestablished.

The meaning is that [the Self] is inexpressible as being an entity and so forth, and is beyond the cause and effect—the real and the unreal—consisting of the primary elements; thus, it is unrelated to this or that [attribute].
And this being so, just as in the case of the word "Ḍittha"...
The primary function of that word operates with respect to a certain unique substance;
just as in the expression "Devadatta is a lion," the word "lion" functions through a secondary (metaphorical) application toward Devadatta, who possesses the quality of courage.

And just as in the expression "a hamlet on the Ganges," the word "Ganges" functions through the mode of operation known as indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to refer to the bank— which lacks the [literal] connection [of being the Ganges]—
so too [is it with] that and that...
How could the Śruti texts function with respect to Brahman, which is the locus of all existence, through various modes of operation? Furthermore,

according to the principle that "the Śāstra has its source in the Śruti" (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.3), since the Śrutis are the means of knowing it, their application to that [Brahman] as its sole expounders must necessarily be asserted.
Therefore, in what manner do those [faculties] operate within that [object] in a direct manner, by way of their primary function?
That manner is the specific distinction (*viśeṣa*).
"Please teach it yourself.

Otherwise, because it would not be a category (padārtha), and because that which is not a category cannot be the meaning of a word's denotation (vācyārtha), it would follow that Brahman is not within the range of the Vedas (śruti). This being established, how much less [could it be known through inference]?
Regarding that, how is it that the Lord—who is the radiance moving above—that state becomes the object of perception for His two devotees?
To this, it was stated at the beginning: "having pointed out the path of the Vedas—which are self-evident (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*)—namely their being centered on the Lord (*bhagavat-paratva*). [110]
In this regard, he states the answer given by Śrī Śukadeva:
the sage said— [he withdrew] the intellect, the senses, the mind, and the vital breaths.
The Lord created human beings for the sake of their mothers, for the sake of worldly existence,
and for his own lack of isolation.

The Lord, the Supreme Ishvara, created the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect for the sake of the "measures" (mātrā) and so forth of living beings (jīva) who follow after [the world], and not that people created them through their own ignorance; thus the doctrine of illusory transformation (vivarta-vāda) is refuted. They are called "māyā" because they are measured (mīyante); it is for the sake of those objects.

"Bhava" means for the sake of existence— that is, for the purpose of performing actions characterized by birth and so forth. "For the self" (ātmane) means for the sake of the self as it travels to other worlds, that is, for the enjoyment of those respective worlds.
The meaning is: for the sake of non-conceptualization, for the cessation of conceptualization, and for liberation;
that is, for the sake of wealth, dharma, pleasure, and liberation.
The meaning of the four quarters is given in sequence.
Here, liberation (mokṣa) also consists in abiding as pure consciousness alone;
and according to the prescribed method of the letters, final emancipation (apavarga) occurs.

Because it has been thus defined by the prose passage in the fifth [chapter], beginning with "He who is the Blessed One" (*yo'sau bhagavān*) and ending with "by means of the loosening of the knot of ignorance which is the cause of various states of existence" (*ananya-nimitta-bhakti-yoga-lakṣaṇo nānā-gati-nimittāvidyā-granthi-randhana-dvāreṇa*), [this devotion] is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
And it should be known as being twofold, characterized by the manifestation of devotion;
for in both cases, there is the cessation of ignorance in the form of conceptual construction.
This is what is meant:
since Īśvara himself created the intellect and other faculties— which are observed to be the means for accomplishing various purposes— for the sake of those respective ends, therefore...

It is understood that he acted toward them by virtue of his fitness as a repository for the power to accomplish those [ends]. In this context, the powers that accomplish the three aims of life (trivarga) are portions of the power of *avidyā* consisting of the function of *māyā*, which is conceptual in nature;
for they are characterized by outward-directed action and are the cause of transmigratory existence through the alteration of one's true nature.
And thus, as long as living beings remain turned away from the Blessed One,

so long is it indeed true that the intellect and other faculties— being primarily composed of the powers of ignorance (avidyā-śakti), which are purely conceptual in nature— possess qualities (saguṇa) and therefore do not directly manifest the qualityless (nirguṇa). But when...
At that time, because the power of consciousness (cic-chakti) manifests within those [objects], it is established that one perceives them directly;
since speech also consists of the intellect (buddhi) and other factors, such conventional usage is likewise established.
This very point is concluded at the end as the established tenet (siddhānta), without distinction.
Thus, O King, has this been described which was our question posed by you,
concerning that which is Brahman and the indefinable.
The mind should also move toward the virtues of women.
Regarding the phrase "thus here, [it is] the mind":

therein, within the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, the power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*) should be understood as being self-luminous with respect to its own non-material nature of supreme bliss and its corresponding qualities, and as consisting of those respective designations with respect to speech.

Therefore, for the sake of establishing the final conclusion that the Śrutis proceed by taking as their support such a non-material (aprākṛta) essential nature and so forth, it is thus established that even human speech possesses the character of the Lord's own activity—as it has been said: "In which [speech], even though not composed verse by verse... (BhP 1.5.11).
And this being the case,
how much more so would such speech and other qualities— possessing a single locus, manifesting directly as the breath of the Blessed One, and being authorless (apauruṣeya)— be his conduct?
Therefore, the Śrutis indeed move directly [toward their goal];
and it will be stated later: "In some cases, one should follow him as he moves in the form of the Unborn."
Regarding the word *nigama*: likewise, it is stated in the twelfth [chapter] concerning the *praṇava*—
it is the direct designator of Brahman, the supreme self, from its own abode.
"It is the eternal seed of the Vedas, containing the secret essence (*upaniṣad*) of all mantras" (BhP 12.6.41).
And in the Śruti: "Om—this is the name of Brahman nearest to It," referring to its most proximate characteristic and so forth.
The meaning is "without any intervention.
For this very reason, the king's intention was: "Tell me, by what manifestor do they move directly?"
In this regard, the objection concerning the literal meaning of the word will be refuted later in the passage beginning with "dyupatayaḥ" (BhP 10.87.41).
Now, as for those Vedic texts which appear to be extroverted by being devoted to the three aims of worldly life (trivarga):
Indeed, it culminates precisely in inwardness;

for [it is] thus: the playful manifestation of the compassion of the Supreme Lord, directed toward the multitude of living beings who are constantly struck by their outward orientation away from the ultimate reality.
The Vedic scriptures, which consist of breaths that culminate in fulfillment, first generate confidence regarding their own subject matter;

then, toward those who— being ignorant of unseen realities and constantly desiring only seen, worldly ends— strive for such goals, they prescribe rites such as the *putreṣṭi* sacrifice to accomplish those very ends.

And then, having inspired confidence in him by demonstrating the utter instability of this worldly life, he [directed him] toward the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices, which give rise to various desires for the next world— characterized by heaven and so forth— and which are wondrous with the marvel of divine bliss.
They cause [the Dharma] to proceed;

then, through their continuous practice of that, they generate a taste for the Dharma itself. Then, for those who have attained a taste for the Dharma and whose internal faculties are purified, there arises an investigation into its meaning.
They fulfill the longing for the bliss of nirvāṇa in those others who possess the knowledge that even the world is impermanent and who are distressed by the fear of saṃsāra;
and the bliss of nirvāṇa is supreme—
It is indeed of the nature of the manifestation of reality.
As it was said by the venerable Sūta:
"For [this is] the dharma that leads to liberation..."
Wealth does not serve the purpose of wealth;
nor is desire for the sake of wealth traditionally held to lead to the exclusive attainment of dharma.
The gratification of the senses is not the attainment of desire;
one should live with only so much as is necessary for life,
in order to seek the knowledge of reality.
"There is no purpose here through ritual actions.

And thus, just as the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties move toward varying degrees of the Supreme Reality through the manifestation of the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) according to the degree of their inward orientation, so too do they proceed with varying degrees of intensity.

Likewise, even the word characterized by sacred revelation (śruti), by following the sequence of the manifestation of the power of consciousness (cic-chakti) and transcending the domain of the three qualities (traiguṇya), becomes focused solely on the state beyond qualities (nirguṇya); thus, it is indeed able to move correctly toward that qualityless reality (tattva). [The qualityless...]
Because it is suitable as a mode of existence;
thus it was said regarding the *praṇava* in the twelfth [chapter]:
"From that arose the threefold *oṃkāra*."
"He who has his origin in the unmanifest, the self-ruling one— that which is the mark (liṅga) of the Blessed Brahman, the Supreme Self. [BhP 12.6.39] Thus it is said.

In that regard, that reality manifests in two ways: as the form of the Blessed Lord (bhagavad-rūpa) and as the form of Brahman (brahma-rūpa). The power of consciousness (cic-chakti) also manifests in two ways: in the form of devotion consisting of His own self-luminosity and so forth, and in the form of knowledge consisting of that [devotion].
Therefore, it has been established in general that the Śrutis consisting of devotion operate upon the Blessed Lord, while the Śrutis consisting of knowledge operate upon Brahman.
Now, in order to state the specific distinction therein, a traditional narrative (itihāsa) concerning Him is introduced.
Śrī Sanandana said:
Having swallowed this world of his own creation,
He lay down together with His potencies.
At the end of that, the Śrutis awakened Him, the Supreme, by means of His characteristic signs:
"Having Himself created this universe, He has withdrawn it at the time of dissolution, absorbing it along with His powers."

Having brought under His own control the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the person (*puruṣa*), and the individual souls who are portions of His portions— the Supreme Lord, who was lying down with eyes closed toward His own effects— the Śrutis awakened Him at the end of that period, when the time of dissolution was nearly over, using words that describe His characteristics or establish His identity, just as one awakens another in the morning.
The meaning is that they praised him by way of eulogy;
thus, his status as the Blessed One (Bhagavat) alone is understood, and not merely that he is a person (puruṣa).
O Blessed One, you alone were here at the beginning as the pervasive Self,
the very essence of selfhood, following the will of the Self.
"Because he is the supreme observer of all things," as stated in the section on the Third Skandha;
for it is heard there that at that time the Puruṣa was included within him. This is an illustration regarding the meaning of the preceding verse.
Just as bards approach a sleeping emperor at dawn with beautiful verses celebrating his heroic exploits, so [should one approach the Buddha].
"His dependents are distressed"—

this refers to the prowess of that sovereign, and not to those beautiful verses which manifest his state of non-distinction. This is the intended meaning of the verse beginning with "the sovereign lying down."
Just as at night,
even while a sovereign is sporting with his queens, because he has abandoned external affairs and remains within the inner apartments, he is described by those people as being simply "lying down."

And at that time, this Blessed One is praised by bards through the artifice of awakening him with verses composed of His own majestic power— He who, though His gaze was fixed upon the affairs of the world, remained hidden in His own abode, sporting with His own retinue.
By the word "dependents" (*anujīvinaḥ*), it is indicated that they do not know His vital points (*marmajña*) in the same way as He does.

Therein, first of all, one's own [nature] is the reality (*tattva*) which is the undivided form of the Blessed One, being experienced through the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*), which is characterized by the service of qualities such as knowledge and which is the cause of right vision (*samyagdarsana*).
The Śrutis, demonstrating the nature of Brahman as that which is to be realized and thus embracing it as such, have said:
"Victory, victory! O Unconquered One, abandon the unborn Māyā, whose qualities are grasped as defects."
Since You have by Your very self acquired all fortune,
O Knower of all potencies, the Veda follows You as You move sometimes as the unconquered Self within the mountains and the dwellings of the world.
O unconquered one! Victory, victory! Reveal your own excellence;
the repetition [of "victory"] is used out of respect.
Here, the term "unconquered" (ajita) refers to you.
By this form of address, the following is obtained:

according to the principle stated in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 6.2.10, "The utterance of Viṣṇu’s name [is effective] because the mind has that [name] as its object," the Blessed One is brought directly face-to-face by means of His name.
By that very indicative mark (*liṅga*), that [form] also becomes of the same nature as the glorious form (*śrī-vigraha*);
one should know this because it is worthy of being brought face-to-face with Him.
For this very reason, in cases of fear, hatred, and so forth, [one should approach] the glorious form.
Its influence is also heard of in such cases as "as if from a flash of intuition" (*sphūrteḥ*) and so forth;
moreover, in this context, both scripture and the experience of the learned have already been established as authoritative.

Therefore, it is established that what arises in the eyes and other senses in the form of the glorious body (śrī-vigraha) is indeed the same [reality] that arises in speech and other faculties as name and form (nāma-rūpa).
Consequently, because there is no difference in the essential nature between the name and the named, the direct realization of the latter follows from the direct realization of the former.

Since this is indeed the case, what more need be said? Elsewhere, as with other things, even the Vedic scriptures proceed toward the Blessed One through conventional designations—such as those based on genus and so forth—and through modes of expression such as "conventional" (rūḍhi) and others, according to the manner of the relationship between a name and the named. Of these scriptures...
The fruits of the creepers that are the designations are, in fact, the names themselves as they truly are.

By the phrase "manifesting excellence," it is shown that through such a connection with the quality of being the most excellent of all, the Vedic scriptures move toward Him by their primary function alone.
And the Śrutis state: "The Vedas do not encompass Your greatness" (ŚvetU 3.7), and "Neither one equal nor superior to You is seen" (ŚvetU 6.8), and so forth.
In this regard, the Śrutis—by manifesting their own devotion through the cry "Victory! Victory!"—show that devotion alone is the cause for the revelation of Him.
They cause [beings] to go. Anticipating the question, "By what activity do they manifest excellence? they say that it is by means of dispelling *māyā* through the granting of their own grace:
"Destroy *māyā*, which is unborn."

Now, is it not the case that what is called *māyā* is a power (*śakti*) whose function consists of both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*)? If so, then by its destruction, there would also be the destruction of knowledge; to this he replies: [It is] "seized by defects" (*doṣa-gṛbhīta*). It is precisely the defect characterized as ignorance—which is the cause of the self-forgetfulness of living beings—that is "seized" (held fast) by it; whereas [the other aspect] is for the sake of causing the remembrance of that [Self].
That [power] by which she possesses the quality characterized by *vidyā* (knowledge);

for she herself, through her own penetration (*svāveśa*), produces the defect characterized by *avidyā* (ignorance) and abandons only a certain *jīva*, at only a certain time, in only a certain manner, and in only a certain place. This is her [nature].
Even the quality known as knowledge, which consists of renunciation, is indeed a defect.
Therefore, having uprooted that [knowledge], grant to all living beings devotion directed solely toward Your own lotus feet; this is the intended meaning.

Therefore, it has been indicated that the Śrutis proceed by way of negating that [Māyā] through their intentional function (*tātparya-vṛtti*), manifesting the Lord’s nature as a mass of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss, while designating His transcendence of it by virtue of His power being fit to destroy Māyā.
And the Śruti passages state: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti,
but the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10),
and "the one unborn female" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.13).
"He is the lord of all, the ruler of all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22); "He indeed is this one who is 'not this, not this,'" and so forth.
Now, having prayed for the destruction of *māyā*, would even my sovereignty and other qualities conditioned by it [also perish]?
Regarding the statement "you wish to destroy [them]," he provides the following resolution: "You," because you, by your very self—
by your own essential nature alone— possess the entirety of all glory, having attained that which is called the three-quarter manifestation (*tripād-vibhūti*).
"You are the possessor of all sovereignty and so forth;
therefore, the meaning is: what is the use of your trivial [notions] or of the sovereignty and other qualities conditioned by them?"

And likewise, regarding the verse "He who, by means of Ajā, [knows] the Ajā," the commentary states: "Indeed, there is no need for the Ajā of the Lord of the multitude of wish-fulfilling cows (Kāmadhenu), which is uninterrupted, blissful consciousness.
Similarly, [it says]: "For unlike others, [he does not require] a place..."

The meaning is that although your sovereignty is eightfold, being delimited by time and so forth, it is nevertheless immeasurable because it is inseparable from the nature of your perfect self. Such is this [verse].
Here, by the word *ātman*, which denotes the mere essential nature (*svarūpa-mātra*), and likewise by the word *bhaga*, the essential nature—
By this term "denoting the qualities of reality" (bhūta-guṇa-vācaka), the following is implied:
words such as *svarūpa* ("own-nature") and so forth, as well as words such as *īśvara* ("Lord") and so forth,
[function] through convention (*rūḍhi*) by taking hold of the mere own-nature, or even by taking hold of the qualities that constitute the own-nature.
They are able to explain it thus:
"The manifest world has the same nature as that which the Blessed One possesses. And there are scriptural passages to this effect.
And the "first" ones are those beginning with [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8]: "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold.

And they say that this is the power of His own nature (svarūpa-śakti), which is perceived by all. It belongs to all living beings (jīva) whatsoever—those whose abodes are the immobile things and whose worlds are the mobile things, i.e., their bodies—and it is entirely...
The meaning is that "O you whose power is the slayer of those [powers]" is an address;
it is inferred that he is a mine of jewels consisting of the waves of various powers within them.

Alternatively: [An objection] might be raised, "Surely by the destruction of the illusion (māyā), there would be a loss of power for the individual soul (jīva), who is its limiting adjunct (upādhi). To this they reply: "Aga" (Come!). It is exactly as before.
The sense is that, on the contrary, by their very own essential power (svarūpa-śakti), there will arise for them a full power that bestows nothing but happiness.
Herein, from the perspective of an impartial observer—
It has been stated that the *śruti* passages proceed by way of characteristic marks;
and the *śruti* passages are those beginning with "Who indeed shall enkindle another? (*ko hy evānyāt*) and "The breath of breath" (*prāṇasya prāṇam*).
[There are scriptural passages such as: "That very one shines" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.2.15);
"At the end of the body, the Lord reveals the liberating Brahman" (Nṛsiṃha Tāpanīya Upaniṣad 1.7);
and "He who has supreme devotion for the God" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.23), and so forth.

Now, one might ask: "How do you know specifically that there is no further task for me through Ajā, and that [the Lord] is a mass of being, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānandaghana), with all His powers (bhaga) fully contained within His own essential power (svarūpaśakti)?
To this they reply with the words "somewhere" (kvacit).

At certain times, such as at the beginning of creation, You move about in the form of a person, sporting with the unborn Māyā; and eternally You move about by Your own essential power, which manifests Your true nature,
consisting of the single essence of truth, knowledge, and bliss— of You, whose nature is thus described, there is this scripture.
One should follow and serve [the teacher] both in the form of sound and in the form of the deity;
therefore, the meaning is that we know everything truly.
The genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*).
This is what is meant:
here, the Veda is of two kinds—that which has the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) as its subject matter, and that which has the absence of the three qualities (*nistraiguṇya*) as its subject matter.
And therein, the object consisting of the three qualities (traiguṇya) is of three kinds. First of all,
one kind indicates that [object] by means of a state of neutrality while taking it as its objective support.
For example, the passage beginning with "from which indeed these beings [are born]" and so forth;
and the second type, which demonstrates His majesty and other qualities by means of descriptions such as His being composed of the three *guṇas* and His being the Lord over them.
Just as in the passage beginning with "Indra is the king of those who have settled," and so forth;
and the third type indicates the supreme reality by means of the elimination of the three qualities (traiguṇya).
This [negation] is also twofold: by way of negation and by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Among these, by way of the former [is stated]: "It is neither gross nor subtle, neither long nor short."
The passage beginning with "Not this, not this" (BAU 3.7.8) and so forth is the latter door;
the passage beginning with "All this is indeed Brahman, you are that very reality" (tat tvam asi) and so forth is the former statement.
Having indicated that everything possesses the nature of Brahman on the grounds of its being born from That,
the portion therein which is manifested as the ultimate basis for the cognition "this is Being" (sad idam) is designated as pure Brahman.

Furthermore, in the subsequent statement, when the referent of the term *tvam* (the "you") is established as being one with the referent of the term *tat* (the "That") by virtue of its nature as the aspect of consciousness (*cid-ākāra*) and its power (*tac-chakti*), it is thereby indicated that the referent of the term *tat* is none other than Brahman itself.
Since the mere knowledge of the referent of the term *tvaṃ* (the "thou") is ineffective without the knowledge of the referent of the term *tat* (the "that"), the term *tat* is introduced.
Furthermore, the transcendence of the three *guṇas* applies to both [referents] here.

It should be understood that where, by means of the elimination of the three guṇas and with reference to them, the attributes pertaining to Him are clearly perceived, there the text has the Blessed Lord as its purport; whereas where they are not clearly perceived, there it has Brahman as its purport.
The subject matter of the three gunas has been explained;
this same [explanation] applies to one who moves about following that which is unproduced (ajayā).
Furthermore, even one who has transcended the three qualities (niṣtraiguṇya) is of two kinds:
one devoted to Brahman and one devoted to the Blessed Lord (bhagavat). As it is said: "Ānanda is Brahman," and so forth.
For him there exists neither effect nor instrument;
neither one equal to him nor anyone superior to him is seen. His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold.
And there is the intrinsic power and activity of primordial wisdom.
And so forth, as in Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8.
This has been explained as "moving along with that which moves by means of the Self. Therefore, according to the Śruti, that state of moving [belongs to the Self].

Success! The direct practice belongs to those who are beyond the three qualities (*guṇas*) by their very nature; for others, however, it should be understood through its syntactic unity with that [direct practice].
The mention of various qualities is made solely for the purpose of dispelling illusion (*māyā*).
Subsequently, having set that [view] aside as entirely untenable, the true nature, qualities, and so forth of the Lord Himself are directly pointed out;
thus, to illuminate the unity of this single discourse, it is this very same established conclusion that is indicated in this opening statement.
And likewise, in the concluding summary, the scriptures declare: "For the Vedas bear fruit in You alone, by the negation of what is not You, culminating in You" (BhP 10.87.41).
And the Madhva... [scriptures also state...]
Those authorized by the Bhāṣya include such passages as, "Neither the eye nor the ear, nor reasoning nor memory—verily, the Veda alone makes him known," and others;
as well as such passages as, "The person taught in the Upaniṣads" (BAU 3.9.26), and so forth. [114]
Now, they point out specifically how [the scriptures] proceed even regarding Brahman, and how, for those who proceed toward Brahman, their ultimate culmination is indeed in the Blessed Lord alone;
they understand this which has been extensively perceived as being without remainder.
Since the rising and setting of the sun occur in the changing world, yet You remain unchanging throughout the day, for this reason the sages have placed their minds, words, and deeds upon You;
how could the steps taken by men on this earth ever be otherwise?
All this is perceived and understood as nothing other than the Great Brahman itself.
How so? Just as every object such as a jar is perceived and seen to be nothing but clay when it remains as a residue apart from its modified form, so too is all this.
The meaning is that it is likewise "great" (*bṛhat*). The reason for this is that from the Great One (*bṛhat*) arises transformation.
The scriptural passages beginning with "from which indeed these [beings arise]" consider that he merges into him;
therefore, the sense is that his similarity to the dead is appropriate.
Then, how is it that there is no modification [of Brahman] either? To this they reply:

"From the unmodified. The meaning is: even so, because of its inconceivable power—according to the principle that "Scripture is the root of [knowledge of] sound"—that which remains strictly unmodified, from that [Brahman it proceeds].

Although here too it is logically consistent that the "Great One" (Bṛhat) possesses power (*śakti*), nevertheless, because it is not presented as having its divine nature manifested (*āviṣkṛta-bhagavat-tva*), it is established as Brahman alone. For if power were entirely abandoned, by the force of the context of its presentation, it would result in [the Great One] becoming a mere nothingness (*tucchatva*).
And therefore, it is Brahman alone that has been cited here.
For this very reason, even agency and so forth were not presented there by means of the example of mere clay.
They say that even this exposition of Brahman ultimately culminates in the Śrī Bhagavatī herself;
hence [the word] "ataḥ" (therefore).
Therefore, even beyond the exposition of Brahman,
the seers— the Vedas— have placed their mental application, that is, their intent, and their verbal expression, that is, their denotation, solely upon You, the Blessed Lord. They have held them fast.
Because the two [terms] refer to one and the same entity,

and because a distinction is merely imagined based on the observation of whether qualities such as "fearlessness" (bhaga) are manifested or not manifested, there is no positing of a different meaning in that case.

How could the footprints of men walking upon the earth—whether they possess right vision or lack it—ever become otherwise than real? Having been placed and deposited upon the ground, they do not fail to reach the earth; rather, they terminate precisely there.
Therefore, the sense is that however they may explain it, the fruit ultimately accrues to you alone. As it has been said:
"And the yoga of knowledge is centered on Me."
"It is devoid of qualities and characterized by devotion;
for both, the single intended meaning is that which is characterized by the word 'Bhagavat'. (BhP 3.32.32)

In this regard, the scriptural passages authenticated by Madhva’s commentary are as follows: "Ah! All names indeed designate that very Person; just as rivers flowing toward the ocean enter into the ocean, even so do all these names enter into the Person. [115]

Thus, it has been stated that by virtue of being the Blessed One (*bhagavat*) and being Brahman, you alone are the object of all the Vedas through both their intended meaning (*tātparya*) and their explicit declarations;
and that [status] is indeed according to reality, not merely conceptual.
Thus have your wise ones said: O Lord of the Three Worlds, having plunged into the nectar of your discourse which destroys the impurities of all the worlds, they abandoned their ascetic penances.

How much more so those who, having shaken off the qualities of time and the latent impressions of their own nature by means of their own glory, worship Your supreme state which is the experience of eternal bliss?
O Lord of the Three! You are the Master of the three—Brahmā and the others—and the one known as Nārāyaṇa, who descends in various incarnations.
The Supreme Person (Puruṣa) is also the Lord (adhipati), for He is the very nature of Uparicara;

therefore, O Lord of all lords, since the ultimate intent and the explicit meaning of the Vedas terminate in You alone, for this very reason the wise, who possess discrimination, [attain] the succession of Your [grace].

Having set aside even that portion of the Veda consisting of ritual injunctions (*pratipādanamaya*), and having plunged with faith into the nectar-ocean of your stories— which leave no trace upon the entire world— and having served you through the power of austerity (*tapas*), whether by its predominance or by its nature as a purifier, [one attains liberation]. Your fame is a sea of nectar, the cause for the destruction of all sins.
They abandoned those karmas;
if even for those practitioners it is thus,
then what need is there to speak of those whose intentions, time, and qualities are shaken off by their own abode— the pure nature of the Self?

The internal organ has been conquered by Your vibration; those who worship that reality called Brahman—the state which is Your own nature consisting of the incessant experience of bliss—having plunged into That, they have abandoned those things, namely the power of Time which is the cause of old age and so forth, as well as the qualities such as *sattva*. What then? [They have abandoned all else.]
The meaning is that they have even abandoned steadfastness in the experience of the measure of Brahman (*brahma-mātrā*).
This is what is being said:
here, first of all, there are three kinds of people—the deluded, the discerning, and those who have accomplished their purpose.
In this regard, with reference to all [beings] indeed, the Blessed One’s teaching of the Vedas is seen to consist precisely in their being free from conceptual construction (*akalpanāmaya*).
For if that were not seen as suchness (*tathātva*), then in reality...

Because there would be no connection with that [the Lord], even the well-known power of the Lord’s narrations contained within the Vedas to remove the sins of the deluded— who lack knowledge of words and their meanings and thus view the entire world as worthless— would not exist.
It is like the capacity of fire or iron to burn when they have not actually been touched. Furthermore,

if that [notion] were merely a product of imagination, those who possess discernment would not engage with it, just as one would not upon hearing of the quality of having fine offspring attributed to a barren woman.
Or, even if they proceed through such possession, they would not abandon their own duty,
just as one who hears that the Ganges is the glory of the king does not resort to other sacred fords. Moreover:
That being the case, those who, by delighting in the Self, have attained their supreme goal, would not at all plunge into discourse concerning that [world] out of disregard for it;
they have already plunged into the lake of nectar and have attributed qualities even superior to it [to that discourse].
It is like a river; and its possession of various qualities is heard in scripture, as in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "That Hari, having gone there, destroys the impurity of the ear. [ViP ?]
In such passages as "it is not so," and in this very context,
"your mother does not know," and so forth.
"In the first [verse], 'his mind captivated by the qualities of Hari' (BhP 1.7.11) refers to the beginning. Therefore,
it is established that the relationship between the Lord and both the qualities and the Vedas— which expound those qualities and so forth— is entirely natural in every respect."
Regarding this, there are scriptural passages beginning with "Om, they know this... and so forth:
"Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows thus. "He is not smeared by evil action; he shakes off both good and evil deeds."
"Thus indeed he does not grieve:
'Why did I do good? Why did I not do [good]? For those who have been liberated worship him, and so forth."

With this in mind—that other verses as well, which demonstrate that statements concerning meditation and the like have the Lord as their ultimate referent, should be applied accordingly—I shall not cite them here.
[Objection: But then, according to your own view, if He is denotable by words, does it not follow that He is merely material (prākṛta)? What [is the answer]?
And because it is that from which even words turn back, unable to reach it along with the mind;
he spoke by means of non-speaking itself: "That which is not expressed by speech, that by which speech is expressed; that which the ear does not hear."
In response to the doubt that in such passages as "that by which this hearing is heard," it is precisely the state of being denotable by words that is negated, it is said:
just as there is a fault in its being directly denotable, so too there is a fault in its being indirectly indicated (lakṣya).
How could it not be so?
For there is no distinction between the two cases insofar as both are objects of the operation of words. Furthermore, it is not that...
It is established by the proponent that, unlike ordinary things, they are not to be designated directly; rather, it is precisely through their non-designability that they are thus designated.
In this very manner, there is the conclusion of those great statements (mahāvākya).

Even the lords of heaven did not reach the end of those [worlds] because of their infinity; yet you too have reached the end of the multitude of worlds within them, for they are indeed possessed of coverings.
Just as dust is carried away by the wind into the sky, so too are the Vedas [carried away] by time.
"For indeed, those things which end in You bear fruit by means of the removal of what is not that.
Here, both the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the qualities (*guṇa*) are each twofoldly indescribable; [this is so] because of their infinity. This...

And because it is impossible to point to it by saying "it is this much," they call that first infinity [the *anantya*]. "O Blessed One, your end (*anta*) is such; you are the lords of heaven and the other worlds."
Even Brahmā and the others did not go there, nor did they know it; why?
Because of its infinity.
"That which has an end is nothing at all;
you do not exist as such, because you, O Ātman, do not go to your own end."
From where, then, does omniscience or omnipotence arise? Regarding this, they say:
"By way of being infinite," that is, precisely by the absence of limits; for it is not so.
The non-cognition of a rabbit’s horn, or the failure to attain omniscience, does not undermine the majesty of one's power;
for the Śruti says: "He who is its supervisor in the highest heaven—he, my dear, knows it, or perhaps he does not know."
[Ṛgveda 10.130.18] They call that very state "the infinite" (anantatva) which is within— that which is inside you; indeed,
oh, it is possessed of a covering.

Masses of cosmic eggs, endowed with seven successive coverings each ten times greater than the preceding, fly about and revolve simultaneously— not in succession— by the force of time like particles of dust in the sky. By this, their inherent infinity is shown through the revolving of infinite Brahmāṇḍas therein.
It should be known as residing in the qualities because it is the substratum of manifold qualities;
and the scriptural passages [state]: "That, O Gārgī, which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which has come to be..."
"Past and future" refers to passages such as *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.7.3;
and "of Viṣṇu, indeed, shall I proclaim the heroic deeds,
he who measured out the earthly realms," etc., refers to passages such as *Ṛgveda* 1.154.1.
Indeed, because it is so, the Śruti texts culminate in you;

therefore, even in the Śruti, after describing an intensity of bliss a hundred times greater than that of the bliss of Prajāpati, it further says, "From whence words turn back... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4).
By means of [the words] "beginning" and so forth, as well as "endlessness," it is stated that Brahman possesses an infinite number of joys beyond the reach of speech. As it has been said:
"It is not to be known as 'such-and-such,' nor is it expressible, nor can it be reasoned about."
"Even the wise, though beholding it, do not know the true form of Meru. Thus [it is said].
Therefore, in this case, its expressibility consists precisely in its being inexpressible;
whereas in passages such as "Truth, Knowledge," and so forth,
there is a direct expression of the essential nature itself.
And they say that in passages such as "the intrinsic nature, knowledge, power, and action," the quality is heard of there in exactly that way;
[this is] the end of existence through the refutation of that [opposite].
Thus [it is said]: having set aside that which is a material object (*prākṛta-vastu*), because [the process] culminates in the self (*bhavat-paryavasānāt*).
This is the meaning:
by such statements as "intellect" (*buddhi*), "knowledge" (*jñāna*), and "absence of delusion" (*asaṃmoha*), all these—modesty (*hrī*), intelligence (*dhī*), and fear (*bhī*)—are the mind (*manas*).

And by the words "not this," etc., all that which was previously designated as ordinary knowledge and so forth is negated by the statements "not this, not this" and "of him there exists neither effect nor instrument," and so on, such that none of it is Brahman.

And yet, that [nature] is denoted by such statements as "truth, knowledge, and so forth," and by such statements as "inherent knowledge, power, and action. Therefore, for them, that knowledge and so forth are not something other than the primordial nature (prakṛti).

The words "knowledge" and so forth terminate precisely in the negation of that [object]; therefore, because it is a reality beyond the scope of the intellect, it is inexpressible. Nevertheless, since some such form exists and is being pointed out, it is also inexpressible.

Likewise, in the case of indirect knowledge— as in the statement "you are the tenth"— one perceives that very object, though it is self-luminous by nature, as clearly manifest within a purified mind through the mere power of the sentence; thus, it is determined that the word of the Śruti possesses the inherent power of self-luminosity.
"Both the Śabdabrahman and the Parabrahman are my two eternal bodies" (BhP 6.16.51); and "because the Veda has the Lord as its very self" (BhP 11.3.44).
"We have heard that the Veda is Nārāyaṇa himself, the Self-existent" (BhP 6.1.40). Or rather, why wait for others? Here, the Lord is immediately apprehended within the heart.
"By the wise who are desirous of hearing, that [should be told] at once" (BhP 1.1.2).
For this very reason, in the passage "the person known through the Upaniṣads" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26), the Śruti makes known that He is accessible solely through the Upaniṣads.
Just as one says "the visual [perception] of form," so too,
by means of the power of self-luminosity inherent in that which consists of hearing (śrutimayī), it dispels the mass of various material objects like darkness and shines forth by itself.

Therefore, even in that case, there is no quality of being demonstrable; for it is not logical to say that the sun is illuminated by its own light in the same way that a jar is illuminated by it, because [the two] are non-different from one another.

And if the position that power and the possessor of power are distinct is accepted, then even "indicatability" [would follow]; in this regard, by means of very non-indicatability, indicatability itself is established.
For this very reason it was said:
In the Gāruḍa [Tantra]: "Because it is not well-known, that is inexpressible; yet it is expressible according to the teachings of all the Āgamas."
"It is remembered as the supreme: the unthinkable is thinkable, the unknowable is indeed knowable.
And in the Śruti: "That is indeed different from this... and so forth.
"From that which is unknown [comes] study. With this in mind, the venerable Parāśara also said:
"In that Brahman, the abode of all powers, the means of knowledge of those who possess such means do not [apply]."
"He who has gone to Hari becomes capable of reaching the ultimate goal and destroys impurity through his hearing. Thus it is said.
Now, since the Brahman known as the Blessed Lord possesses manifest power, it follows that the Veda is of the very nature of the power of self-luminosity.
And therefore, how can there be the manifestation of Brahman, whose power has not yet been manifested?
It is said: in our view, even its manifestation is [due to] the Lord.
It is by power alone. As it has been said: "And my own majesty is designated by the term 'Supreme Brahman'."
"You shall obtain that which has been favored by me and revealed in my heart through your inquiries.
Thus it is said; yet these [teachings] do not fall into the state of being illuminated by another.
Because Brahman and the Blessed Lord are non-different entities,
it has been stated here that even any instruction regarding Him given by means of worldly terminology is possible, as it is sustained by that very Vedic revelation through its conformity with it.
Therefore, at the time of studying that [scripture],
there is certainly no prohibition regarding the word "That" (tat), which consists of the power of devotion to Him, because it is entirely an outpouring of His essential nature and potency.

Rather, it belongs solely to that which consists of the play of the mind; thus, everything is faultless. For this very reason, in the *Suparṇa-śruti* it is said: "That which they do not smell, they smell; that which they do not see, they see. Regarding their nature and its derivatives: [they perceive] what is not perceived, and they see what is not seen.
That which they do not hear, they hear; that which they do not know,
they know.

// 10.87 // The Śrutis [speak] of the Blessed Lord. // 109–116 // [117] Now, it is said that there is but one single essential nature which shines forth both as power (*śakti*) and as the possessor of power (*śaktimat*). Of that power...

Its nature as the essential self has been described; that which shines preeminently by virtue of possessing those powers attains the designation "Bhagavat," and this has already been explained. And that very same [reality], in its state of being power—

In order to demonstrate that she who shines preeminently receives the name Lakṣmī, some of her many divisions— she being infinite due to the distinctions of her own functions— are shown, as follows: by Śrī, Puṣṭi, Gīr, and Kānti.
He is served by Kīrti, Tuṣṭi, Īlā, Jayā, Vidyā, Avidyā, Śakti,
and Māyā.
Śakti is in the form of Mahālakṣmī, constituting His very own nature;
she is the internal great power (mahā-śakti) of the Blessed One, who is the primary basis for the application of the word "power" (śakti).
Māyā is the external power (bahir-aṅga-śakti), while Śrī and the others are the functional modes (vṛtti-rūpa) of those two; this should be understood everywhere. Among them, regarding the former:

"Bheda" means distinction. "Śrī" refers to the prosperity belonging to the Lord (Bhagavat), but this is not the form of Mahālakṣmī, because she is the primordial power (mūla-śakti). This will be explained further ahead.
The distinction of the north is prosperity (*śrī*); it is the *jāgatī* meter and the attainment of wealth.
It is with reference to this very [prosperity] that such statements as "Prosperity does not abandon me, even though I am detached" are made. Since...
And it was said by the venerable Nārada at the conclusion of the Fourth Canto:
"He who is self-perfected [bestows] prosperity upon those who follow after it, as well as upon the lords of men and the gods who seek it."
"How could a man who knows the true flavor of devotion not abandon this world, which is governed by his own circle of servants? (BhP 4.31.22).
In that regard, association with those who seek Him, such as the Lord of the two-footed beings (the Supreme Person), is what one must rely upon for subsistence.

Likewise, it is heard that she herself appeared from the Ocean of Milk in the form of the beloved of the Lord himself and, by her very sight, brought about the reappearance of the Fortune of the Three Worlds that had been lost due to the curse of Durvāsas.
The same applies to the others as well. In that context, *ilā* means "the earth" (*bhūḥ*), and by way of illustration, it also refers to "play" (*līlā*).
Furthermore, in that regard, the distinction from the former is knowledge (*vidyā*).
The cause for the awakening to reality is a specific modification of that mental state called consciousness; it is a distinction of the subsequent [state],
the door of illumination for that very knowledge,
characterized by the removal of ignorance.
O Blessed One, the cause of the meditative realization of His omnipresence and other attributes is a particular state of the function of love-bliss consisting of the maternal sentiment and so forth.
For this very reason, He is called the "impeller of the arts of knowledge of the cowherd women" in the *Tāpanīya* Śruti.
This too should be explained at the appropriate occasion:

that distinction of the latter [ignorance]— which is a specific modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) and is the cause for the transmigrating being's forgetfulness of its own true nature and so forth— is,
by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), also [the cause] of the former.

Sandhinī, Saṃvit, Hlādinī, Bhakti, Ādhāra, Śakti, Mūrti, Vimalā, Jayā, Yoga, Prahvī, Īśānā, Anugrahā, and others are to be known. Here, Sandhinī herself is Satyā; Jayā is Utkarṣiṇī; Yoga is Yogamāyā; and Saṃvit is Jñānā and Ajñānā.

It should be understood that *śakti* is pure being (*śuddha-sattva*). The distinction is as follows: *prahvī* is the cause of manifold and infinite capacities, while *īśānā* is the cause of the power of universal authority.
In the same way, the others for the northern [direction] should be understood according to their respective cases.
Thus, even here, the modes of illusion (*māyāvṛtti*) are not explained in detail.
Because it is practiced externally;
whereas in the root [text], the person who has partaken of the service is based on being situated at a distance.
And likewise, in the thirty-seventh chapter of the tenth book, the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa was praised by Nārada as follows:
"A mass of pure consciousness, established in His own nature..."

We take refuge in the Blessed One, whose every purpose is accomplished, whose desires are never in vain, and who, by his own splendor, has eternally brought to rest the flow of the qualities of *māyā*.
I bow to You, the Lord who rests in Himself, by whose own creative power all particular manifestations have been fashioned,
and who has now assumed a human form for the sake of divine play.
"I am born as the leader of the Yadus, Vṛṣṇis, and Sātvatas.
This is the meaning of these two verses:
that which is pure consciousness, the supreme reality (*parama-tattva*), is itself the condensed form of Śrī...
That whose body [is such]:

wherein all objects—such as sovereignty and the rest—are properly attained (*āpta*), meaning eternally established or full, by its own configuration (*sva-saṃsthayā*), that is, by its own form (*svarūpa-kāreṇa*) or by its own power (*svarūpa-śaktyā*). For this very reason...
There exists no desire for the worldly task, which is utterly trivial, futile, and vain—[the word *avāñchita*] refers to one whose longing (*vāñchā*) is directed toward such things.

Anticipating the objection that a connection with even the undesired is sometimes observed, he says: "By his own splendor," meaning by the power of his own essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*), he is eternally withdrawn, being endowed with a power that has become distant [from worldly objects].
"Devoid of that which consists of the qualities (guṇas)"—

let us go for refuge to that Blessed One. Likewise, let us go for refuge to You, the Blessed One known as Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who are the Lord Himself through Your own portion as the inner controller (antaryāmī).
I bow even to him who, though being the Supreme Person (puruṣa), is the Lord (īśvara). Of what nature is he? By his own inherent power (svarūpa-śakti), he is self-supported;
yet by his own creative illusion (ātma-māyā)—where "ātman" here refers to the individual soul (jīvātman)—he makes himself appear as such through that illusion directed toward it.

Māyā is that conceptualization (*kalpanā*) by which all particular forms (*viśeṣākāra*) have been fashioned without exception, or rather, that conceptualization which, through its own creative power (*ātma-māyā*)— that is, its inherent capacity (*svarūpa-śakti*)— has fashioned its own summit (*svāgra*) such that it possesses all particularities without exception.
"Of what kind is he whose power [is such]?"—
because at this present time of Your manifestation, even that Lord has entered into You, the Blessed One.
For the sake of that play which consists in the simultaneous manifestation of various respective powers, he has assumed— that is, brought near and manifested—
the human form (*narākṛti*), being the Supreme Brahman according to the traditional teaching; thus, he is called the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*).
By which [he is characterized]— he further qualifies that very person as the leader (dhurya) of the Yadu, Vṛṣṇi, and Sātvata clans. Of those...
"Carrying the burden of love for those who possess constant attendants.
Alternatively, in the root verse, the word "by power" (*śaktyā*) is the qualifying attribute (*viśeṣya-pada*) in every instance.
Śrī is the primordial form (mūla-rūpa); Puṣṭi and the others are her portions (aṃśas). Vidyā is knowledge; perfect (ā) knowledge is devotion (bhakti).
Because it is stated, "The royal science, the royal secret," and so forth,
Māyā is the external limb;
however, its functions, such as Śrī and the others, are to be understood as distinct.
The remainder is the same.

Therefore, in this section concerning the pure Bhagavān, once the enumeration has been finalized specifically regarding the functions of His essential nature and powers, this [point] must be discerned.
First, since the single reality alone possesses the nature of being, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), its power (*śakti*) is likewise one, though it is divided threefold.
This has been stated in the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*:
Śrī Dhruva says:
"Bliss, existence, and consciousness— these three are one in You, who are the foundation of all things."
"Causing both joy and suffering, it is mixed;
but not so in You, who are devoid of qualities.
Thus it was explained by the Svāmins.
Hlādinī is that which causes delight; Sandhinī is continuous consciousness, the power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti).
It is one, primary, and non-deviating—meaning it is identical with His own essential nature. That [power] is all...

Because the perfect abiding of everything is established in You alone— who are the substratum of all— and not in individual souls, that threefold nature consisting of the *guṇas* does not exist in You.
He explains that very point with the word "hlāda" (bliss).
Regarding "the mixed [feeling] causes distress":
that which arises from mental clarity and causes joy is *sāttvika*; that which causes distress during the separation from sense objects and the like is *tāmasika* because it causes distress.
That which is mixed with both [of these] and produced by sense objects is *rājasī*.
The reason for this is that it is devoid of the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva* and the rest.
This has been stated in the *Sarvajñasūkti*:
The Lord (Īśvara) is Being-Consciousness-Bliss embraced by the cooling consciousness;
the individual soul (jīva) is that same [Being-Consciousness-Bliss] enveloped by its own ignorance.
The source of the accumulation of all afflictions.
Thus, in [Bhāvārtha-dīpikā 1.7.6],
they are to be understood as Sandhinī, Saṃvit, and Hlādinī through progressive excellence;
and that being so:

Just as "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) is the cause for the cognition of all pots, so too this Blessed One— though in some places traditionally taught as being the very nature of existence— is here designated as having the form of "Being" (sat) in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone"; thus,
He bestows and sustains that existence (sattā).
She is the one who brings about the attainment of all places, times, substances, and so forth, and she is the unifying power (*sandhinī*);
likewise, although she is of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid*), she is called *saṃvit* because by her means one perceives and causes [others] to perceive.
Likewise, it should be discerned that the consciousness which, by its intense nature, cognizes and causes one to experience that joy in the form of bliss is called *hlādinī*.
Thus, since that fundamental power (*mūla-śakti*) is established as having a threefold nature, [it possesses] self-luminosity (*sva-prakāśatā*) by virtue of that.

By its characteristic—that is, by a specific mode of its activity—the essential nature (svarūpa) itself, or the power of essential nature (svarūpa-śakti), manifests as qualified; that is pure being (viśuddha-sattva).
And that [pure being] is the manifestation of that [essential nature] independently of anything else.
Because its function consists of the knowledge that makes [objects] known, it is indeed consciousness;
because it lacks contact with *māyā*,
it possesses purity.
And it was said by Mārkaṇḍeya to the sage Śrī-Nārāyaṇa in the twelfth [chapter] regarding that being’s state as being other than the material nature (prakṛti):
"O Lord, O friend of Your own self, sattva, rajas, and tamas— "
Although the causes of this world’s creation, maintenance, and dissolution consist of Māyā,

they are assumed by Him as His pastimes for the sake of peace; yet these are not composed of pure goodness (sattva), for other than them, there are no means to quell the calamities, delusions, and fears of men.
Therefore, O Blessed One, here in this world, those who are skilled worship Your pure body, which is dear to You;
for the Sātvatas desire that essence (sattva) which is the form of the Supreme Person.
"Since the world is neither fearlessness nor self-bliss, nor anything else.
The meaning of these two [verses] is as follows:
O Lord, even that which consists of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* is merely the play (*līlā*) performed by Your own *māyā*.

Of what nature are they? They are the causes of the maintenance and other states of this universe; nevertheless, it is that which consists of *sattva* alone that leads to tranquility—that is, to supreme happiness—and not the others, which consist of *rajas* and *tamas*. Not only that—
The difference between these two is merely the absence of tranquility;
however, regarding their practice, it is undesirable as well, which is why he says "misfortune" (*vyasana*).
Therefore, O Blessed One, the skillful and proficient worship and serve Your white body in the form of Śrī Viṣṇu, which is composed of pure goodness (sattva) and presides over divine play;
they do not worship any other form, such as those of Brahmā or Rudra.

Likewise, among your living beings, those who worship— that is, follow— the pure body, which is solely devoted to goodness (*sattva*) and possesses the characteristics of a devotee of the Blessed One, such as the forms of Svāyambhuva Manu and others; [they do not fall].
But not in the form of Dakṣa-Bhairava and the like;
for she is your own beloved, as well as mine, because she brings peace to the world.
But is it not well known that even my own essential nature consists of *sattva*?
If so, how can that too be merely composed of illusion (*māyā*)?
"No, no," say the Sātvatas, the followers of the Śrī-Bhāgavata; they maintain that sattva is the very form of You, the Puruṣa, which they desire as illumination,
and from which sattva the world [arises].
That which is called Vaikuṇṭha shines forth;
it is that very state of fearlessness, self-bliss, and the nature of the bliss of the Supreme Brahman, and not any other quality of goodness born of material nature.
Here, by the word *sattva*, a specific function of the power of one's own nature (*svarūpa-śakti*) characterized by self-luminosity is expressed;
this pure *sattva* is designated by the term *Vasudeva*.
"In that which is traversed, the person is uncovered" (BhP 4.3.21);
according to these words of Śrī Śiva,
the cause for the manifestation of that which is beyond the range of perception is the quality of *prakṛti*.

The term *sattva* is used because it conforms to the established definition of impure *sattva*, and because it attains its connection [to the subject] as a specific form of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) existing in such a manner;
and thus, its own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*)—
It has been stated that, by virtue of being its very mode of existence, [the Self] is of the nature of its own essence.
That "fearless bliss of the Self" was spoken of with the intention of emphasizing its power, because [it is said] "from which the world [proceeds]."
If this were a different meaning, there would be a contradiction of the vow that the Lord’s form is nothing but His pure essential nature (*śuddha-svarūpa-mātra*) in passages such as BhP 2.8.2,
and there would also be a loss of the quality of being "fearless" (*abhaya*) and so forth; otherwise, it would be something else.
If the single word *rajas* and *tamas* were repeated twice, a cognitive burden would arise;
furthermore, since the previous [word] is also not different, both are referred to by the dual number alone.
Therefore, there is [a distinction] from what is well-known.
The other is *sattva* as constitutive of one's own nature (*svarūpa-bhūta*).

This is the view of the commentator on the passage beginning with "That which is in the eleventh [cakra], this body, the arrangement of the three worlds" (BhP 11.4.4), where it is said that knowledge arises from itself; [it refers to the body] from whose constitutive *sattva* the body—

By the phrase "the knowledge of the supported" (*bhṛtāṃ jñānam*), just as at the end of the hymn to Brahmā in the passage "this was practiced by his friends," it is described as "other than the manifest" (*vyaktetaram*)—meaning other than the manifest insentient world (*jaḍa-prapañca*), consisting of pure goodness (*śuddha-sattva*), and so forth;

likewise, in passages such as "The supreme *rajas* of the Sun, the Jātavedas, the splendor (*bhargas*) of the Lord" (*paro rajaḥ savitur jāta-vedā devasya bhargas*), [it is described] by Śrī-... [text truncated].
In the *Bharata-jāpya*, that same view is expressed through such passages as:
"The Supreme King is beyond *rajas* and beyond *prakṛti*, consisting of pure *sattva*," and so forth.
Therefore, it is heard in scripture that the natural qualities, such as *sattva* and the rest, belong only to the individual soul (*jīva*) and not to the Lord;
as it is said in the Eleventh [Book]: "The qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* belong to the *jīva*, but never to Me."
Thus it is said; and in the Śrī-Bhagavad-Upaniṣad:
"Whatever states of being there are—whether characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa)..."
Know them to be from Me alone; yet I am not in them, and they are not in Me.
Deluded by these three states consisting of the qualities, this entire world does not recognize [Me].
Me, who am beyond these and imperishable.
For this divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the gunas, is difficult to overcome;
yet those who take refuge in Me alone [cross over it].
They cross over this illusion.
As it is said in the tenth [chapter]:
"For Hari is truly devoid of qualities (nirguṇa)."
The Person is beyond primordial nature;
He is the all-seeing witness.
By worshiping Him, one becomes free from the material qualities.
In the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "Wherein the Lord, the primal qualities such as sattva and the rest do not exist..."
"May that primordial Person, pure among all pure things, be gracious.
And likewise, it was said by Devendra in the tenth [book]:
Your abode is a pure being, peaceful, composed of austerity, and free from passion and ignorance;
this flow of the qualities is merely illusory.
"There exists for you no further succession of births"—
this is the meaning.
*Dhāma* refers to the power of manifestation that constitutes one's essential nature (*svarūpa*).
He states its purity through two qualifications:
"that which has destroyed rajas and tamas" and "consisting of austerity."
In this context, "austerity" (tapas) means knowledge, according to the Vedic scripture: "He performed austerity.
It consists of austerity—that is, its essential nature is abundant knowledge—and is free even from a trace of dullness.
The meaning is "devoid of.
Just as [it is said], "the self consists of knowledge and is pure," even *prakṛta-sattva* (ordinary materiality) has been excluded. For this very reason...
This flow of qualities such as goodness (sattva) and the rest is illusory; it does not exist for you, because that [flow] is a mere attachment resulting from ignorance.
For this very reason, Brahmā and the others addressed the Blessed Lord with these words, supported by reasoning.
You resort to pure *sattva* for the stability [of the world], a body that serves as the means for the welfare of embodied beings through Vedic rites,
yoga, austerity, and meditative absorption.
O Creator,
if this innate being of mine were not that which purifies the distinction between knowledge and ignorance, people would not strive for Your worship.
"You are inferred by the manifestations of Your qualities, and whoever or whatever quality is manifested by You.
This is the meaning.
Because it is luminous by virtue of that [consciousness], you take recourse in—that is, you manifest—a body fashioned as non-different from it;
what kind of being is this? It is pure, unlike any other.
Even though it is unmixed with *rajas* and *tamas*, because it is by nature material (*prākṛta*) and thus permeated by an element of insentience (*jāḍya*), it does not possess specific purity;
however, this [purity] exists by virtue of its being the essence of the power of its own nature (*svarūpa-śakti*).
The meaning is that because even a fraction of that [impurity] is not touched, there is extreme purity.
For what purpose does he resort [to this]?
It is for the sake of stabilizing the minds of embodied beings upon his own lotus-feet during their worldly existence.

The underlying sense is that your primary purpose is solely to bestow the bliss of devotion upon all devotees; this is known from Śrī Kuntī’s words in BhP 1.8.19: "for the sake of prescribing the yoga of devotion. Of what nature is that form? It is the *upāyana*, the receptacle or support, of all *śreyas*, that is, of all the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).
The meaning is that [the Lord] has the nature of eternal, infinite, supreme bliss.
Therefore, the intention is that this designation of a distinction between You and Your body is merely figurative (*aupacārika*).
Therefore, by whatever form one person offers worship— that is, honor— to another form as its very object,
by what means is this done?
The meaning is: "by means of the Vedas and so forth which have you as their object.
Even though [the worship] is established as being primarily an offering to you through those common [texts] that are indeed offered [to you], [it is still not sufficient].
Because the body is independent;
because such a body is not to be depended upon, they clarify that it is of the nature of its own essence (*svarūpa*) by virtue of being the cause for the manifestation of such a body.
If this being— which is your own innate consciousness (*vijñāna*)— is that which you experience,
meaning its nature consists of the power of self-luminosity (*sva-prakāśatā-śakti*),
then that [self-luminosity] would not exist.
In that case, however,
the very manner in which your self-luminous experience (*anubhava*) manifests constitutes its cleansing— that is, it attains purity;
this alone is what remains in the world, for not even a trace of your experience persists.

The meaning is as follows: [An objection is raised: "Surely the experience of pleasure and so forth may occur through the very qualities (*guṇa*) of the *prakṛti*-nature; what is the purpose of including the term 'one's own' (*nija*) there? To this, he replies:
The meaning is that you are merely inferred through the manifestation of your natural qualities, but not directly perceived;
or else, [the meaning] is "of yours."

If that which is the form of consciousness (*vijñāna-rūpa*), the eradication of the differentiation of ignorance, and one's own innate being (*nija-sattva*) were not to exist, then You would not manifest; rather, You would be inferred only through the manifestations of the qualities of material nature (*prakṛti*), such as goodness (*sattva*) and the rest. But by the manifestation of Your own innate existence, You are indeed directly perceived—this is the meaning. That...
To clarify this very point, they state that there are two types of inference therein: "that by which a quality is manifested" and "that by which a quality is manifested through another.
This refers precisely to that which is not of the nature of the self (asvarūpa-bhūta). [Prākṛta-]

The meaning is that sattva and other qualities are your inferential marks (liṅga) either simply by virtue of having an invariable connection with you, or simply by virtue of being manifested solely by you—
just as, for example, the dawn is [the mark] of the sun.

Just as the proximity of sunrise is a mark (*liṅga*) [of dawn], or as smoke is a mark of fire; therefore, in both cases, it is logical that for you there is an absence of its being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*). Such is the sense. Thus, in this way, for a being who is not of the ordinary nature (*aprākṛta-sattva*), by which [means] its own self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*)— [The text continues: ...is established. Furthermore, since the Lord is the very nature of the self-luminous consciousness, He is not an object of cognition; rather, He is the subject (*pramātṛ*) himself. Therefore, because the relationship between the cognizer and the cognized does not exist, the Lord is not an object of inference. Nor is He an object of verbal testimony (*śabda*), because words function by denoting objects through their conventional usage (*saṃketa*), and since the Lord transcends all convention, He cannot be expressed by words. Consequently, the Lord is not an object of any means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, the statement "the Lord is not an object of knowledge" is established.
