It has been established that the direct realization of you, who are self-luminous, occurs [for such a person]. In this regard, those who consider the so-called *viśuddha-sattva* (pure being) to be merely material (*prākṛta*), devoid of *rajas* and *tamas*, and [consequently view] its effect as the Blessed One—

However, those who imagine [the Self] to possess conflict and so forth have not been favored by anyone; for since it is by nature inherently tranquil due to the absence of any connection with *rajas*, and because its form is one of universal indifference, agitation is impossible for it. Furthermore, being composed of pure knowledge (*vidyāmaya*), it consists merely in the illumination of things as they truly exist.
Because it is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatva*),
and because it is unfit for other conceptual constructions;
as it has been said regarding that which is beyond the scope [of thought]:
The cause for being an object of experience is the quality of *sattva* inherent in nature;
*rajas* is present when the object of experience possesses many forms;
and *rajas* is also present when those many forms are concealed.
Likewise, when there is mutual indifference, it is *sattva*; when there is assistance, it is *rajas*;
and when there is injury, it is *tamas*.
[The attributes] such as being an object of experience, [and] abiding, creating, and destroying; and [the attributes] such as indifference and so forth.
Now, if even a trace of *rajas* were to be admitted therein, the term "pure" (*viśuddha*) would be redundant; therefore, enough of that doctrine!

If one were to consider that [the mind] is defiled by the impurity of passion (*rajo-kleśa*), then the state of purity would be rendered meaningless; therefore, enough with this shattering of the jar of their doctrine.

In this regard, this very pure being (*viśuddha-sattva*), when the aspect of *sandhinī* (sustenance) predominates, is the power of support (*ādhāra-śakti*); when the aspect of *saṃvit* (consciousness) predominates, it is self-knowledge (*ātma-vidyā*);
and when the essential aspect of *hlādinī* (bliss) predominates, [it is the power of love].
The secret science:
the form is that which primarily possesses the three powers simultaneously;
herein, by means of the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti).
The abode of the Blessed One shines forth;
as it has been said: "That which the Sātvatas desire as the form of the Puruṣa is Sattva, from which the world [arises]" (BhP 12.8.40).

Likewise, through the science (*vidyā*) consisting of the two-fold nature of knowledge and its characteristic function that impels it, the knowledge which has that function as its form and which resides in the devotee shines forth.
In this same way, [the science] characterized by devotion and that which impels it—

Through the secret science (*guhya-vidyā*) consisting of the two modes of activity (*vṛtti-dvaya*), devotion (*bhakti*), which is of the nature of joy and takes the form of those very activities, shines forth. These two alone are made explicit in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* within the hymn to Lakṣmī:
"The science of sacrifice (*yajña-vidyā*) and the great science (*mahā-vidyā*)."
"The secret science shines forth;
and you, O Goddess, are the self-knowledge that bestows the fruit of liberation. [ViP 1.9.118] Thus it is said.
The science of sacrifice is ritual action;
the great science is the eightfold yoga;
the secret science is devotion.
Self-knowledge is wisdom;
because You are the support of all those things, the meaning is that You alone are the bestower of those various forms, of diverse liberations, and of other various fruits.
Then,
through his form, the venerable body consisting of the supreme reality manifests; this very [body] is called Vasudeva.
This was stated by Mahādeva in the third chapter of the fourth book:
"The pure being denoted by the word Vasudeva, wherein the Person (puruṣa) moves unobstructed."
"And within that being, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the Adhokṣaja, is indeed envisioned by my mind.
This is its meaning: "Pure" means existing through the function of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*), and thus devoid even of a trace of insentience (*jāḍya*).
That very same [principle], being especially pure, is designated by the word *vasudeva*.
To the question, "Whence does it derive its nature as *sattva* or its status as *vasudevatā*?", he says: because in that [state] the Person (*puruṣa*), Vāsudeva, is perceived.

It is manifested. First, in the initial case, its nature as existence is evident because it is equal to existence as established in the world by virtue of being the cause for making what was previously outside the range of experience now within the range of experience.
In the second case, however, the meaning is as follows:
He is known as Vāsudeva because he is perceived within Vasudeva; thus the Supreme Lord is well-known.
And He is perceived as pure being (*viśuddha-sattva*).
Therefore, the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is determined by the well-known meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*).
Consequently, based on the etymological derivation *vaṃ devaṃ vāsayati* ("it causes the god to dwell") or *vasaty asmin* ("the god dwells in it"), [the word] *vasu* [is established].
Likewise, he is called *deva* because he plays (*divyati*) and shines (*dyotate*). He is both that and he himself, thus he is Vāsudeva.
He is Dharma himself, for he is the desired wealth of men.

Alternatively, he is Vasudeva because he shines forth by means of the eight *vasus*, which are the meritorious characteristics of the Lord's nature. Therefore, he is the pure being (*viśuddha-sattva*) designated by the word "Vasudeva.
Thus, by virtue of being the cause of the Lord’s knowledge—which is itself the singular embodiment of self-luminous light—[he is so called].
Isolation is sattvic knowledge,
while that which is characterized by doubt is rajasic;
knowledge pertaining to primordial nature is tamasic.

In many places, such as at the beginning of Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.25.24, which states, "It is remembered as residing within the self and devoid of qualities," it is established that through hearing knowledge of the Blessed Lord, one attains the state beyond the *guṇas*;
and herein is realized the characteristic of self-luminosity, which constitutes the function of the pure potency (*svarūpa-śakti*) understood by the term "pure" (*viśuddha*).
This is evident from that [statement].

And thus, in the phrase "it is perceived in existence" (*sattve pratīyate*), the locative case (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended to express the instrumental sense (*karaṇa*). He clarifies precisely this state of existing through its own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti-vṛttitva*).
Being unobstructed and devoid of covering,
it shines forth;
if it were a material entity (*sattva*), then in that case, it would be determined as merely a reflection.
And thus, the sense is that its manifestation would occur only through being concealed therein, just as a face is manifested in a mirror by virtue of being contained within it.
He states the resulting meaning: "In such a being, eternally..."
The meaning is that the Blessed One, thus manifesting himself, is "specifically ordained" (vidhīyate) by me—that is, contemplated—by means of the mind.
That reality (sattva), having attained identity [with the mind], alone can be so contemplated; otherwise, it simply cannot be thought of by the mind. This is the final conclusion.

One might object: "Why not simply contemplate him with the mind alone? What is the use of that being? To this he replies: For [he is] Adhokṣaja; that is, he by whom the sense-born knowledge (akṣaja) of the senses has been cast down (adhaḥkṛta), meaning transcended.
In the reading *namasā*, the word *anu* is read in place of the word *hi*.
And thus, manifesting through the power of self-luminosity alone— known as the "pure being"— it is merely followed and served by means of salutation and other such acts.
The meaning is that it is not revealed by anyone at all.
Thus, it is understood that this very [reality], manifesting solely as invisible, is served by us through invisible means such as prostration;
in this way, the thematic consistency of that section is also perceived.

Likewise, since the pure being who manifests the form of the Blessed One possesses both the nature of a *mūrti* and the status of Vasudeva, for that very reason it is well known that his lawful wife possesses the nature of a *mūrti* during that particular manifestation.
And it should be understood that the illustrious Ānakadundubhi attained the state of Vasudeva;
here, he appeared as one characterized by faith, nourishment, and so forth, being a partial expansion of the Lord's power in the form of his sister.
Through association with the term *pāṭha*, it is understood that the embodied form (*mūrti*) is a manifestation of a portion of His power; as in [BhP 1.3.9]:
"In the fourth creation of the portions of Dharma, the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa... and so forth.
And by the word *kalā*, power (*śakti*) alone is denoted;
therefore, since that [power], characterized as *śakti*,
is seen to have the fruit of the manifestation of the Blessed One known as Nara-Nārāyaṇa, [it arises] from the pure one known as Vasudeva.
It is determined that its very nature is *sattva*; thus, it is also said that "form" (*mūrti*) is its designation, for form is the arising of all qualities. *Nara-*...
Regarding the phrase "the two sages Nārāyaṇau" (BhP 4.1.52):
the construction with the preceding verse is that she gave birth to those two, from whom the manifestation— the appearance— of the Lord, who possesses all qualities, arose.

The meaning of "form" (*mūrti*) is that it is the cause of the manifestation of the one called the Blessed Lord, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*); likewise, because it is seen to be the fruit of His manifestation,
and because of its identity with Him, even the venerable Ānakadundubhi [possesses] pure goodness (*śuddhasattva*) and so forth.
Existence is to be known;
and that was stated in the ninth [chapter]: "Vasudeva is the abode of Hari."
"They call him Ānakadundubhi.

Otherwise, the qualification "the abode of Hari" would be rendered meaningless. Thus, by means of pure *sattva*, which predominates in one or another specific portion such as *hlādinī* and so forth, according to its respective nature—
The manifestation of Śrī and the others must also be discerned;
therein, their nature as perfection with respect to the Blessed One, and their nature as the bestower of perfection upon those to be favored by him, constitute [perfection].
The state of being born from a portion (*aṃśaja*) and so forth should be understood as the threefold nature of the world.

In that regard, those [energies], being formless as mere pure power (*kevala-śakti-mātra*), abide in a state of complete union with the body and other aspects of the Blessed One; thus, they are the presiding deities (*adhiṣṭhātrī*) over them.

Furthermore, it should be understood that there is also a twofold nature: by way of being form (*rūpa*) for material things, and by way of being their obscuration; this is the general direction [of the argument].

// 10.39 // Śrī Śuka said: // 117 // [118] Thus, that very power of His own nature (svarūpa-śakti) which possesses infinite functions is here none other than Lakṣmī herself, existing in embodied form within a portion of the abode of the Blessed Lord; so he says:
"The divine Śrī is inseparable from Hari himself, being his very own self (ātman).
And the commentary states: "She is the non-departing power (śakti) of Hari; the reason for this is that she is his very own self, his essential nature."

The meaning is that because its nature is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), there is no difference between them. By this, it is implied that *māyā*— referred to in passages such as BhP 2.5.13, "by whom, being ashamed, it was not able to stand in the path of his vision"— is not [the same as] this [consciousness].
In that regard, non-decay is as follows; in the *Śrī-Hayaśīrṣa-pañcarātra*:
"The Supreme Self is the Lord Hari."
Its power is here declared to be Śrī;
the goddess Śrī is called Prakṛti, and Keśava is remembered as Puruṣa.
"Without Viṣṇu there is no Goddess,
and without Hari there is no lotus-born one. Thus it is stated in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
That Śrī, the mother of the world, is eternal and inseparable from Viṣṇu,
just as Viṣṇu is omnipresent.
"O best of the twice-born, it is exactly so. Thus [it is said]. Elsewhere:
"In this way, just as the Lord of the World..."
"Janārdana, the god of gods, takes an incarnation, and Śrī likewise acts as his companion. [ViP 1.9.142] Thus it is said.
The nature of consciousness is also described in the Skanda Purāṇa: "But that which is the other, the imperishable, is Prakṛti, whose form is insentient."
Śrī is declared to be the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti), the consciousness that rests upon Viṣṇu.
They call that the supreme imperishable, the imperishable beyond the beyond;
Hari alone is the possessor of all qualities.
"Thus the three syllables have been declared.
For this very reason, in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa itself, it says: "The divisions of time such as *kalā*, *kāṣṭhā*, *nimeṣa*, and so forth..."
May that Hari, whose power is not subdued even within the range of Kālasūtra, be gracious toward me.
May that Viṣṇu, who is called the Supreme Lord even though he is pure, be gracious toward us through his metaphorical designation.
"The Self which belongs to all embodied beings"—
thus it is explained here by the commentators themselves:
"Time itself, consisting of *kalās*, *kāṣṭhās*, *nimeṣas*, and so forth, is like a thread."

The Sūtra is the director of the activities of the world; he whose power or fortune does not operate within its sphere or domain—because it is non-different from his own nature, that [power] is eternal and does not depend on time; this is the meaning.
Therefore, because there is no difference in its essential nature, it is described as "pure."

Now, one might object: "If Lakṣmī is non-different from His essential nature, how then is He called the 'Lord of Lakṣmī'? To this he replies with the words "it is said": She is both *parā* (the Supreme) and *mā* (Lakṣmī); He who is her Lord is, though pure and absolute, spoken of [as such] by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), under the influence of a conceptualized distinction.
The second word "yat" (which) refers to what is well-known;
having intended this very thing, the venerable Brahmā requested [the Lord] in the third verse:
"O bestower of boons upon those who have surrendered, may You delight [us] with Your own power."
"Whatever he shall do, having assumed these qualities, let my mind apply itself even as he manifests this prowess of his own, so that I may abandon both worldly action and impurity. (BhP 3.9.23)
Therefore, as for that which was said:
"Seeing that great marvel, Śrī herself was sent by the gods."
Because she had never before seen or heard of such a thing, she did not approach him, being filled with doubt.
Thus it is said regarding the manifestation of Śrī Nṛsiṃha in [BhP 7.9.2].
Śrī Sūta [said]: "In this way, He whose singular form is existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda), who is endowed with His own inherent, inconceivable, diverse, and infinite potencies... [119]

The state of being a property (*dharmatva*) is itself the state of being a substratum (*dharmitva*); non-differentiation is itself manifoldness with differentiation; formlessness is itself having form; pervasiveness is itself the state of being the middle;
and reality is itself [the ultimate], and so forth—such is their mutual [identity].

He is the treasury of infinite, contradictory qualities; His own form is the Śrī-vigraha, which is gross yet subtle, distinct, self-luminous, indivisible, and His very essential nature; and He is the primary and sole possessor of the name "Bhagavān" in its true sense.

Manifesting such infinite forms through His own body, He is captivated by the Goddess Lakṣmī, whose beauty is characterized by the manifestation of powers corresponding to His own nature; shining with a form that encompasses the specific manifestations of His own splendor within His own abodes, He is the playful display of the power of His essential nature.

The Blessed One is He whose nature is wondrously marvelous through His characteristics, extraordinary qualities, and divine pastimes; who delights in Himself through such attributes as being the Self; whose essential reality is Brahman, manifesting in a form common to all living beings; whose marginal power (*taṭastha-śakti*) is known as the individual soul (*jīva*), which finds its sole life in Him as its own support; and whose quality of self-manifesting power is revealed through the infinite phenomenal world. Thus says the learned.
It is manifested by words whose referents have been apprehended.

In this regard, it is not reasonable for the ignorant—who do not perceive another entity possessing that intrinsic nature—to harbor disbelief; therefore, [the author] speaks in order to inspire faith in those who desire to know.
In that regard, they say that while it is established by one [means of knowledge], its being an object of knowledge for the ignorant is not so; rather, it is to be known solely through the Veda.

Who indeed here knows, alas, that foremost abode of those born later, from which the Seer emerged, followed by both classes of gods? At that time, neither being nor non-being existed, nor did the force of time.
When one lies down there, one should not draw any scripture over oneself.
Alas! O Blessed One, who in this world—being of later birth and subject to recent origin and destruction—could know or understand You, the foremost and eternally perfected Being?
Stating that the Lord is eternally established while another is posterior in time, they declare the absence of any cause for [the latter's] knowledge;
for it is from you alone that the seer Brahmā has arisen.
All those who are more recent than this [period] are likewise included.
However, when you— having withdrawn the Veda that makes yourself known through scripture, and having drawn it back into Vaikuṇṭha—
lie down and close your eyes toward the affairs of the world, at that time, for the souls remaining behind...
There is no means for such knowledge;

because at that time, the body is neither existent— such as the gross ether and so forth— nor non-existent— such as the subtle mahat and so forth— nor is it composed of both the existent and the non-existent.
And there is no velocity of time;

since that [velocity] would have to be caused by an irregularity in time, and such being the case, at that place and at that time, not even the sense-faculties, the vital breaths, or anything else exist.
This is the meaning:
because it pertains to the state of emanation, and because there is a sense of internality created by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the body and so forth.
Due to the influence of time and karma, because their minds are defiled, they lack the capacity for such focused attention;
yet even at the time of dissolution (pralaya), when there is not even a slight interval [between them], they likewise [lack it].
"Because of the absence of the means [of knowledge] due to the deep sleep consisting of the great darkness of ignorance regarding the Vedas, you do not possess the capacity for direct experience.
Thus say the Śrutis:

"You do not know him who generated these [beings], for something else has come between you. From whom words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained him—who truly knows? Who here has declared it? [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1]
From where has this emanation come? From where did it proceed?
The gods are later than its emission; who then knows from whence it first came into being?
It is one, unmoving, yet swifter than the mind.
The gods did not attain this before;
it moved forward, surpassing others as they ran, while it stood still.
In it, Mātariśvan places the waters.

"There is no eye, no ear, no reasoning, and no memory; indeed, the Veda alone makes Him known"—such are the scriptural texts (*śrutayaḥ*) concerning the Blessed Lord. Now, with three verses, he describes how the wise, preceded by that [knowledge], experience Him directly through devotion alone: [10.87–10.89] "O Great-armed One, You are not perceived by the eye, nor by speech, nor by the other senses, nor even by the mind. By what means, then, can You be seen? Tell me, O Lord of the World. "O Supreme Person, neither by austerity, nor by action, nor by gifts, nor by rituals, nor by study, nor by renunciation, are You seen as You truly are. But by single-minded devotion, O Source of the World, You may be known and seen in Your true nature. "By those whose sins have been destroyed by the fire of knowledge, who are purified by the penance of devotion, and who have become one with Brahman, You are seen within themselves, O Puruṣottama. [119] These are the scriptural texts regarding the Blessed Lord. [120] Now, with three verses, he states that the wise, preceded by that [knowledge], experience Him directly through devotion alone: [10.90] "The wise perceive You, O Great-Souled One, as the Self abiding in their own hearts, by means of the eye of wisdom sharpened by meditation and disciplined through yoga. [10.91] "But those whose minds are unsteady, who lack self-control, and whose intellects are distracted by various objects, do not perceive You, O Lord of Yoga, even though they strive with devotion. [10.92] "Therefore, O Supreme Person, grant us that devotion by which we may know You, see You, and enter into You, O Unfading One, O Source of the World. [120] Thus ends the tenth chapter. The eleventh chapter follows. The Blessed Lord said: "Listen, O mighty-armed one, to this most secret teaching, which is the king of sciences and the king of secrets, the supreme purifier, understood by the realized ones, and practiced by those who follow the path of yoga. [11.1] "This is the sovereign secret, the supreme purifier, the realization of all the Vedas, the holy discourse on the Adhyātma (the Self), the ultimate goal of knowledge, and the supreme means of purification. [11.2] "It is the eternal religion, easily performed, imperishable, and directly experienced by the wise. Those who disregard this law, O Parantapa, do not attain Me, but fall into the cycle of birth and death. [11.3] "I am the source of all beings; from Me everything proceeds. Thinking thus, the wise worship Me with single-minded devotion, permeated by the knowledge of the Adhyātma. [11.4] "Constantly glorifying Me, striving with firm resolve, and bowing down to Me, they worship Me with devotion, ever-disciplined and firm in their vows. [11.5] "Others, too, perform sacrifices to Me alone, offering them according to the ordinances of the Vedas. I am the recipient of the sacrifice, and I am the lord of the sacrifice; indeed, I am the sacrificial offering itself. [11.6] "Others, offering the sacrifice of wealth, sacrifice with the sacrifice of austerity, and others with the sacrifice of yoga; and there are those who offer the sacrifice of knowledge, all of whom worship Me with the sacrifice. [11.7] "I am the *ṛc*, I am the *yajus*, I am the *sāman*, and I am the *hotṛ*, the *adhvaryu*, the *udgātṛ*, and the *brahmā* priest. I alone am the sacrifice, the oblation, the fire, and the act of offering; I am the father, mother, sustainer, and grandfather of this world. [11.8] "I am the object of knowledge, the purifier, the syllable *Om*, the *Ṛk*, the *Sāman*, and the *Yajuṣ*. I am the goal, the sustainer, the Lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, and the friend. [11.9] "I am the origin and the dissolution, the support, the resting place, the seed, and the imperishable seed. I give heat, I withhold and send forth the rain; I am immortality and also death, as well as being and non-being, O Arjuna. [11.10] "Those who know the three *Vedas* and drink the Soma, purified of sin, worship Me with sacrifices and seek to reach heaven. Having attained the meritorious world of the gods, they enjoy divine pleasures in the celestial realm. [11.11] "When they have enjoyed the vast pleasures of that heavenly world and their merit is exhausted, they enter the mortal world again. Thus, following the injunctions of the three *Vedas*, they obtain the state of coming and going. [11.12] "But those who, worshipping Me with exclusive devotion, meditate on Me and strive for Me, for them I secure safety from the ocean of saṃsāra. [11.13] "Even those who are devoted to other deities and worship them with faith, they too worship Me alone, O Son of Kuntī, though contrary to the prescribed rules. [11.14] "For I am the enjoyer and the lord of all sacrifices. However, they do not recognize Me in truth, and therefore they fall. [11.15] "Those who worship the ancestors go to the ancestors; those who worship the spirits go to the spirits; and those who worship Me come to Me. [11.16] "If one offers a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water with devotion to Me, I accept that offering made with love by the pure-hearted. [11.17] "Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give away, and whatever austerity you practice—do that as an offering unto Me. [11.18] "Thus, with your mind fixed on Me, you shall overcome all attachments born of karma by My grace. And when you have attained perfection, you will come to Me. [11.19] "I am the same to all beings; I have no enemy and no friend. But those who worship Me with devotion abide in Me, and I too abide in them. [11.20] "Even if a person of extremely evil conduct worships Me with undivided devotion, such a person should be regarded as righteous, for he has rightly resolved. [11.21] "Swiftly he becomes virtuous and attains eternal peace. Know for certain, O Kaunteya, that My devotee never perishes. [11.22] "For, O Parantapa, even those who are of low birth—women, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—even they attain the supreme goal by taking refuge in Me. [11.23] "How much more so the holy Brahmins and the devoted royal sages! Having attained this transient, joyless world, worship Me. [11.24] "Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and prostrate yourself before Me. So shall you come to Me alone; I promise you this truly, for you are dear to Me. [11.25] "Abandoning all duties, take refuge in Me alone. I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve. [11.26] "If you say, 'I cannot abandon all my duties,' then, O Parantapa, focus your mind on Me, practice yoga, and be devoted to Me. [11.27] "Even if you do not excel in yoga, yet performing actions for My sake, you shall attain perfection. [11.28] "If you are unable even to perform actions for My sake, then, controlling your mind and restraining your senses, engage in the yoga of renunciation. [11.29] "If you are unable to practice even this yoga of renunciation, then, surrendering the fruits of all actions to Me with self-control, practice yoga with the mind fixed on the Supreme. [11.30] "Better is wisdom than the practice of yoga; better than wisdom is the renunciation of the fruits of action. From the renunciation of fruits comes peace. [11.31] "If you are unable to fix your mind steadily on the Supreme, then perform actions for My sake with the mind disciplined by yoga, free from attachment. [11.32] "Knowledge is superior to action; meditation is superior to knowledge; and the renunciation of the fruits of meditation is superior to meditation; from that renunciation, peace follows immediately. [11.33] "He who hates not, desires not, is free from the pairs of oppos
An ignorant person does not see you, the Supreme Self,
nor do they realize you even today through the methods of meditative absorption;
how then could others perceive his mind, body, or intellect?
"Created by the emission [of the Lord], we are unmanifest.

As for others who are later in time, how could they see You or understand You? The reason for their being later in time is that they possess the mind, the body, and the intellect—these being the effects of *sattva*, *tamas*, and *rajas*—and it is through these that [the later ones perceive].
The various creations of gods, animals, and humans have been produced;
even therein we are unmanifest, so how could we see? This is the meaning. [121]
To this he replies: "Then what do others see there?
Those who possess bodies perceive the qualities (guṇas) dominated by the three gunas, or indeed darkness (tamas)."
Those whose minds are deluded by my māyā do not perceive you as established within themselves, for they lack outward illumination;
those who identify with the body do not know you, even though you are perfectly situated within them.

However, they perceive only the qualities (guṇas), and at times they see only darkness (tamas) alone, because for them, the intellect (buddhi) consisting of the three qualities is indeed the primary principle (pradhāna).
Due to their dependence on the intellect (*buddhi*), they perceive objects during the waking and dreaming states;
however, in deep sleep, they perceive only darkness, and not You, who are the self-nature of all those who are free from qualities and delight in the Self, and who have become the very Self.
The reason for this is everywhere:
since their minds are deluded by your māyā— or by the māyā of that [other]— nevertheless, you will come to know through investigation.
He says this because you are not within the range of knowledge for those like us, but only for devotees:
"I [know] you, who are a mass of knowledge, as my own nature..."

How can I, a deluded person, contemplate that which is realized in the hearts of Sanandana and others, whose delusions regarding the distinctions of the qualities of *māyā* have been utterly destroyed? [BhP 9.8.23]

How can I fully comprehend You, the treasury of supreme power whose nature consists of manifold wonders? What is Your true form? You are a mass of consciousness, an embodiment of the singular essence of truth, knowledge, and infinite bliss;
therefore, as stated in the *Sahasranāmastotra*, "Your body is indefinable."
This is the meaning:

because you are a mass of pure consciousness (*jñāna-ghana*), you are not an object of knowledge; furthermore, even though you are the subject of investigation, I am one who is overwhelmed by the qualities of *māyā*.
"Capable in investigation. [The opponent asks:
"In that case, what is the proof for my being such as you describe? To this, he replies:
"By your own [cognition]."

The meaning is that it is to be contemplated, investigated, and directly experienced by sages such as Sanandana and others who know the reality of the Blessed One, and by whom Māyā— consisting of the delusions produced by the various modes (guṇas)— has been utterly destroyed through their being, devotion, their own self-nature, or even through its manifestation.
Therefore, just as the sun— though its quality of luminosity is not admitted by owls— nevertheless possesses that very quality as it is perceived by others, so too,
although Your possession of those qualities is inconceivable to those of limited vision, it is nonetheless directly perceived by the wise who are Your devotees.
The meaning is that it is indeed established.
And thus says the Śruti:
"The Self-existent pierced the openings outward."
Therefore, one looks outward and not at the inner self; but some wise man, desiring immortality, beheld the inward self with his vision turned back. (Katha Upaniṣad 2.1.1)
Devotion alone leads him; devotion alone reveals him to him;
a person is under the sway of devotion.
Devotion alone is more abundant.
[Māṭhara-śruti]:
"He alone whom this [Self] chooses is able to attain Him;
to him this Self reveals His own form. [Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.23]
Aṃśumān [worshipped] Śrī Kapiladeva. // 120–121 //
In the Vivṛti, both Brahman and Bhagavān [are explained].

Thus concludes the *Śrī Bhāgavata-sandarbha*, which contains the essence of the teachings of Śrī Rūpa and Sanātana— who were disciples of the feet of the divine Lord Kṛṣṇa Caitanya, the incarnation whose purpose was to purify the Kali-yuga by distributing his own worship— and who were the recipients of honor from the assembly of all the kings of Vaiṣṇavas.
